title: Looking to Wisconsin
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: Francesca Hong at a Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary debate. Nam Y. Huh/AP Today’s notice: Learning lessons from Michigan to use in Wisconsin. New polls in Maine and Iowa. Comer plans to wrap up Epstein investigations while Democrats plot more. And: Inside the weird politics of data centers. THE LATEST Democrats get ready to do it again. Another progressive candidate, this time in Wisconsin, is running circles around the party establishment and scaring leaders about a key race in a key state. DSA member and state lawmaker Francesca Hong seems set to walk away with the nomination in next week’s gubernatorial primary. But now, for some odd, out-of-the-blue, strange reason, there are some questions about the polls. “It’ll probably be closer than people think based on the results in Michigan,” a Democratic strategist told NOTUS’ Christa Dutton . Campaign officials for Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley , the candidate the establishment wants to win the primary, popped a memo yesterday saying they, too, think the polls are wrong. Once again, the Democratic establishment has assembled to back one of several candidates running in a primary: Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers has been campaigning hard with Crowley, whom he urged to get back in after he dropped out earlier in the cycle. Is that really the lesson Michigan taught? NOTUS’ Manuela Silva spoke to Democratic senators about what they took away from Michigan’s Senate primary when it comes to deciding whom to endorse. Sometimes it’s easy, said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who offered the example of a candidate like Roy Cooper in North Carolina. “There are other places where the fight is pretty even, and in those situations, I would prefer that leadership just let it play out,” Murphy told Manuela. Some places are getting a little messy. Take Montana, for example, as NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández explores, where the establishment is backing an independent over the Democratic nominee. Some senators noted that the tools the establishment throws at races — i.e. the millions spent attacking Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in her Senate bid — are clearly not working anymore. “Voters are just tuning that bullshit out,” retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minnesota) said of the cash flowing against Flanagan. What about any lessons for the left next week? One of that side of the party’s kingmakers seemed to suggest people should not pay too much attention to Wisconsin. “To be honest with you, I met Francesca a couple of years ago,” Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) told reporters. “I haven’t talked to her since. It’s not the race that we’re involved in.” “We’re very much involved in Peggy Flanagan’s race in Minnesota,” he . “I hope that Peggy Flanagan wins.” Open tabs: Max Miller resists pressure to drop reelection bid (AP); Darline Graham Takes Over Lindsey Graham’s Leadership PAC (NOTUS); After Michigan Loss, AIPAC Weighs a Second Effort to Defeat El-Sayed (NYT); Inside the GOP hemp wars (Axios) From the campaign trail First on NOTUS: Two new PAC-funded battleground polls. Polling as a, well, concept took a hit in Michigan on Tuesday night, but that doesn’t mean political strategists aren’t still spending a ton of money on surveys to inform their spending plans and other campaign maneuvers. In that spirit, we offer an exclusive look at two polls from groups with pockets deep enough to buy the expensive ones. Maine: Democrats weathered the primary storm? New numbers from Senate Majority PAC (the spending arm of Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer ) shows freshly minted Democratic nominee Troy Jackson with a slight lead over Sen. Susan Collins , the longtime Republican incumbent. NOTUS’ Christa Dutton got the SMP memo , which found Jackson up 49% to 45% over Collins, with 6% undecided. The memo also details why Collins may be more vulnerable this year than the last time she ran, in . Iowa: Democrats see momentum in the 2nd Congressional District. House Majority PAC (the spending arm of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries ) is trying to win the seat being vacated by Rep. Ashley Hinson after she became the Republican nominee for Senate. Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris in the district by 10 percentage points . A new HMP poll found Democratic nominee Lindsay James with 46% to Republican Joe Mitchell ’s 45%. The survey gave credence to the idea that Trump is a drag on Republican candidates even in Republican places — Trump’s favorability rating is underwater in the poll, 44% fave/53% unfave. From the Hill The state of House Oversight’s Epstein investigation will be largely determined by the voters in November, NOTUS’ Stephen Neukam reports . The committee’s chair, Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky), says it’s time to wrap things up, produce a report and ask the DOJ to consider criminal prosecutions. Democrats on the committee, led by Rep. Robert Garcia of California, say there’s much more to do and want to keep the investigation going if they get the majority. “There’s no question that the investigation will continue into the next couple of years,” Garcia told NOTUS. From the White House Trump in Las Vegas: “The polls say we do better against the communists. So he won, and so I think I’m happy.” Trump also in Las Vegas: "When I watch Abdul, he’s full of shit." More from NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause . NOTUS PERSPECTIVES After Abdul El-Sayed’s primary win, Republicans’ rhetoric got real ugly, real fast. Leading the charge was Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who yesterday held a hearing titled “Hidden in Plain Sight: Confronting the Muslim Brotherhood Network in America.” None of Cruz’s colleagues showed up — but Dana Milbank was there . NOTUS METRO Local news: Talk to Tom: Restaurant Recs for D.C., Maryland ... and Germany! By Tom Sietsema Sports desk: Commanders to Sign Stefon Diggs, Shoring Up a Shaky Receivers Room , by Martenzie Johnson NEW ON NOTUS Data center politics continue being just so weird. The ongoing division among Democrats over data center construction — moratorium-ers vs. regulation-ers, basically — is getting more complicated, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports . Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) today will propose a new excise tax and the elimination of tax breaks for data center construction. His plan is not to stop the construction of new centers but rather to ensure there’s some public benefit from them, if only just in tax revenue. That’s part of a growing list of policy ideas Democrats are kicking around to address the electorate’s AI skepticism. Things are weird in MAGA politics, too. In a deep dive, NOTUS’ Mara Hoplamazian reports that the first year of Trump’s effort to accelerate data center infrastructure by clearing away regulatory and permitting hurdles — a promise kept to the tech titans who supported his candidacy — has not actually boosted data center construction. But it has helped spread the data center backlash to red places, often over the same issues his administration is trying to ease oversight around: water quality, air quality and the speed at which centers are built. More: Republicans Roll the Dice on Their Farm Bill , by Tyler Spence Congress’ Watchdog Is Still Struggling to Get Answers on DOGE , by Natalie Alms Max Miller’s Corporate Backers Go Silent on Embattled Congressman , by Dave Levinthal NOT US Mullin’s immigration balancing act grows more precarious , by Myah Ward and Eric Bazail-Eimil for Politico C.I.A. Sets Up Secret Cuba Task Force as Trump Pressures Havana , by Adam Entous for The New York Times Our Fauci Diaries, Ourselves , by Molly Fischer for The New Yorker Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com . And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr, Brett Bachman and Andrew Burton. Photo by Nam Y. Huh/AP.

title: Wisconsin Democrats Doubt a Progressive’s Prospects After Michigan Results
author: Christa Dutton
summary: Two gubernatorial candidates’ camps are drawing opposite conclusions after Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow victory on Tuesday
content: Stakes for Wisconsin Democrats are high in the state, which Trump won by less than a percentage point in . Nam Y. Huh/AP Photo In Wisconsin, a progressive gubernatorial candidate is polling far ahead of the other candidates before the battleground state’s Democratic primary next week. That was the story in Michigan, too: Polls showed Abdul El-Sayed handily beating Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of Tuesday’s Senate primary — but he had barely edged out a victory by the time the race was called the next morning. Now, some Democrats wonder if the same will come to pass in Wisconsin, where polling has shown state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist , leading her opponents by double-digit margins for weeks. Among the most doubtful is Hong’s leading opponent, David Crowley, who previously suspended his race in July because he wasn’t gaining traction before reentering 10 days later. Tuesday’s disconnect between polls and election day realities in Michigan brings Milwaukee County’s executive to one of the most optimistic points of his campaign so far. His team sent out an internal memo on Wednesday telling supporters his race is similarly closer than polls indicate. “Results in Michigan Tuesday night showed polling that failed to appropriately capture and reflect the primary electorate and well overstated the position of the race frontrunner,” the memo, first reported by WISN , says. “Democrats are in the driver’s seat in Wisconsin to choose David Crowley and have the best fighting chance against Tom Tiffany in November.” If next week’s voter base resembles those of and , the primary “does not have a prohibitive front runner,” the memo continues. While El-Sayed’s win shows how a socialist candidate like Hong can similarly ascend, Michigan’s uneven polling shows how challenging it is to pull off accurate primary surveys, said Barry Burden, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Madison — especially in Wisconsin and Michigan, where voters of any party can opt to participate. “There are questions about where Hong stands,” Burden said. “There’s an opportunity for Crowley, and the Michigan results might be an indicator for him that it’s still a possibility.” Wisconsin and Michigan are two of the country’s most consequential battleground states. Crowley’s camp argues Stevens’ better-than-expected performance proves more moderate candidates can still make good showings despite a recent progressive surge within the party. “We don’t have to talk in theoreticals anymore about how this might work,” said a Democratic strategist who backs Crowley, given anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “Yeah, Haley didn't win, but she lost by one point. But this isn't us just trying to explain what our theory of the case is. … There is more money coming through the door today. There is more enthusiasm.” Hong’s campaign, meanwhile, considers El-Sayed’s victory a harbinger of success in Wisconsin for the party’s left-most flank, which saw several candidates win Democratic primaries in New York City and Denver ’s heavily blue districts. Michigan showed that working-class people are “ready for something different,” Hong said in a statement to NOTUS, adding that her campaign has “never taken the size of any projected margin for granted.” “Polls are snapshots, and Michigan was another reminder that campaigns are won by organizing and turning out voters,” Hong said. Stakes for Wisconsin Democrats are high in the state, which Trump won by less than a percentage point in . The governor’s mansion, currently occupied by Democrat Tony Evers, has alternated between Republican and Democratic administrations since the 1970s. And the left’s gubernatorial candidate pool has and flowed significantly this summer — even prompting a lawsuit from the state party over the ability to recast ballots that was eventually dismissed. Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her campaign finance filings. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes ended his campaign last week shortly before the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety. Crowley himself had dropped out of the race briefly before reentering with Evers’ endorsement. Whoever advances from the Aug. 11 primary will a tough race against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. State Navigate, a polling firm that mostly focuses on state legislative races, concentrated on including more rural, low-income and Republican voters after seeing Michigan surveys miss those groups, executive director Chaz Nuttycombe said of a new survey coming out this week. A poll the organization conducted in late July showed Hong up by 29 points. “It’ll probably be closer than people think based on the results in Michigan last night,” said another Democratic strategist in Wisconsin, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “I think people thought that it was going to be a little more lopsided than it ended up being, and that’s probably what’s going to happen here in Wisconsin.”

title: Are Montana Democrats Abandoning Their Own Candidate?
author: Raymond Fernández
summary: Democratic leaders are backing an independent Senate candidate in Montana. The Democrat is livid.
content: Robert Yoon/AP Democrats are facing an unusual obstacle in their push to create as many paths to a Senate majority as possible this fall: a Democratic nominee who refuses to quit. Democrat Alani Bankhead is set to Republican Kurt Alme in Montana’s Senate election — the kind of race that would be a reach for Democrats in a normal year but could be on the table in a favorable political environment this year. The problem is Democrats are rallying behind independent candidate Seth Bodnar, who they think actually makes that long shot a possibility. But with both candidates running, beating Alme is nearly impossible. “[Republicans] know that if it’s head-to-head between Bodnar and Alme, Bodnar wins the damn race,” former Montana Sen. Jon Tester, who has endorsed Bodnar, told NOTUS. Bankhead is livid with national party leadership, who she thinks is leaving her out to dry. In an interview with NOTUS, she accused Democratic leaders, nationally and in the state, of “using all their power and money to try to make Montanans accept the person that they pick.” Bankhead alleges Tester has collaborated with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to circumvent the democratic process by backing a preferred candidate, an allegation Tester denies. On top of that, it’s not even clear what would happen if Bankhead were to withdraw before next week’s Aug. 10 deadline. There’s a legal dispute, which lawyers briefed the state Democratic Party on, over whether the party would have to name a replacement for the party line should Bankhead quit. Bankhead has said repeatedly she is not considering exiting the race, “short of God” telling her to drop out. “Montana law says no matter what — [even] if I die — the state party still has to replace me on the ballot,” Bankhead told NOTUS. “No, I’m not dropping out.” In June, shortly after the Democratic primary, 17 state legislators wrote a letter to Bankhead and Bodnar, urging one of them to drop out. “Every week that passes makes it more difficult to unify supporters, consolidate resources, and mount the strongest possible campaign for November,” the legislators wrote. The lawmakers stopped short of supporting either candidate’s campaign. “Based on the information currently available to us, Seth appears to have an advantage,” they wrote. “At the same time, we recognize that [Bankhead] has only recently secured the Democratic nomination.” The state had at least one Democratic senator for a until . But it’s not currently at the top of national Democrats’ priority list as they try to take the Senate majority in November. “I’m just not tuned in on Montana,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS. “I’ve been doing Michigan and Minnesota and Georgia and North Carolina.” Several of her colleagues involved in other Senate races echoed that sentiment, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont). But Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate majority, and some seats currently held by Democrats — including in Michigan — are in reach for Republicans, putting pressure on the party to devise multiple paths to victory. Bankhead, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and counterintelligence agent who won the state's Democratic primary with over 48, votes in June, faces myriad challenges. Bankhead’s campaign had only raised just under $60, by the end of June compared to the more than $3.2 million Bodnar has raised since launching his campaign . Bankhead accuses the DSCC of “starving” her campaign of money — and she is facing mounting pressure from former Democratic leaders in the state to drop out. A Tavern Research poll conducted in mid-June, showed an Alme-Bodnar tie in a hypothetical head-to-head, while Alme led Bankhead 56-44 in a hypothetical two-way race. Some polls show Bodnar leading Alme if Bankhead were to drop out. There has been a run of Democratic Senate nominees withdrawing to clear the path for a two-way race with an independent candidate. Democratic nominees have dropped their campaigns in Nebraska, South Dakota and Idaho, giving a boost to independent candidates in each Republican-leaning state. Bodnar, the former president of the University of Montana and a West Point-trained former Green Beret, entered the race as an independent in late March. He has secured the endorsement of major Democratic-aligned groups, including Montana Conservation Voters and VoteVets — the largest progressive veterans’ organization in the U.S. The group previously supported Bankhead . Bodnar also has been endorsed by Tester and former Democratic Sen. Max Baucus, among other leaders. Bodnar’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. Bankhead described herself as being up against the entrenched party establishment. “Old guard political leaders want to stay in power and control, and they're trying to use the last bit of power that they have to wield their influence to maintain the status quo,” she told NOTUS. Schumer’s office did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. The DSCC referred NOTUS to the organization’s comments to Semafor , where DSCC executive director Devan Barber said “The DSCC partners with viable campaigns who have a path to victory, which Ms. Bankhead does not.” Montana’s Senate seat is open because Republican Sen. Steve Daines abruptly withdrew in March and endorsed Alme, who had filed to run the same day. Concerns over splitting the Democratic vote have local leaders convinced that keeping Bankhead on the ballot will hand Republicans an easy win in the state. Bodnar, Tester said in the interview, is “the kind of person who’s willing to sit down and listen, and make a decision based on facts, not on conspiracy theories. And for that reason, he’s head and shoulders above the people who he’s running against.” Tester also says Bodnar’s candidacy is viable not because he is an independent, but because “he is somebody that understands politics,” working families, high costs, agriculture and the “shit that this president with support of the Congress have done.” While most Senate Democrats NOTUS spoke to repeatedly said they had not been paying close attention to the Montana race, some said they were relying on Tester to know the best path to contention in the state. “I have a lot of respect for Tester, and so I kind of defer to him in terms of just what can be done,” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey told NOTUS.

title: Trump's Economy Speech Veers Into an Extended Riff on Communism
author: Ben T.N. Mause
summary: The president dedicated several minutes of his Las Vegas speech to denouncing Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin’s Francesca Hong.
content: President Donald Trump speaks at an event at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa in Las Vegas, Wednesday, Aug. 5, . Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo President Donald Trump came to Las Vegas on Wednesday to rally voters on the economy and tax relief. But, after a pivotal week for left-leaning candidates in Michigan and Wisconsin, he couldn’t help but turn to communism. “You lose your home, you lose your apartment, and that’s where the communists will take us,” Trump said. “You got to nip it in the bud.” The president’s broadsides at the Red Rocks Casino came during a nearly 75-minute rally, evoking repeated cheers from the audience. Trump diverged from his economic remarks multiple times, including minutes-long segments calling out this week’s main characters: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who edged out moderate Rep. Haley Stevens by a narrow margin, and Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, who went viral over old posts describing a hatred of Thanksgiving (and Christmas, and Halloween). El-Sayed’s primary win was the latest example of left-wing challengers succeeding against more moderate, establishment-backed Democrats. It’s a shift that has coincided with a deepening party splinter since Trump entered office — and one Republicans hope to take advantage of during the summer campaign season by amplifying distrust of communism to push more centrist voters away from progressive candidates. El-Sayed’s victory makes that effort easier, Trump said Wednesday. “The polls say we do better against the communists,” the president said. “So he won, and so I think I’m happy.” Trump has been attacking communism for some time, but he gained fresh ammunition this week after more of Hong’s past commentary — including wanting to abolish Thanksgiving and voicing disdain for other holidays — circulated ahead of the state’s Aug. 11 primary. A member of the Wisconsin General Assembly and the Democratic Socialists of America, Hong has also been criticized for past calls to abolish the police, among other left-wing positions. But her Turkey Day opinion — which Hong has since walked back, telling Politico on Wednesday that it’s actually her favorite holiday — was a welcome talking point and easy target for Republicans. Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany’s campaign even reposted comments from Hong’s own press team . Trump blasted her on Wednesday as he called communism “the greatest threat to our country,” including both World Wars, Pearl Harbor and 9/11. “And in Wisconsin, the communists have a woman who said that the holiday of Thanksgiving should be immediately abolished, and the police — the police only exist to, quote, ‘uphold white supremacy,’” Trump said, calling Hong a “lunatic.” “We can’t let them get into office.” Republicans have a lower opinion of socialism than Democrats, who are the only partisan group to view the ideology more positively than capitalism, a Gallup poll found. Those dynamics have been present in Michigan and Wisconsin’s primaries this month: Multiple polls show Hong with a dominant lead in the primary race, and surveys conducted prior to the Thanksgiving comments’ resurfacing showed her virtually tied with Tiffany for the general election. And El-Sayed will Republican Mike Rogers, who posted a video calling his opponent a “radical leftist” on Wednesday. “But everyone, every time this has happened ... you go through squalor. And add the word again: filth, crime, death, destruction, embarrassment,” Trump said. “When I watch Abdul — he’s full of shit.”

title: Darline Graham Takes Over Lindsey Graham’s Leadership PAC
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: The newly inaugurated senator is now listed as a “leadership PAC sponsor” for her late brother’s well-funded political committee.
content: In an unusual move, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) is inheriting the leadership PAC of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Sen. Darline Graham just inherited an unconventional asset from her deceased brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham: his federal leadership PAC. Federal records reviewed by NOTUS now list Darline Graham as Fund for America’s Future’s sponsor. Filings from earlier this year listed Lindsey Graham as the PAC’s sponsor. Such a sibling-to-sibling transfer of a senator’s political action committee is decidedly uncommon. “There's little official guidance from the FEC specifically addressing the transfer of a leadership PAC after the death of its sponsoring lawmaker,” Michael Beckel, the director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a nonpartisan political reform organization, told NOTUS. “In practice, most leadership PACs associated with deceased or retired lawmakers are eventually wound down or terminated rather than transferred to another politician.” After Lindsey Graham died last month at the age of 71, the treasurer of the leadership PAC — long-time Republican operative Cabell Hobbs — could have moved to wind down the committee and dispose of any remaining funds by donating to certain political committees and charitable organizations or refunding donors, according to FEC rules. Hobbs declined to comment on the matter when reached by phone Wednesday. Darline Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sponsorship transfer. Although Darline Graham inheriting both her late brother’s Senate seat and leadership fund is unique, it is “not surprising” because “the stars aligned in this case,” Beckel said. South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s term, and she decided to seek a full term after President Donald Trump told her to run. Graham Trump ( , AR: 1.50)During the election cycle, Fund for America’s Future has raised more than $ , through a variety of donations and cash transfers, FEC records indicate. It ended June with about $70, cash on hand after having spent much of what it’s recently raised. It is incredibly common for lawmakers to have leadership PACs; 96% of the 119th Congress — out of members — have leadership committees, per Issue One. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) is the only senator who does not have this type of PAC. The committees allow lawmakers to donate to other campaigns, which builds their political network. “Money in the leadership PAC helps you buy friends and allies, so being able to raise money and dole that out to other politicians is a way for her to be helpful to the team,” Beckel said. But Fund for America’s Future isn’t the only PAC that’s thrown its support behind Darline Graham. The Security is Strength super PAC, which has been affiliated with several committees supporting Lindsey Graham, has pledged millions to bolster his sister’s campaign. The committee announced a $ , digital ad buy for Darline Graham on Wednesday, with TV spots attacking one of her opponents, Rep. Russell Fry (R-South Carolina). Republicans in South Carolina will have the chance to vote for a new nominee in a special election on Aug. 11, because Lindsey Graham had already won the nomination for his party in June. Darline Graham is set to Rep. Ralph Norman, former Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, businessman Mark Lynch and Fry in the special election. Whoever advances will be running against Democratic opponent pediatrician Annie Andrews in the general election in November.

title: Say My Name, Say My Name
author: Marissa Martinez
content: Abdul El-Sayed departs following a news conference at the Spirit of Detroit shortly after winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Wednesday, Aug. 5, , in Detroit. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for August 5, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Michigan finally has its Democratic Senate nominee in Abdul El-Sayed , whose razor-thin race was called this morning after weeks of touting expectations for a blowout victory. His previous opponents, Rep. Haley Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow , have lined up behind him. What do his potential colleagues think? A quick search among Michigan Dems shows only Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet and Sen. Elissa Slotkin ’s personal X accounts have congratulated El-Sayed by name today. Rep. Hillary Scholten ’s personal account issued a congratulatory statement that did not name the Senate nominee. Retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters — who says he’ll back El-Sayed — bashed reporting that showed the candidate up by double digits based on internal polling. He told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic it was a “technique as old politics itself. We saw polls that were questionable right from the start for me.” The NSRC put up its first attack ad today, calling him “Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed — the most radical Senate candidate in America.” “That’s the only play they got,” El-Sayed told voters this morning. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war.” THE HILL The allegations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) prompted different statements from the House’s two women’s caucuses. Democrats called for his resignation, while Republican Women’s Caucus Chair Kat Cammack said she respected the Ethics Committee’s need to follow due process. Cammack, who is working to tackle workplace sexual misconduct on the Hill, called the situation “painful” for everyone involved: “My heart especially breaks for the little girl caught in the middle.” The Senate confirmed CDC director nominee Erica Schwartz , the agency’s first permanent director in nearly a year. THE ADMINISTRATION Donald Trump’s helicopter taking off triggered an air-traffic safety incident at DCA yesterday when Marine One potentially got closer than the acceptable range between aircraft. A California judge held the Homeland Security Department in contempt for allegedly slow-rolling an order to produce data from last year’s controversial Los Angeles immigration raids. Trump sought to shield his business finances from the BBC in a defamation lawsuit in an emergency stay motion today. THE STATES Amir Hassan , the Trump-endorsed candidate in MI-8, trailed Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points after yesterday’s primary — even though Smith had already dropped out of the race. Smith accepted his nomination in a statement today. Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid in MI-13 to state Rep. Donavan McKinney , and conceded the race today. New Mexico’s attorney general is suing Todd Blanche and the DOJ for allegedly blocking access to unredacted Epstein files, as “one of the few jurisdictions that still may have an opportunity to hold Epstein’s associates accountable.” STRANGER THAN FICTION Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

title: Rep. Shri Thanedar Loses Reelection Bid to DSA-Backed Challenger
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: He narrowly lost his primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney.
content: Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid to a progressive challenger after two terms representing Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, the Associated Press projected Wednesday. Thanedar, who admitted to NOTUS this week that he struggled to garner support from his congressional colleagues, was down by 4 percentage points to state Rep. Donavan McKinney with nearly all of the votes counted. Thanedar conceded in a statement Wednesday, adding his name to the slate of incumbent Democrats who lost their primary to candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressive groups. “It was a tough election cycle and, in the end, the voters of the 13th District chose him to represent them moving forward,” Thanedar said of McKinney, a lifelong resident of Detroit. Several members of the Congressional Black Caucus also backed McKinney to represent the 13th District, an area with a large population of Black residents. McKinney campaigned on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending military aid to Israel — a topic that loomed over Democratic primaries in Michigan. McKinney previously told NOTUS he saw constituents’ economic struggles as inseparable from the federal government funding Israel’s attacks on Palestinians and working alongside Tel Aviv on a “war for no reason with Iran [that costs] $1 billion per day.” “People around the country are just tired of status-quo politicians,” McKinney told NOTUS. The DSA endorsed McKinney in July, saying he would “fight for strong union jobs, environmental justice and for universal childcare.” Thanedar, a retired entrepreneur and scientist, largely self-funded his reelection campaign. He had picked up endorsements from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) and Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana). When previously asked by NOTUS if he wished he had more congressional support, Thanedar said, “No, no, I have plenty.” “It’s not like a high school,” Thanedar said. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.”

title: Waiting for Michigan
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: An attendee wears a pin reading "STOP DATA CENTERS" during a primary election night event for Abdul El-Sayed. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Today’s notice: Hope you wanted the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan to go on longer. Max Miller says he has friends in high places. Latest on Todd Blanche’s nomination. Redistricting’s next steps. Private health info leaked with Fauci’s journal. And: Bond market warning signs. THE LATEST The dreaded third option: When the polls closed in Michigan last night, the idea was that Democrats would get clarity on the questions that have plagued them throughout the primary season. A big win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would mean the left could fight off big outside money and wave off pesky worries about electability. A clear win by Rep. Haley Stevens, the establishment pick, would signal that battleground Democrats weren’t ready to take the same ideological risks as safely blue places — and let party leadership breathe a little. El-Sayed remains ahead of Stevens, but the margin is too narrow for there to be a clear winner early this morning. That means the argument about the party’s future goes on. It was a proverbial Groundhog Day for this Democratic primary cycle, and the little guy saw his shadow — forecasting at least six more weeks of Democratic Party angst. Bring on the Wisconsin primary! One thing we definitely learned last night: time to really stop listening to the polls, right? There were a lot of them in this Senate primary and in most cases they were, uh, not accurate . Open tabs: Chuck Edwards Ends His Reelection Following Harassment Allegations (NOTUS); Iran reports positive signs in Hormuz talks with Oman (Al Jazeera); Armed Man Arrested at Trump’s LA Golf Course Ahead of the President’s Visit (NOTUS); Former GOP Sen. Jeff Flake backs Jon Ossoff (AJC); Arizona’s Democratic Governor Set to Pick a Republican Running Mate (NYT) From the Hill Rep. Max Miller says he has allies: The embattled Ohio Republican vowed to stay in his reelection race, called for a House Ethics investigation of his conduct and asserted powerful people still have his back, NOTUS’ Adora Brown writes . “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else, they’re standing behind me,” Miller told CNN. “No one has told me to get off the ballot.” Johnson hasn’t publicly joined calls for Miller to step down and didn’t respond to a request for comment. Todd Blanche drama gets one more act: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said yesterday that she’ll vote against Blanche, Trump’s nominee to be attorney general. That means Blanche must win over at least one of the two remaining Republican holdouts in the Senate to be confirmed, NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports . The senators to watch: Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Bill Cassidy (R-Lousiana). From the redistricting wars Redistricting rekindled: Maryland statehouse Democrats passed a constitutional amendment yesterday that would make it easier to redraw congressional lines ahead of the election, NOTUS’ Manuela Silva reports . And miles away in Missouri, the state’s top elections official blocked a petition challenging a Republican-passed map aimed at eliminating Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver ’s seat. THE BIG ONE Rand Paul’s doxing problem: When the Kentucky senator made public the journal kept by Anthony Fauci last week, Paul also released personal medical information of more than 20 individuals, NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports . What’s included: Names, diagnoses, symptoms and test results of individuals. Two of the people identified by name alongside their medical details were children, Margaret writes. (One of those was the child of Trumpworld players Stephen and Katie Miller, as we first reported .) Some are very public figures like Joe Biden , and others appear to be private individuals whose medical history was posted for the world to see. And those individuals are understandably angry. “If I was a victimizer in the Epstein files, my name would have been redacted,” Leslie Adelman , whose name and medical condition were posted in the document dump, told NOTUS. (Adelman gave permission to use her name in Margaret’s story.) “Instead, I am an innocent and productive member of society, who has donated her time and body to NIH for research that will benefit millions of people — yet MY name and information is blasted to the national news.” NOTUS PERSPECTIVES When Trump called Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz “seriously retarded” last year, it was part of a disturbing pattern. “The use of slurs in general is up,” according to one expert. “But nothing comes near the numbers we’re seeing on the R-word.” Today at NOTUS Perspectives, Sadie Dingfelder explains why this particular insult has become the defining slur of the Trump era. ON NOTUS PODCAST From your favorite podcast app: As the Senate prepares to head home for August recess, some Republicans want to stay behind to pass the SAVE America Act, even if they lack the votes. NOTUS’ Igor Bobic is joined by Avani Kalra and Al Weaver to discuss the inner machinations of the Senate Republican Conference and President Trump’s “dog with a chew toy” focus on the voting act. NEW ON NOTUS Bad signs in the bond market: Last week’s unexpected surge in bond yields — primarily triggered by doubts about the Fed’s commitment to fighting inflation — could hit small- and medium-sized banks hard if the market doesn’t calm, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports . The implications for the U.S. economy, not to mention the midterms, are potentially huge. Volatility in the bond markets helped push Trump to back off of his “Liberation Day” tariff scheme, which corrected the situation quickly. But the spike this time was less sudden and has gotten less attention, Jeff writes, and it may also be harder to resolve. More : Mike Lindell Steps Down From MyPillow to Focus on Minnesota Governor Campaign , by Jenna Monnin FEMA Cut Staff Without Planning for Future Work, Watchdog Says , by Natalie Alms Freedom Sponsors Failed to Disclose Donations — A Potential Lobbying Law Violation , by Taylor Giorno NOT US US diesel prices overtake Biden-era average , by Myles McCormick for the Financial Times At least 12 states cyberattacks on their water systems, sources say , by Luke Barr, Jack Date, Katherine Faulders, Josh Margolin and Aaron Katersky for ABC News Ronald Lauder, a Billionaire G.O.P. title: A House Candidate Who Dropped Out Beats Trump's Pick in Michigan
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: Amir Hassan lost by double-digit percentage points to Thomas J. Smith, who accepted the nomination despite dropping out of the race last month.
content: President Donald Trump listens as Republican congressional candidate Amir Hassan speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground in Michigan. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) A Michigan Republican endorsed by President Donald Trump lost his primary election to a candidate who dropped out of the race but remained on the ballot, the Associated Press projected Wednesday. Amir Hassan, a former federal law enforcement officer from Flint, Michigan, trailed retired engineer Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points. Smith suspended his campaign to represent Michigan’s 8th Congressional District in July. The pair were vying to flip the seat held by Democratic incumbent Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. Trump-endorsed candidates have won about 97% of their primary elections in , according to a July 10 review by Ballotpedia . Hassan is the only Trump-backed House candidate in Michigan who lost his primary. Trump brought Hassan and other candidates onstage during a rally in Michigan on July 27, where the president made reference to Hassan’s family ties to industry giant General Motors. At the rally, Hassan told attendees that they were putting “this country back on the map because we have a leader who stands up for us.” Hassan acknowledged his apparent defeat in the early hours on Wednesday. “The fight has just begun,” Hassan wrote on X . “Service never stops.” Smith accepted the nomination in a statement early Wednesday to The Detroit News . He said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet." “I look forward to working with Speaker Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s America First agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” Smith . The Michigan Secretary of State’s office did not immediately reply to a request for comment on whether Smith can proceed with his nomination despite his decision to officially withdraw from the race. After dropping out, Smith had backed another candidate, Al Lemmo, who came in last with about 16.4% of the vote. McDonald Rivet ran unopposed in her Democratic primary election.

title: Michigan Hands the Democratic Establishment Another Brutal Loss
author: Alex Roarty, Elena Schneider
summary: Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow win is a low point for the center-left as Democrats head toward November.
content: Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Democrats will remember as the year their party’s establishment lost its once total control of the primary process. Instead, it was outmaneuvered and overwhelmed by a progressive insurgency whose chosen candidates, backed by a furious liberal base, smashed their way to victories. It’s a low point for the center-left that Democratic leaders can climb out of, party strategists say, but only with a radical readjustment of how they operate. The result of Michigan’s Senate Democratic primary Tuesday — in which outspoken progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens — was arguably the sharpest blow yet. Stevens lost despite having a huge cash advantage, outspending him 11-to-1 in ads, and running a playbook that had worked for moderate candidates for years, including during Hillary Clinton’s and Joe Biden’s presidential campaigns. El-Sayed winning only narrowly, despite his own campaign’s expectations of a blowout victory, just poses more questions of what if anything the party establishment could’ve done differently to head off the rising left. The choice to support Stevens was emblematic of a larger problem with how party leaders anoint candidates, said some Democratic strategists, and a failure to properly understand just how angry their own party’s voters were with the old way of conducting politics. “They value seniority over talent, a fundraising rolodex over ability to make genuine voter connections, institutional comfort over the anger and change that voters are actually demanding,” said Lis Smith, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked for a candidate in the race who dropped out , Mallory McMorrow. “If you put up establishment slop against DSA candidates who may have bad ideas but are exciting and speak to the anger of American voters, Democratic voters are going to choose DSA and far-left candidates, until we get our act together.” Democratic voters, said another party strategist, were “shouting from the rooftops” about their anger. “If we don’t actually respect and respond to this frustration, we’re gonna wind up with heads in a basket,” said the party operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Democratic Party leaders counter that they have mostly gotten their way in primaries this year and more importantly, could be poised for a big midterm election in November in part because of successful candidate recruitment. Democratic Senate candidates from Texas to North Carolina lead in public polling as President Donald Trump’s approval rating sags to all-time lows. Gas prices are still high, and voters say they’re still feeling the cost-of-living pinch. Those environmental factors have put not just the House in play but also the Senate, an unlikely possibility just two years ago. Both the Democratic National Committee and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quickly rallied around El-Sayed after his win. DSCC chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Democratic Senate leader Sen. Chuck Schumer said in a statement that El-Sayed had “inspired thousands of Michiganders” and that the party is united behind him. But Tuesday’s result in Michigan was only the latest setback for Democrats in Washington this year. In June, Maine Gov. Janet Mills lost her primary race in an embarrassing landslide to political newcomer Graham Platner, despite an endorsement from the DSCC. (Platner later exited the race .) Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado failed to clinch his gubernatorial race, which revolved around his closeness to Washington leadership . The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has lost three races in California, Arizona and Maine, where it spent money on its preferred candidate. The party has also seen progressive candidates win some House races in which the party establishment split its support among multiple candidates. That happened again on Tuesday night in Michigan, where progressive activist Will Lawrence beat two moderates in a swing district. And a handful of incumbent Democratic House members, from Colorado to New York , have lost their reelection races to Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated candidates, a rarity in a party that traditionally has valued its incumbents. “It’s not the end of the center-left, but they need to do a better job of consolidating earlier rather than letting multiple go in the same lane," said Kevin McKeon, a Democratic strategist who works on Senate and House races. Of course, establishment Democrats still have successes to claim this cycle. Of the 13 candidates on the DCCC’s coveted Red to Blue endorsement list, 10 have won their respective primaries. The DSCC recruited former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola into their respective Senate races without any incident, instantly putting the trio of states into play. In Iowa, the establishment-backed candidate, state Rep. Josh Turek, also won a contested primary. That’s something DSCC aides are all too happy to point out. “Senate Democrats created a path to win a majority thanks to all-star candidate recruitment, formidable campaigns, and a winning message,” Tommy Garcia, a DSCC spokesperson, said in a statement. “Democratic candidates are out-polling and out-raising their Republican opponents, and in November we will win the majority — which no one thought was possible a year ago.” Democrats are even more bullish on taking the House majority than the Senate, in part because of investments in many key races. “Everyone agrees that the stakes could not be higher for November,” Viet Shelton, a DCCC spokesperson, said in a statement. ”The DCCC is doing everything possible to ensure Democrats win the biggest majority possible and Congress can actually deliver for the American people again. Every poll is proving we are (still) well positioned to do just that.” Center-left Democrats are quick to point to November as the ultimate scorecard for the wings of the party. “It's worth remembering,” said a Democratic consultant granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly, that progressive won primaries in Omaha, Nebraska, and Syracuse, New York, a pair of battleground House districts. But Democrats “went on to win the majority in without winning either of the Omaha or Syracuse seats.” Some Democratic leaders expressed optimism that the party losing some primaries was ultimately good — that it could help expose leaders in Congress to new ideas and energy. “I actually think this is a healthy debate to have,” said Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who has endorsed candidates running against the party establishment this year and previously served as the chair of both the DCCC and DSCC. “I think we need this kind of churning in the Democratic Party.” Even so, party leaders have problems beyond this year’s primaries. Schumer has calls from some candidates and activists to step aside, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been on the receiving end of frustration from some activists and candidates. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin has been beset by crises since taking over last year, dogged by controversy over the party’s fundraising tactics and a botched autopsy report. And Michigan isn’t the last crucial test the party will this primary cycle. In Wisconsin, a democratic socialist candidate is favored to win the gubernatorial primary next week, in part because other Democratic candidates failed to consolidate support or gain traction. “Since I've been paying attention to politics, the Democratic Party has never been as weak and unpopular as it is now,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a liberal grassroots group. “And I think that’s just an empirical fact.” Levin has been critical of Democratic Party leadership since Trump’s inauguration last year, arguing they haven’t been forceful or creative enough in their opposition to the president. He, like others interviewed for this story, said he thought the base’s frustration with party leadership was more about its failure to defeat Trump in and the perception it has done little to thwart him while in office. Even among Democrats who have represented battleground districts, there’s a concern the party isn’t offering “bigger, bolder policy ideas this year” and the party hasn’t “been inspiring enough,” said former Rep. Susan Wild. “Voters are looking for [an] actual strategy for how we are going to be different, what our plan is,” Wild said, citing “Medicare for All” and subsidized child care as potential policy platforms. “You can’t just talk about an affordability agenda without talking specifics.” During the second Trump administration, Danielle Butterfield, president of Democratic super PAC Priorities USA, voters have identified a “vacuum in Democratic leadership.” “In a world where our party doesn't have any lever of government, our leadership is failing in crazy ways,” Butterfield said. “It has created this circular firing squad of everyone else saying, ‘Maybe someone else will step up.’ And progressive Democrats are the ones who are meeting the moment, and people want that.” Butterfield pointed to the difference she saw in the ads from El-Sayed’s and Stevens’ campaigns. She believed El-Sayed did a better job explaining to voters exactly how he proposed to make their lives better, centered on passing “Medicare for All” and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “As a whole, progressive candidates are meeting that anger more vividly,” she said. “And we're seeing that play out in these primaries.”

title: Missouri Elections Official Blocks Petition Challenging GOP-Friendly Redistricting Map
author: Manuela Silva
summary: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said the petition had the requisite number of signatures but was still “unconstitutional.”
content: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.” David A. Lieb/AP Photo Missouri’s top elections official squashed a challenge to Republicans’ new congressional map that could net them one more U.S. House seat, waiting until the last possible day to block a petition that would have triggered a statewide vote on the gerrymander. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, on Tuesday rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.” “At issue is not the number of signatures turned into the challenge, the new congressional map, but the fact that the referendum itself is null and void by virtue of the fact that it is unconstitutional,” Hoskins said at a Tuesday press conference. “Therefore, House Bill 1, the Missouri First map, continues to be the law of the land.” Hoskins also said that Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway agreed with his choice. At the press conference, Hoskins said he was “confident in the stance” he's taken, and that the government is “prepared to go to court.” That chance will come soon: People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that led the original petition, confirmed in a statement Tuesday evening that it plans to announce details regarding future litigation tomorrow. The Missouri General Assembly pushed through a new map targeting Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s heavily Democratic district, becoming one of the first states that moved to redistrict after President Donald Trump pushed state lawmakers to redraw their congressional maps to more heavily favor Republicans. Signed into law by Kehoe last September, the map carves Missouri’s largest city, Kansas City, into three congressional districts. Shortly after the assembly pushed the new lines through last fall, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered over , signatures to force a referendum. In Missouri, a petition with enough signatures triggers a veto referendum, or a statewide vote on the law in question. The group filed the signatures in December. Hoskins had until 5 p.m. Tuesday to decide on the legality of the petition — the same day as Missouri’s primary elections. Hoskins was widely expected to not certify the signatures, previously saying that any signatures gathered before the campaign was approved by his office constituted “ a misdemeanor election offense ,” a claim his office later clarified and corrected . “Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, wrote in a statement. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year, and we won’t stop now. There are more than enough signatures, verified by election authorities, to qualify the referendum.”

title: Mike Lindell Steps Down From MyPillow to Focus on Minnesota Governor Campaign
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: The CEO is stepping away from his role to focus on his Republican primary after facing a new string of controversies this month.
content: Mike Lindell rose to prominence for supporting President Donald Trump’s attempts to contest the results of the election and has a slate of lawsuits and legal challenges since — including during his current gubernatorial run. Steve Karnowski/AP MyPillow founder and CEO Mike Lindell says he’s stepping away from his post at the company to focus on the Minnesota governor’s race. "After 22 years of leading MyPillow, I know the company is ready for its next chapter and I know Minnesota cannot wait," Lindell wrote in a press release. "This decision is not about walking away. It is about stepping forward to serve.” Lindell rose to prominence for supporting President Donald Trump’s attempts to contest the results of the election and has a slate of lawsuits and legal challenges since — including during his current gubernatorial run. His decision to focus on the upcoming Aug. 11 primary comes as he battles questions about his residency eligibility and a campaign law violation lawsuit. Lindell said the move will allow him to dedicate his “full time, energy, and attention" to the campaign and Minnesotans, while former MyPillow President James Furlong takes over as CEO — a position Lindell has held since he founded the company in . He also reduced his stake in the company to a minority share, but he will remain on MyPillow's board of directors. The Minnesota Republican Party last week asked state officials to clarify the residency rules concerning gubernatorial candidates after reports that Lindell was registered to vote in Texas — the second time in a month the state party has cast doubt upon his candidacy. According to Minnesota’s constitution, gubernatorial candidates must live in the state for at least one year before the election. “The Republican Party does not want Minnesotans who vote for any candidate for Governor to find, after the fact, that their vote was effectively wasted because the candidate did not meet constitutional qualification that could and should have been clarified in advance,” Alex Plechash, the state party chair, wrote in a letter to the Minnesota secretary of state. On Monday, Lindell sent TV station KSTP pay stubs that show he’s paid taxes in Minnesota since at least August . “I don’t know why Alex Plechash, or whatever his last name is, and what he has against me,” Lindell said. “But ever since I got Donald Trump, the president’s endorsement, he has viciously attacked.” The Minnesota secretary of state’s office told the network it does not have the “investigative authority” to review residency claims and deferred to the state Supreme Court. Lindell is currently facing a lawsuit alleging he violated campaign finance rules by distributing promotional pillows at a July 4th parade. He told WCCO the allegations were a “set-up hit job” and he felt “very confident that there was no violations." Lindell's social media accounts have been banned or restricted by several platforms for pushing election fraud claims, including Twitter and YouTube in . He launched multiple social media platforms in response to these restrictions. On Tuesday, Lindell said his Facebook advertising accounts had been restored after calling on Meta to look into his gubernatorial ads apparently being blocked by the platform. Lindell, whom Trump endorsed in July, has also several legal actions related to his false claims that the election had been stolen, including a House committee subpoenaing his phone records in during its Jan. 6 probe. Lindell targeted voting system companies with claims of election fraud, leading to a $1.3 billion lawsuit from Dominion Voting System, now known as Liberty Vote, in . The voting hardware company confidentially settled its defamation suit earlier this month after a former Republican election official purchased the voting company in October. In a separate case last year, a federal appeals court ruled Lindell did not have to pay a $5 million award to a software engineer after he mounted a “Prove Mike Wrong Challenge” over claims China interfered in the election. A recent poll found Lindell leading the Republican field at 35%, followed by Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth at 26% and Kendall Qualls, who earned the state party's endorsement, at 11%. Whichever candidate wins the GOP nomination is likely to Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who has steadily outraised her Republican opponents.

title: Democrats in Congress Don't Like Shri Thanedar. He Hopes Voters Disagree.
author: Christa Dutton
summary: The lawmaker faces a democratic socialist challenger in a blue Detroit-area district.
content: “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress," said Rep. Shri Thanedar. Bill Clark/AP How much does it matter if a lawmaker’s colleagues are indifferent about him in Congress? According to Rep. Shri Thanedar, a wealthy lawmaker who represents Michigan’s 13th Congressional District and who has become one of the left’s targets, not much. The popularity contest that matters is among voters rather than his congressional peers. On Tuesday, voters will choose between Thanedar and Donavan McKinney, a young, Black state lawmaker and democratic socialist who grew up poor in Detroit. The House primary has flashes of the different identity crises Democrats are facing this year: How left is too left? Is being an incumbent a net negative when voters are this angry? How important is racial representation? Then there's the one unique twist: Not even Thanedar's colleagues know what to make of him, which he concedes. “It's not like a high school,” Thanedar, acknowledging apathy from his colleagues about his primary challenge , told NOTUS. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.” Thanedar, who emigrated from India in and worked as a janitor until he became a pharmaceutical executive, is arguing that he should keep his job in Congress because he understands the struggles his district faces. While some of his colleagues have said that they do not care whether he leaves Congress, he has the backing of party leaders, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar. “My constituents know my story,” Thanedar said. “They know my struggles, and I am more like Detroit because Detroit has struggled, but Detroit never gives up.” McKinney, meanwhile, is campaigning on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending American military aid to Israel. He’s backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), numerous state lawmakers, local government officials and progressive groups like Sunrise Movement and Justice Democrats. His campaign is hoping to carry the momentum created by progressive victories across the country, including in several New York City House primaries and Colorado’s 1st Congressional District, to a battleground state. “People think this movement is just in New York or just in California or just in certain states,” McKinney said. “This is across the board, and you can win purple states like Michigan. You can win in Middle America. You can win in toss-up country.” One example of how much he’s leaning into the anti-incumbency sentiment is his reluctance to support Jeffries as speaker of the House if Democrats win the chamber. “I don’t have a decision yet. I just want a conversation,” he said. He that while he’d love to see a Black speaker, he wonders if Jeffries can help Democrats keep the majority next cycle. “How long does he want to be speaker if he actually gets elected speaker?” Other primary races in Michigan are also testing how progressives perform in a purple state. Climate activist Will Lawrence is hoping to defeat two centrist Democrats in a swing district — but if he pulls it off, Democrats are wary of his chances of beating Republican Rep. Tom Barrett. The state’s marquee Senate primary also has establishment Democrats sweating over whether their pick, Rep. Haley Stevens, will beat out progressive Abdul El-Sayed. But this primary is where groups like Justice Democrats, who tapped McKinney as its first recruit of the cycle, are hoping to close the loop. “[This primary] embodies the entire fight that we are having in the broader Democratic Party right now, which is — are we going to be a party that is represented by multimillionaires serving the interests of billionaires, or are we going to let working class communities be represented by working class people?” said Usamah Andrabi, the group’s spokesperson. Many Democrats in the district think Thanedar secured his last two wins because the Black vote was split among multiple candidates, making this head-to-head matchup a serious threat to the incumbent. The race isn’t a clean split between progressives and establishment Democrats. The district has a long history of Black representation, and that has prompted several members of the Congressional Black Caucus, like Reps. Summer Lee (D-Pennsylvania) and Steven Horsford (D-Nevada), to break with Jeffries and other party leaders in endorsing McKinney over their colleague. Several Black state lawmakers in Michigan are also rallying behind McKinney. The Supreme Court’s dismantling key protections of the Voting Rights Act and the elimination of majority-minority districts around the country through redistricting are motivating voters to support him, McKinney said. “Allies are allies, but unless you’ve lived what I've lived, you won't be able to advocate the way I'm able to advocate,” said state Rep. Stephanie Young, chair of the Detroit Caucus in the statehouse and a McKinney supporter. Thanedar said that Black constituents supporting him in the race are doing so because of his track record. “For them, it’s not about the race of the candidate. It's about who can help them, who can bring more federal dollars home,” he said. “Their concern is about who can fight hardest against Trump, and there's nobody fighting harder than me against Trump and the Trump administration.” He also has six members of the CBC backing him, including Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) and Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana). Asked if he wished he had more support from members of Congress, Thanedar said, “No, no, I have plenty.” There’s also the matter of financing. While Thanedar largely self-financed his campaign, he has been criticized by his opponent for being financially supported by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and crypto industry. Thanedar rejected the idea that he is indebted to corporate donors and pointed to progressive super PACs like American Priorities, a pro-Palestine super PAC meant to counter AIPAC, spending on McKinney’s behalf. Thanedar’s campaign had about $5 million in the bank on July 15, according to a pre-primary Federal Election Commission report , and he loaned his campaign $2.1 million . McKinney has raised $1.3 million and had nearly $ , in the bank as of July 15. For McKinney, funding is a key part of his pitch of why he should replace Thanedar in Congress. “This election is about the many versus the money,” he said.

title: Democrats Are Launching a New Way to Coordinate With Outside Groups
author: Alex Roarty
summary: A new agreement between Swing Left and official Democratic infrastructure could be a template for future data-sharing and coordination.
content: Bastiaan Slabbers/Sipa USA via AP The Democratic National Committee and a liberal organizing group have struck a first-of-its-kind deal among Democrats to seamlessly share voter data collected on the campaign trail, bolstering coordination between outside organizations, party committees and individual campaigns. The agreement was reached between Swing Left, the Democratic Data Exchange (the Democratic entity that houses the party's voter data), the DNC and the Association of State Democratic Committees. It is in part an effort to retrofit how the party conducts its field programs up and down the ballot. The goal is to allow Democrats to effectively pool their resources to most effectively and efficiently engage voters. Officials say they hope the agreement becomes a template for deals between other outside groups and the official Democratic Party infrastructure. “The DNC is committed to organizing year-round, ensuring Democrats up and down the ballot have the infrastructure to win in , , and beyond,” Catherine Tarsney Kahle, the DNC’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. “We are proud to partner with Democratic Data Exchange and Swing Left to put critical, ground-level voter data directly into the hands of campaigns nationwide and look forward to continuing that work with others.” Outside groups that ran door-to-door voter outreach efforts were for years legally prohibited from coordinating with candidates and the party infrastructure; they were able to share only a subset of the data they collected from voters, which officials say was of limited use. But a advisory opinion from the Federal Election Commission allowed the two sides to collaborate with their field programs. This deal takes the newly allowed coordination to the next level, allowing all parts of the wider Democratic ecosystem to share the entirety of the data they collect from each individual interaction with voters, and to do so instantly. “That's what this agreement does,” said Yasmin Radjy, executive director of Swing Left. “It allows every volunteer conversation to strengthen campaigns, state parties and organizations across the country. It will help Democrats compete in while ensuring we're not starting from scratch again in .” Swing Left has launched a revamped effort this election cycle to reach independent and Republican-leaning voters, hoping its new field program can help Democrats win congressional majorities in purple districts and states. Some Democratic officials believe the party has fallen behind Republican-backed field programs in recent elections, especially after Donald Trump's campaign successfully identified and persuaded many voters who don’t often turn out to vote. They hope the Democratic Party, boosted by agreements like these, can catch up in this year’s midterm elections.

title: Normies’ Left Turn
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Jenna Monnin
content: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Today’s notice: Why some normie Democrats are backing El-Sayed. Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race gives DSA its biggest test yet. Moreno says his ex-son-in-law congressman is unfit for office. The DNC strikes a first-of-its-kind info-sharing deal. Why some candidates can’t say no to corporate cash. Democratic senators reject DSA’s push to axe the Senate. And: Trump’s plan to supercharge local immigration enforcement. THE LATEST What’s happening in Michigan? The defining Democratic primary of the cycle — the Senate race between Rep. Haley Stevens and former Wayne County health department chief Abdul El-Sayed — is not only about how the left learned how to win, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports . It’s just as much about how badly the mainstream Democratic Party has lost trust. Alex examines the average, normie Democrats — Boomers, relatively affluent, Clinton-supporting types — who are on the El-Sayed train. Many of them voted against El-Sayed in , when he ran for governor as the left’s alternative to Democrat Gretchen Whitmer . He notched only 30% of the primary vote. But polls are showing him comfortably ahead in Tuesday’s Senate primary. Progressive activists say privately that they think these voters’ movement toward candidates like El-Sayed is less about a newfound acceptance of lefty policies like single-payer health care, and more about anger with the Democratic establishment, Alex writes. Many Democrats once skeptical of Stevens now think she might have turned the corner in using attacks against her as slights against the whole state — but the election may hinge on whether normies take a ride with the left’s loftier ideas instead of the establishment’s status quo. The big example, of course, is the debate around Israel. NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed connects the dots, tracing how the debate has become a simple way for many Democrats to find the outsider fighter they’re looking for. “Palestine is a credibility test now,” said Greg Krieg of the American Priorities PAC, which was built to counter AIPAC. “If voters think you won’t be honest about it, they won’t trust you on anything else.” The Michigan primary could be summarized in one sentence: El-Sayed is unabashedly pro-Palestine, Stevens is benefiting from millions in AIPAC spending, and that’s all many primary voters need to know. Open tabs: Gulf States Pressed Trump to Hold Off on Iran Strikes and Pursue Talks (WSJ); For sale: early access to Trump's Truth Social posts (NPR); Republican Sen. Kennedy says he ‘wouldn’t bet my house’ on Blanche being confirmed (The Hill); RFK Jr. targets Fauci and pushes medical misinformation in fiery CNN interview (CNN); Former Texas Congresswoman, Fort Worth's first female mayor, Kay Granger dies (CBS) From the campaign trail Democratic socialists are facing their biggest test yet in Wisconsin’s chaotic primary for governor. It’s easier for Zohran Mamdani ’s wing of the Democratic Party to find its footing in deeper blue states like New York, but Francesca Hong ’s candidacy gives Dems the chance to assess a DSA-aligned candidate in a battleground state. Some voters have a “real fear” that Hong’s connections to the DSA won’t fare well in a state Trump carried in , NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports . “In a super, super purple state, I’m worried she’s not going to catch the people on the fence,” said one attendee at a Hong campaign event in Franklin, Wisconsin. But Hong sees the rise of the DSA brand as a way to bridge gaps in the party’s voting base, saying it’s successful “especially among the voters who are hardest to reach, which are Gen Z and millennials.” The road to reelection is getting rockier for Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) after his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said Miller should seek professional psychological help and “should not serve in the House,” citing allegations of domestic abuse against his daughter and granddaughter, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin and Reese Gorman report . That came after Miller livestreamed a 20-minute denial of the accusations yesterday, vowed to keep running for reelection and posted files, videos and audio recordings to Dropbox. But the numbers already weren’t looking good for Miller. His Democratic opponent in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, Brian Poindexter , is polling at 44% to Miller’s 39% with 16% undecided, according to a recent poll conducted by a Republican firm and reviewed by NOTUS. That’s in a district Trump won by 11 percentage points in . Sharing is caring, or at least that's the message the Democratic National Committee hopes other outside groups take from its first-of-its-kind deal with the liberal organizing group Swing Left to seamlessly share voter data collected on the campaign trail. The DNC is hopeful that the deal can serve as a template for future collaboration after the FEC opened the door to sharing with outside groups. “It will help Democrats compete in while ensuring we're not starting from scratch again in ,” Yasmin Radjy , executive director of Swing Left, told NOTUS’ Alex Roarty . The life of the corporate donation taker. It’s chic in Democratic politics to say no to business-linked political action committees, but NOTUS’ Oriana González and Kadia Goba find it doesn’t protect members from the intense pressure to raise big sums — all the time. “I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” said one Democratic lawmaker caught in the middle. “That's fucked up.” Democrats without major name recognition or national donor networks say taking corporate contributions can save them literally hours of call time per week. That plus eagerness to help battleground races pushes some former corporate-donation rejecters into sighing heavily and taking the money. From the Hill The Senate prefers not to be abolished, thank you. “No,” Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) said flatly when NOTUS asked about the plank in the new Democratic Socialists of America platform calling for the Senate to be eliminated in favor of a unicameral legislature. Our Igor Bobic reports zero takers to the idea among senators who caucus with the Democrats. NOTUS METRO Sign up for our local newsletter , written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman. Local news: Let’s Talk About the Massive Parking Garage Trump Wants to Build at Dulles , by Martin Austermuhle NEW ON NOTUS The Trump administration plans to supercharge immigration enforcement with $1.6 billion in grants to state and local police agencies through September , NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports . The push far exceeds previous federal funding for the (g) program, which allows for coordination between federal and state entities on enforcement efforts. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin recently called the program “the greatest partnership we can have.” More: Trump, Burgum Blast Pirro For Dropping Reflecting Pool Damage Case , by Angie Orellana Hernandez Rep. Marcy Kaptur Hospitalized After Hit-and-Run Crash in Ohio , by Jenna Monnin Trump Sticks by ‘Anti-Weaponization’ Fund Ahead of Blanche Confirmation Vote , by Angie Orellana Hernandez NOT US How a Top Law Firm Went From Standing Up to Trump to Bending the Knee , by Michael S. Schmidt and Jessica Silver-Greenberg for The New York Times The Democrats’ Biggest Donors Have Gone on Strike , by Maggie Severns, Laura J. Nelson and Ken Thomas for The Wall Street Journal MTG Teams Up With Tucker Carlson and Thomas Massie to Plot New Political Party , by Sean James for Mediaite WEEK AHEAD Today Jay Clayton to be sworn in as director of national intelligence. title: Wisconsin Is DSA’s Biggest Test Yet
author: Elena Schneider
summary: Democratic socialist Francesca Hong has risen to the top of a chaotic gubernatorial primary, with major ramifications for Democrats’ future.
content: “The Democratic brand is struggling. The Republican brand is struggling,” Hong told NOTUS. “The Democratic Socialist brand is starting to rise." Kayla Wolf/AP Photo/Kayla Wolf. FRANKLIN, Wis. — The first, second and third questions for Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong at her meet-and-greet Thursday night revolved around her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America. Voters described a “real fear” she can’t win a general election for governor, questioned whether she’d tailor her policy platform to reach swing voters and asked for a primer on “what we can say to others when that concern comes up.” This standing-room-only event captured Hong’s appeal — a packed, generationally diverse crowd, surrounded by dozens of hand-drawn signs for the once little-known state legislator — but it also reflected the angst of voters here. At times, it bordered on group therapy, with voters airing their concerns over Hong’s ability to win the governor’s race in a closely divided state that President Donald Trump won two years ago. “In a super, super purple state, I’m worried she’s not going to catch the people on the fence,” said Faith Casselman, a 32-year-old medical education coordinator who attended the event. This anxiety has defined much of the primary itself, as Hong’s opponents insist the state assemblymember would be unable to beat Rep. Tom Tiffany, the likely GOP nominee. As DSA candidates rack up victories in blue cities and districts, tapping into a deep discontent within the Democratic Party, Hong’s candidacy is the first test of it in a battleground state. The results, say Democrats in Wisconsin and Washington, will offer clues for how the party’s electorate might assess a potential DSA-aligned candidate, like New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, in the presidential primary. “The Democratic brand is struggling.
