The Republican brand is struggling,” Hong told NOTUS in an interview. “The democratic socialist brand is starting to rise, especially among the voters who are hardest to reach, which are Gen Z and millennials.” That isn’t a satisfactory answer, though, for some Wisconsin Democrats. “If you’re trying to explain what DSA is or isn’t, you’re losing,” said a Wisconsin Democratic consultant not working with any of the gubernatorial candidates, who was granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, one of Hong’s opponents in the Aug. 11 primary, is left trying to make the argument that Wisconsin is not like the heavily Democratic places where the DSA has flourished this year. “New York City and the state of Wisconsin” are “different,” he told a dozen voters in the town of Baraboo, many of whom nodded along. But as has been true in other major races this year, from Colorado to Maine to New Jersey, the Democratic establishment has struggled to fend off the rising far left. Wisconsin has turned into the most vivid showdown of those competing wings. Democrats in the state have seen a cast of traditional candidates rise and fall over the past month — all while that wing of the party has failed to coalesce around a single alternative. In early July, Crowley dropped out and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, when it appeared she was uniting moderate support. But Rodriguez dropped out just over a week later, after her campaign acknowledged widespread campaign finance irregularities. Crowley opted to get back into the race with an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers, who had previously said he’d remain neutral; backers of another candidate, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, decried the move as fracturing the center-left bloc again. But then Thursday, Barnes, who’d been polling second-highest behind Hong, dropped out . In a video, he said the “front-runner is clear,” but the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel soon after published a story about concerns within the party that Barnes had allegedly used his political role to facilitate sexual relationships. Crowley, along with state Sen. Kelda Roys and former Evers administration official Joel Brennan, were all polling in single-digits, while Hong hit 38 percent support in a Marquette University survey conducted in late July. About a third of voters were still undecided. “It’s a collapse of the establishment combined with the bumbling of a bad situation,” said Steve Schale, a national Democratic consultant. “The socialist doesn't have to get to 50 percent to win. It requires the normie class — mainstream, establishment, whatever it is — failing to recognize that threat and rally around one person.” In Wisconsin, several voters described the primary campaign as “chaotic” and “unsettling,” or “basically a reality show,” as Caitlin Hapsel, a 38-year-old Greendale resident at Hong’s event in Franklin, put it. Nyaga Kariuki, a 25-year-old Milwaukee voter, said “the moderates just did not get themselves together.” Moderates’ disarray is worrying Eleanor Chiquoine, a 72-year-old voter from Sauk County who was happy to learn at Crowley’s event in Baraboo that Barnes had dropped out — “Oh, that’s good,” she said. She worries that Hong is “unelectable” but she hasn’t been able to settle on another option. “Whether it is fair or not, being labeled, in this state especially, as a democratic socialist, then that might be a harder sell than you think, and that’s my concern,” Chiquoine said. She left with a Crowley yard sign, but she said she planned to keep it in her dining room until she finally picks a candidate. Those are the kinds of voters Crowley needs to win over in less than two weeks, a tall order for a candidate who’s still trying to build his name recognition outside Milwaukee and with early voting already underway. Crowley, in an interview with NOTUS, said he sees a “clear path to consolidate these undecided voters” that’s “based off of my experience” leading Milwaukee County and as a state legislator. He’s now making an all-out sprint to introduce himself to voters, helped by a surge in fundraising since he jumped back into the race. Another Wisconsin Democratic operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly and not affiliated with a gubernatorial candidate, argued that 60 percent of the electorate “doesn’t want to vote for Fran,” giving Hong a “hard floor and low ceiling” of support. “There are enough voters out there, and if Crowley can muster enough resources and reach them, he can really do something here,” the operative said. “But that’s a narrow path.” Republicans, Crowley said, have picked Hong as their preferred candidate, pointing to the $3 million in TV ad spending the Republican Governors Association has dropped boosting her. In a post on X last week , Tiffany previewed his own line of attack on Hong, describing her as “a card-carrying socialist committed to abolishing the police, the Senate, and prisons.” “That should make us pause a little bit, right?” Crowley said at his meet-and-greet in Baraboo. “If they have an opportunity to pick our nominees and say, ‘Oh, this is what communism looked like, or this is what socialism looks like,’ what does that do [to] defining who we are?” Hong, a single mother and restaurant worker, has already started to define herself with voters, particularly younger, more liberal ones. Like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Hong has tapped into a potent organizing network, activating 7, volunteers and campaigning aggressively online. In answer to the voters who wanted to know how she’d combat labels of communism, Hong said her campaign has put out “clarification videos on our positions” and urged voters to zero in on Tiffany’s record. “Bringing it back to policy is how we combat that word that, you know, they called Joe Biden and Tony Evers,” she said. “We don't even have a $10 minimum wage in our state, let alone $19, so what makes you think we're going to make socialism happen?” Eddie Phanichkul, a Democrat who is running to flip a state Assembly district in suburban Milwaukee and attended Hong’s event in Franklin, acknowledged that “the socialism and the communism part is going to be a challenge.” But he said he believed they could “overcome that challenge because we just have to talk to people.” In an interview with NOTUS after speaking to a few dozen voters at a community garden in Milwaukee, Hong said, “Wisconsin is ready for a democratic socialist governor because we're fighting for the things that people are asking for” and “a growing number of voters who feel left behind and unheard.” “Electability is the person who wins the most votes,” she said when pressed on how she’d appeal to voters come November. “I’m a proud democratic socialist. I’m not advancing a brand. I'm focusing on the policies, the socialist policies that improve lives.” But some Wisconsin Democrats, particularly those focused on down-ballot state legislative races, don’t buy that argument. Some privately fret that Hong’s candidacy, and her DSA labeling, could make flipping state legislative seats more difficult and that money from Democratic donors would dry up. In the districts where there are “data center fights, she might turn into a folk hero, and other places, it may be more complicated,” said a third Wisconsin strategist who is not involved in the gubernatorial primary. “People are incandescent about prices, the Iran war and data centers, so the question is, is all of that enough to overcome the kinds of attack ads Tiffany will surely be running the day after the primary.” It’s Hong’s positions on the “defund police” movement that gives those Wisconsin Democrats the most heartburn, they said. “She’s somewhat backed off of that, but the receipts are there, the tweets are there,” the first Democratic consultant said. In , Hong posted several times in support of defunding the police after the police shooting of Jacob Blake, a Black man, in Kenosha, Wisconsin. When a voter at the community garden event asked about her posts, Hong said, “We're in a different political climate than where we were five years ago, where the fearmongering of ‘defund’ is not as much of a priority when we're able to shift to the issues.” Pressed on her position in the interview, Hong said her “values are established.” “How I believe I can make sure that we have laws that reflect those values, that may evolve, but again, I think it's more important about what I'm going to do, and I'm going to be investing in things that we know would prevent crime,” she said. “I won't defund the police, and I cannot.” DSA supporters, who gathered for their national meeting in Chicago over the weekend, are keeping a close eye on Wisconsin. Pennsylvania state Rep. Chris Rabb, a DSA-backed candidate who won his own multicandidate congressional primary this year, said that “if Hong wins, it will affirm that the platforms of democratic socialist candidates are more broadly embraced by a diverse electorate than corporate media and institutionalists within our electoral duopoly care to admit.” The DSA does have some political history on its side. At the Franklin Public Library event, one voter brought up Wisconsin’s legacy as the first state to elect a socialist to Congress, in . “Don't apologize for being a democratic socialist,” the voter told Hong, rushing to shake her hand. “That's part of Wisconsin's tradition. Welcome.”

title: Israel Is Defining Michigan's Primaries. Progressives Say That's Why They're Winning.
author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed
summary: The debate among state Democrats is proving to be a microcosm of the discussion happening nationally within the party.
content: Abdul El-Sayed, left, is running against Rep. Haley Stevens for the Democratic nomination for Michigan's Senate seat. He could become the country’s first Muslim senator, and has both condemned Israel and said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.” Kristen Norman/AP Photo Rep. Haley Stevens recently lobbed a stunning accusation at her rival in the race to be Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed. “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens wrote Thursday on X . Stevens is not Jewish. But she has received nearly $30 million — a record amount — in support from forces that have long dominated American discussion of Israel, the self-proclaimed Jewish state: the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and affiliated groups. El-Sayed, who could become the country’s first Muslim senator, has both condemned Israel and said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.” Asked about her comments by a reporter on Saturday, Stevens responded: “There’s been a lot of talk from my opponent throughout this race about AIPAC, about foreign policy,” and mentioned El-Sayed campaigning with the streamer Hasan Piker, saying Piker “has been very antisemitic.” Piker has previously rejected similar characterizations of his views. Stevens’ campaign did not respond to an inquiry from NOTUS about her comments regarding El-Sayed. Earlier in the week, Donavan McKinney, who is making a primary challenge against Rep. Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, told NOTUS that as he campaigns, voters have demanded a “redistribution of resources” with clear implications for the U.S.-Israel relationship. As people speak of working three jobs or rent swallowing most of their Social Security checks, he sees their dire straits as inseparable from Washington choosing to fund Israel’s ongoing attacks on Palestinians and collaborating with Tel Aviv on “a war for no reason with Iran [that costs] $1 billion per day.” Israel is inescapable in the dynamics around Michigan’s Tuesday primaries, making the elections there a microcosm of the larger debate within the Democratic Party over U.S. support for the country. An overwhelming majority of Democratic voters think the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, according to a late-June Quinnipiac poll. And the views of the American public writ large on the issue have trended downward in recent years — with a drastic split emerging between the preferences of the Democratic base and party leadership as the last Democratic president, Joe Biden, fueled Tel Aviv’s punishing offensives in Gaza and Lebanon. Nationally, candidates and activists urging drastic changes to the U.S.’s Israel policy are now deeply enmeshed with those demanding an overall change to the Democratic Party’s positions and style, saying it has been soft on both Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump. The establishment is pushing back: Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan’s Democratic governor, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have endorsed Stevens against El-Sayed, and chief House Democrat Rep. Hakeem Jeffries backs Thanedar against McKinney. Schumer and Jeffries are firm Israel supporters. Will Lawrence, another insurgent House candidate tied to the party’s left flank, is battling two establishment-friendly rivals in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District. Yet while political convention once recommended deference to hardline Israel allies, the situation in Michigan suggests rising forces in the Democratic Party are cementing a different strategy: being loud and proud in questioning Washington’s entanglement with Tel Aviv. The midterms follow the cycle, in which American support for Israel first became a dominant national concern among Democrats. Like the current slate of progressive candidates, including El-Sayed and McKinney, those questioning Israel then intense pushback presenting them as needlessly divisive, and defenders of the U.S.-Israeli status quo still cite that election. The argument — pushed by voices like Rep. Dan Goldman (D-New York), a staunch Israel backer unseated in a primary this summer — is that the Uncommitted campaign, which began in Michigan and urged Democrats in several states to reject Biden in their primaries votes to send an electoral message to shift his Gaza policy, hurt the party. Goldman argued on X that Uncommitted “was significantly responsible for Trump 2.0.” Abbas Alawieh, an Uncommitted co-founder, is now running for state senate in Michigan with the backing of many of the organizations supporting fellow progressives. Alawieh has said he voted for Kamala Harris, and Uncommitted’s defenders say its goal was to warn Democrats about a vulnerability so they could win. Today, Israel skeptics say the success of their movements in Democratic primaries in Colorado and New York earlier this summer has already demonstrated the growing popularity of changing the American relationship with Israel. Rather than treat Michigan as definitive, they hope it will entrench a trend — and be influenced by momentum elsewhere. “This is a national movement too,” McKinney said, recalling his trip to Denver in June to campaign for Melat Kiros, a fellow challenger to a Democratic incumbent who entered national politics because of the Gaza war. “To see the energy on the ground — We were like, ‘I hope it spreads.’” He continued: “People around the country are just tired of status quo politicians.” Kiros and fellow progressives, including two others who won primaries this cycle, have stumped for candidates in Michigan during the primary races’ final weeks, and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), a progressive leader, visited the state to campaign for McKinney and El-Sayed last month. Locally, their coalition includes figures like Eboni Taylor, who’s running for state senate and whom Sanders has endorsed. Ed Rushton, an adviser to Taylor, cast the fight against AIPAC as similar to a deeply local issue: He said its operations resemble those of Detroit-based energy company DTE, in focusing on silencing critique from politicians from both parties — rather than supporting a positive agenda — and pumping excessive money into races. Stevens’ opponents argue, for instance, that there is no guarantee AIPAC and its partners will continue supporting her through November should they succeed in quashing El-Sayed. The alliance among progressives means they can vouch for each other to those who might be skeptical of one, Rushton noted — including those wary of growing discussion of Israel in politics, and those highlighting the issue. Some voters and even elected Democrats in Michigan have expressed concern about the political influence of Arab Americans, the community to which El-Sayed and Uncommitted’s leaders belong. At a recent campaign stop at a senior-living center, Rushton said, a person said they did not want “these Arabs to run the show,” an apparent criticism of Taylor’s endorsement from Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D), the sole Palestinian American in Congress. “I almost appreciated them saying that” for the chance to respond, Rushton said, to what he calls “an attempt to remarginalize Arab Americans disguised as a reclaiming of the Democratic Party” after the loss to Trump. “Across the state, 70, white women voted for Whitmer twice and voted for Trump in . Yet somehow this is an Arab issue?” Rushton told NOTUS. He said Taylor responds to similar comments while canvassing by describing her personal trust in Tlaib, El-Sayed and Alawieh. Stevens has falsely claimed El-Sayed led Uncommitted and rejected Harris in . Usamah Andrabi, the communications director for the progressive group Justice Democrats, said the Michigan progressives can jointly “build power for the working class in working class communities” while using the experience to their own benefit, to argue that mainstream Democrats enabled the rise of a Republican trifecta federally. “The establishment has spent so many years trying to convince everyday people they cannot challenge the billionaire class … [now] it is up to the establishment whether they want to use the campaigns we’re building as a roadmap,” he said. Justice Democrats formally endorsed McKinney and is, per Andrabi, “supportive from afar” of El-Sayed and Lawrence. Part of that blueprint is a clear position on Israel. Greg Krieg of the American Priorities PAC, which explicitly aims to counter AIPAC spending, told NOTUS: “Palestine is a credibility test now. If voters think you won’t be honest about it, they won’t trust you on anything else.” American Priorities has spent more than $ , in Michigan, he said. Progressives say a central part of their strength is the excitement that drives grassroots ground organizing. In Michigan, they have the benefit of several aligned campaigns running simultaneously, “working to change the of Congress for something much bigger” in terms of a policy shift, said Beth Miller, the political director of the organization Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP) Action. Her group’s endorsement of El-Sayed was its first Senate endorsement and itself an indicator of the Democratic evolution on Israel: JVP is explicitly anti-Zionist. Miller traced the development to years of work by organizers focused on what she called American “complicity in Israeli apartheid and ethnic cleansing” that has grown significantly since the Gaza war began in October . El-Sayed was long on the group’s radar, she said, “not coming in trying to ride the coattails.” Alongside his message, JVP emphasizes “the truth there is no ‘Jewish’ opinion on Israel or Palestine – as long as there has been Zionism, there have been anti-Zionist Jews,” Miller said. Amid the optimism among progressives, they still have determined detractors in Michigan — including among Democratic voters and persuadable Trump voters, groups from which their candidates will need support in November. The handling of Israel is a particular focus for those who remain leery, though seemingly more over its impact on domestic politics than policy choices abroad: Stevens supporters argue El-Sayed and allies focused on pushing the party over Gaza created unnecessary and even dangerous negativity at a party convention in April. On Thursday, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is Jewish, said she will not attend the state party’s August convention over fears for her safety. Nessel’s critics say their opposition to her is over her attempted prosecutions of anti-war protesters at the University of Michigan. Some Democrats maintain that the party and voters it needs won’t coalesce around progressive candidates in the general election, and those divisions could aid the GOP, with some hinting they might never back El-Sayed if he triumphs over Stevens. Meanwhile, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ campaign is projecting confidence over the surge for the left and Democratic infighting. "If you think calling to defund the police, abolishing private healthcare for autoworkers, and campaigning with an influencer who said, ‘America deserved 9/11’ are winning messages, I have news for you: Michiganders aren’t buying it,” Alyssa Brouillet, Rogers’ communications director, said in an emailed statement to NOTUS, including an apparent reference to Piker. Miller cast cold water on that GOP logic and said the progressives are focused on overall success. "What we need to beat Republicans in the general election in and then again in are people who are absolutely unapologetically un-bought and very clear in their values,” she said.

title: A Normie Democrat Revolt Is Pushing Abdul El-Sayed Toward Victory
author: Alex Roarty
summary: “The only reasonable thing seems to be: Burn it down and start over, and make it different,” one Michigan organizer said.
content: The frustration normie Democratic voters feel with their own party is in part responsible for the defeat of establishment-backed politicians this year. Jose Juarez/AP Photo/Jose Juarez. WILLIAMSTON, Mich. — Kent Tisdale spent most of his life voting for Republicans before he started voting for Democrats, even backing Donald Trump in . The 70-year-old retiree can even remember that his biggest concern backing Mitt Romney in was that the GOP presidential nominee wasn’t conservative enough. He is now seriously considering supporting Abdul El-Sayed in Tuesday’s Senate Democratic primary. Tisdale, now a member of his local Indivisible chapter, said Trump’s presidency and the deluge of money in politics led him to El-Sayed, whose passion has impressed him even if the candidate’s politics are further left than he’d like. “I don’t feel I’ve changed that much,” said Tisdale, who spoke to NOTUS while attending an event for a local House candidate. “But I feel the environment has changed.” In Michigan and across the country this year, voters like Tisdale are transforming Democratic primaries — and potentially putting the party on a different path as it heads into the presidential campaign. Rank-and-file Democratic voters who once naturally inclined toward establishment-backed candidates are instead supporting — or at least showing an openness to — lefty candidates they would have previously believed to be outside the political mainstream. They’re driven by disappointment in old-guard Democrats’ inability to beat Trump in and a growing sense that the country’s politics need a fresh direction. It’s that change in the electorate that, more than anything this year, explains why El-Sayed is now favored to beat Rep. Haley Stevens in Tuesday’s Senate primary in Michigan. Stevens is running the type of campaign — backed by key party endorsements, support in the Black community and plenty of money — that has helped centrist Democrats like her defeat progressive challengers for years. That pattern held for Hillary Clinton in and Joe Biden in . But the voters on the receiving end of that effort are in a much different place than they were in , much less or . “So many people feel the same way I do, that something needs to be done,” said Jan Cohen, who founded a local Indivisible chapter last year. “And the only reasonable thing seems to be: Burn it down and start over, and make it different. We have to take the stands and do everything we can.” Cohen voted against El-Sayed in when he ran for governor against Gretchen Whitmer. But she said she’s grown frustrated with Michigan Democratic leaders recently, worried they no longer seem to be pushing progressive policy through the state and upset at their support for Stevens. The frustration normie Democratic voters feel with their own party is in part responsible for the defeat of establishment-backed politicians like Janet Mills in Maine’s Senate race, or the handful of defeats of Democratic incumbents in safe blue House seats. In nearby Wisconsin, Democratic voters look poised to nominate a democratic socialist for governor in that state’s open gubernatorial race despite protests from party leaders like Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers. El-Sayed, a former Wayne County, Michigan, health director, earned just 30% of the vote against Whitmer in . That sort of defeat had become the norm for progressive Democrats, most crucially during each of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns. In those races, the senator from Vermont was unable to break through with many middle-of-the-road Democratic voters, especially in the Black community, and was ultimately pushed back by a party establishment that emphasized electability and realistic policy goals. Polls now show El-Sayed in a strong position ahead of Tuesday’s primary, leading Stevens by a double-digit margin in a spate of recent surveys, despite tens of millions of dollars spent against his campaign by outside groups. Stevens officials maintain the congresswoman has a chance to win Tuesday, dismissing polls as underestimating the support of her core voters. Some of the frustrated voters, including Tisdale, have also not actually made up their minds despite their openness to El-Sayed, expressing some reservations about his ideology and electability in the fall. And even progressive activists say privately they think the movement of these voters toward candidates like El-Sayed is less about a newfound acceptance of lefty policy platforms like single-payer health care and more about their anger with the Democratic establishment. Some Stevens supporters acknowledge that El-Sayed has tapped into a deep frustration in the party, pushing his candidacy to a stronger position than many expected was once possible for a candidate with his politics. “Abdul has drafted behind that uneasiness with our party,” said Lon Johnson, a veteran Democratic strategist in the state. “He has done a good job of drafting behind it, and corralling it.” “This year is very, very different than ,” said another Democratic strategist supportive of Stevens’ campaign, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “And I don’t like what that means for our party’s prospects, but that’s the way it’s going. People are pissed.” In a gaggle with reporters after a campaign event last week, El-Sayed said he personally had changed a lot since his race, noting he’s gone from a 32-year-old first-time candidate to a 41-year-old with two kids. He said he believes his message resonates much more deeply with the electorate now than it did then. “The bigger change is not really me,” he said. “The broader public has come through a lot. In the ensuing eight years, we’ve had a pandemic. We’ve lived through one full Trump presidency and then another quarter of one. We’ve watched an inflation crisis. And the central point that I was making is that Trump is not the disease, he’s the symptom. And I think this time around, after his ... first reelection, I think people understand that. “There’s something about having been saying the same thing for the better part of 10 years, since I jumped into public service,” he said. El-Sayed said he didn’t think the party’s failure to defeat Trump in was the root of voters’ frustration, instead blaming the simmering rage on Democrats’ inability to make people’s lives easier in tangible ways. El-Sayed’s pitch to voters hasn’t deviated this campaign. Before talking to reporters last week, he rallied with supporters in Lansing with a message focused on Israel’s wrongdoing in the Middle East, a single-payer health care system and a vow to take money out of politics. His final campaign ads feature progressive leaders like Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York). “I want you to remember that you're walking the same exact path as all of those folks who fought for everything coming from abolition to native rights to women’s suffrage to LGBTQ rights to religious freedom to ending Jim Crow, to building an America where we had unions, the folks who showed up to sit down and stand up for rights, the folks who gave us Medicare and Medicaid,” El-Sayed told supporters last week in Ypsilanti. “You are walking that path.” Polls indicate that El-Sayed still has some of the same struggles that have traditionally plagued progressives, especially with middle-aged and elderly Black voters. Stevens is counting on their support, along with older white union voters, to give her a chance at victory, and has developed her campaign to win them over. But Democrats say that many suburban voters who once considered themselves ideologically and temperamentally moderate before Trump’s victory in have entered their own state of rebellion. Their anger can be harshest for candidates like Stevens, Democrats say, who was first elected in but hasn’t been able to stop the GOP’s advance since entering office. “The base is so angry at normal Democrats who were around back then and are exactly the people who said, ‘We’ve got this,’” said a second Democratic strategist, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “And they didn’t.” Tisdale, a resident of Williamston, is still interested in candidates with more centrist politics, too: He spoke to NOTUS here at a meet-and-greet event for Matt Maasdam, a moderate Democrat running in the state’s 7th Congressional District. (Maasdam and Bridget Brink, another candidate with the support of local Democrats, are both in danger of losing to a progressive activist.) But even as a man who said he’s never voted for Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, despite living in her old House district, Tisdale said El-Sayed’s “passion level” might give Democrats a needed jolt to take on Trump. It’s why he says he and others, including his wife, are considering voting for the insurgent. “We think that kind of energy is how you fight back,” he said.

title: DSA Wants to Abolish the Senate. Bernie Sanders Says 'No.'
author: Igor Bobic
summary: Democrats across the caucus dismissed the idea of restructuring Congress.
content: Sen. Bernie Sanders backs many progressive proposals to overhaul the government, but opposes a DSA plan to eliminate the Senate. AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana Jose Luis Magana/AP Democratic Socialists of America, a group that’s gaining momentum across the country, is pushing to scrap the U.S. Senate and replace it with a unicameral legislature. Senate Democrats aren’t on board. “It's in the Constitution, and it is a critical component of the United States government to pass legislation with the House,” Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly told NOTUS. “In my view, that is not a serious recommendation.” “I don't even know what they mean by that. I don’t have any idea,” a befuddled Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. Even Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who’s long called himself a democratic socialist, isn’t on board with the proposal. “No,” Sanders told NOTUS. He declined to elaborate, saying he had a flight to catch. The DSA’s new platform , unveiled earlier this month, calls for expanding the social safety net and making sweeping changes to the federal government. Those include abolishing the Senate, the presidency, and the Supreme Court. Those institutions would be replaced with an “executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress,” as well as an expanded House of Representatives with multiple political parties instead of the current two-party system. Those ideas would require approving an amendment to the U.S. Constitution, a major hurdle in a polarized political environment. “The Senate is a very undemocratic institution,” Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, said in an interview on C-SPAN. “I talked a bit about democracy, a small ‘d’ democracy, and that’s really important to us. We want democratic representation of all people who live in this country.” The DSA platform, titled “Workers Deserve More,” has drawn attacks and ridicule from top Republicans who are seeking to tie some of its controversial ideas, such as abolishing the police, to the Democratic Party and its candidates ahead of November’s midterm elections. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist and front-runner in the Wisconsin governor’s Democratic primary race, for example, is facing questions about the platform and her past comments calling to abolish the police. “I do not support the full platform of the national DSA, and I am not endorsed by DSA national. What democratic socialism is, is a form of government that puts working-class people first,” Hong said in a debate last week, backing away from a social media post in which she called to abolish the police. Some Democrats believe their party isn’t doing enough to marginalize the democratic socialist movement, which recently claimed victories in local and congressional races in New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado and Washington, D.C. According to a recent CNN poll , about a third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists. “These people sat in a room and said, ‘How much crazy shit can we cram into a platform?’ Like, ‘Yeah, abolish the Senate? Sure, why not. Hey, abolish the presidency? Yeah, sure, why not?’ That's crazy shit,” Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, who has broken with Democrats on several key issues, told NOTUS. “I'm unique, I'm the only Democrat that will call it out.” But other Democrats downplayed the rise of DSA, arguing that most people who consider themselves to be far-left progressives ascribe to more popular ideas like taxing the rich and providing universal health care. “I know people in Richmond who align with DSA who don't want to abolish the Senate,” said Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine. “They don't want to abolish the presidency. If you ask them, ‘Why are you DSA?’ they will say, ‘I'm a Democrat, but I like DSA because I don't like the concentration of wealth.’” New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said his constituents are more concerned about their economic situation and having health care rather than “proposing things that would require a constitutional amendment,” which he called “farcical at this point.” Still, Booker, a potential Democratic presidential candidate, said he did support other structural reforms such as granting statehood to Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, as well as changing equal state apportionment, which gives every state two senators, no matter its population. “The Senate does have things that our founders never imagined, like the fact that North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, Idaho and Montana have 10 senators and they have less population than Los Angeles County, and that's really problematic,” Booker said. “But there are things that really focus on the real issues of people that we can get done here, that I think we should be organizing around.” Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, meanwhile, argued that voter frustration with how the Senate operates could be addressed if its members stood up for the system of checks and balances as laid out in the U.S. Constitution. “I think that we need to do something about a supine Senate. There’s a lot of madness happening right now in the White House that this body could do something to address if there was any courage,” Warnock said, before adding, “If my Republican colleagues had any moral courage.”

title: Saying Bye to July
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: President Donald Trump. Alex Brandon/AP Today’s notice: Well, that was a long month. Senators’ odds for a Blanche confirmation. Ryan Mackenzie returns Adam Kidan’s money. Democratic AGs say they’re gonna have a big cycle. The winding paths of two South Carolina political careers. And: Regulating the wokeness out of AI is harder than it sounds. THE LATEST Who’s happier to see July end? Mercury’s second retrograde ended eight days ago , but that was not enough to stop a seemingly endless torrent of terrible, horrible, no good, very bad headlines that have bedeviled both sides this month. Donald Trump started the month with stormy weather almost canceling his Fourth of July fireworks. It proved to be a sign of things to come. The war with Iran flared back up, the economic indicators went back down. The courts pummeled him, forcing him to pay E. Jean Carroll and withdraw subpoenas issued to New York Times reporters in an attempt to find out who leaked that the much-ballyhooed new Air Force One was not exactly ready for prime time. The last week brought some astoundingly bad polling numbers, increased oil prices , the Senate refusing to do his bidding on the SAVE America Act and acting Attorney General Todd Blanche ’s nomination for the permanent gig sputtering. What didn’t happen: The hot MAGA summer of lowered prices and talk of tax cuts some Republicans hoped for. If a shellacking comes from voters in November, remember how things never gelled in July. The Democrats did their best to have a worse month than the GOP. The Graham Platner -pocalypse showed the left has a lot to learn about picking primary candidates. Several embarrassing faceplants by DCCC-backed candidates showed the establishment also has a lot to learn about that. Oh, also parts of the DNC appear to be a dumpster fire — the parts of it that aren’t being actively scammed by fraudsters, that is. Democratic primary voters in Maine were, of course, disenfranchised cuz of all that , and now thousands more might see their votes wasted in the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary. A lot of people did what they were asked to do in Wisconsin and voted early for one of the two candidates who dropped out this month. What this portends: If Democrats manage to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory in November, just remember how they spent their July. What comes next? Let us again consult the astrology charts: The Lion’s Gate Portal opened up Tuesday, peaks Aug. 8 and stays open until the 12th, which happens to be a few days after the Senate leaves for recess. We have no idea what these words actually mean but it’s all about cosmic alignment, according to NOTUS’ Manuela Silva — letting go of the old and being clear about your intentions moving forward. Open tabs: Trump Announces Deal for ‘Complete Disarmament’ of Hamas (NOTUS) Midterm election fears run high, poll finds (Semafor); Senate Finance Republicans kill bid to stop Trump IRS audit-immunity deal (Politico); Taco Bell’s Plan to Win Back Customers After Cyclospora Outbreak (WSJ); Joe Rogan warns liberals against trying to turn Texas blue (Fox) From the Hill Blanche’s odds: Todd Blanche has had a bumpy week. Is Trump about to be rebuked by the YOLO Caucus? Or is this just some noise before the Republican-controlled Senate gives the Republican president the nominee he wants? Manuela asked senators their odds for Blanche’s eventual confirmation as attorney general. They changed throughout the day, but not by much. “I would say, based on the comments that I’ve seen coming from the White House, not very good,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said earlier in the day. “67.7%,” YOLOer (and part-time bolo -er!) Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) joked after Trump’s Truth Social post suggesting he’d withdraw Blanche’s nomination if Tillis and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) don’t get on board. “You know, I can be really hopeful and say I hope that that happens before we leave,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) said. “But it wouldn’t surprise me that what we have to do is hold the nomination off until September.” “I believe we will,” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said when asked if the Senate will see Blanche confirmed. Any timeline predictions for that, senator? “Nope!” “I’m not in that at all. So I have no idea,” Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin) said. From the campaign trail Refund incoming: Pennsylvania’s 7th: Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie returned a donation from Adam Kidan , a convicted fraudster whom Trump pardoned three days after he donated to Mackenzie, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports . The refund comes one day after Avani reported on the donation. Mackenzie faces Democrat Bob Brooks in one of the most competitive House races in the country. First on NOTUS: Democratic AGs say internal numbers show wind at their backs. A new state-of-the-race memo marking -ish days till the general election from the Democratic Attorneys General Association suggests the group is poised to capitalize on the outsize attention attorneys general have seen in the lawsuit-heavy Trump 2.0. DAGA has raised $20.3 million since Jan. 1, a total that is close to double what it raised in the cycle. The memo points to internal polling the association says shows Democrats can “flip 2-3 seats from red to blue” in November. THE BIG ONE Un-woke-ing, another job AI cannot actually do: The Trump administration is trying to regulate “wokeness” in artificial intelligence. What that looks like in practice is turning out to be difficult to define as the General Services Administration tries to draw up contracting language for the second time, NOTUS’ Natalie Alms reports . The government’s draft language says it would test systems for bias, but it’s unclear how to do so. Even if a bias test can be spun up, contractors would have to pay decommissioning costs if their software is found to be swayed too woke, and could legal exposure. “That’s a huge penalty for something that I think is such a mushy framework,” Jessica Tillipman , associate dean for government procurement law studies at GWU, told Natalie. NOTUS METRO Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman. Local news: D.C.’s Worst Landlord Is Its Housing Authority , by Zara Norman Sports desk: The Commanders’ Defense Has Made a Strong First Impression at Camp , by Martenzie Johnson NOTUS PERSPECTIVES “I came to Michigan expecting to dislike El-Sayed’s candidacy,” writes Dana Milbank today at NOTUS Perspectives . Instead, he reached a very different set of conclusions: that the Michigan Democratic primary isn’t really an ideological civil war, and Abdul El-Sayed isn’t as scary as the establishment thinks. NEW ON NOTUS A tale of two South Carolinians: The career arcs of Mark Sanford and Lindsey Graham tell the story of the modern Republican Party, NOTUS’ Paul Kane writes . Once close friends — Graham was the godfather to one of Sanford’s sons — the pairs’ political fortunes took a divergent course after Trump changed the GOP. Graham got on board, Sanford never really did. Tracing their steps over the years, Paul details the path that has led to perhaps the most unlikely place: Sanford running a long-shot bid against Graham’s sister in the Republican primary for Graham’s old Senate seat. More: Defense Hawks Challenge the White House Push for a Narrow Reconciliation Bill , by Joe Gould and Avani Kalra Democrats Mobilize Over Fears Trump Will Deploy Troops to Polls , by Joe Gould and Kadia Goba Judge Appears Skeptical of Trump Administration’s Arguments About Anthropic Posing Security Threat , by Hamed Ahmadi Trump-Themed Passport Rollout Goes National , by Jenna Monnin NOT US Bipartisan Anger Grows at Pentagon’s Delayed ‘Forever Chemicals’ Cleanups , by Hiroko Tabuchi for The New York Times ‘It’s the honor system’: New Jersey’s noncitizen voter registration brings private worries into the open , by Matt Friedman for Politico A new media ecosystem is taking root on the left, reshaping Democratic politics , by Ali Swenson for The Associated Press Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com . And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr and Andrew Burton. Photo by Alex Brandon/AP.

title: How Lindsey Graham and Mark Sanford’s Friendship Defined 30 Years of Republican Politics
author: Paul Kane
summary: Once close friends, the South Carolinians’ paths chart the Republican Party’s evolution.
content: Disagreements over President Donald Trump were too great for former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (left) and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-South Carolina) to overcome. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) No relationship better tells the story of the modern Republican Party than that of Mark Sanford and Lindsey Graham. The former governor of South Carolina and the late senator were once as close as two politicians could be. But like so many political alignments — and friendships — over the last , disagreements over President Donald Trump were too great to overcome. Eight years ago, Graham said turning against Trump was the reason Sanford had been cast aside in the primary for his Charleston-area House district, despite nearly a quarter-century of ideologically consistent conservatism. “What happened here? I think for the first time, Mark misread the tea leaves, and being in for a while became a liability. So he's on the wrong side of new versus old,” Graham told me at the time. Two days after his defeat, Sanford called it “a Faustian bargain that's going on right now.” “I'll pander to you if you pander to me,” he said of Trump. Sanford declined to say whether he included his friend Graham in that bargain. The two entered the House together in as part of the Newt Gingrich-led Republican revolution, giving the GOP a majority for the first time in 40 years. They were rabble-rousers back then, and in the years to come, Sanford seemed made in a conservative laboratory for a presidential ticket. Graham evolved into a type of bipartisan wheeler-dealer that’s now a dying breed in the Republican Party. In a twist of fate that stretches from the Appalachian Trail to Argentina, it was Graham who received the equivalent of a state funeral this week, first with a service inside the Capitol Rotunda and then with Trump as the main eulogist at the National Cathedral. And it was Sanford who, a few days earlier, stood alone in his backyard, filming a video to launch a long-shot bid to get back to Congress. He’s one of many Republicans trying to win the nomination to replace Graham. “Lindsey’s death is a reminder to all of us how short and precious life is,” Sanford said in his less-than-two-minute video . Lindsey Graham ( , AR: 1.50)He cited his father’s death from Lou Gerhig’s disease, his status as a grandfather and his wish to finally tackle the national debt and shrink the size of federal government — the issues that launched the duo onto the national scene in — among his reasons for running. He never mentioned that he and Graham were once so close the late senator was godfather to Sanford’s youngest child. And he never mentioned that Trump, who supported Sanford’s primary opponent in , has endorsed Graham’s sister, Darline, who is now serving as interim senator. Sanford attended Wednesday's service for Graham in South Carolina, but he was not among the more than dozen politicians, TV personalities and conservative activists asked to speak at memorial events over two days. While he declined NOTUS’ interview requests this week, Sanford has tried to paint his rise, fall, rise and fall in politics as a selling point to South Carolina Republicans in this snap primary to be settled in just a couple weeks. Mark Sanford ( , AR: 1.50)“All of the ups and downs and what not that I’ve had in life — that all of us have had in life — give us a little bit more humility, give us a little bit more empathy, give us a little bit better perspective, I think, in later chapters in life,” he told a local TV news interviewer on Monday. The two were more aligned than not in those earlier chapters. Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) let out a solid 10 seconds of laughter when asked Wednesday about his early memories of Graham and Sanford. “Two of the most colorful members of our class,” said Wicker, who served as master of ceremonies two years ago for the class of reunion in the Capitol’s Statuary Hall. In , Graham played a leading role in an attempt to throw Gingrich out as speaker, with support from Sanford and other Republican rebels. During the campaign, while their state’s senior Republican leadership lined up behind Texas Gov. George W. Bush, Graham and Sanford signed on with Sen. John McCain’s team. They traveled their state in McCain’s Straight Talk Express bus and warmed up the crowds for the Arizona senator, who sometimes called them his “running mates,” already knowing their ambitions. Two years later, Sanford won the governor’s race and Graham won his Senate seat, launching them higher into national politics. GRAHAM MCCAIN ( , AR: 1.50)When McCain clinched the nomination, punctuated by a big win in South Carolina, Graham stood at his side. Sanford remained neutral in that presidential primary, perhaps a sign that his conservative politics diverged from that of Graham and McCain. Then suddenly, it seemed Sanford’s political career was over. His affair with an Argentinian woman became public in June after he had gone missing for days and aides gave false assertions he was hiking the Appalachian Trail when he was actually in Buenos Aires. Many Republicans called for his resignation, and state legislators began impeachment proceedings. But one friend gave him as much support as could be expected. “I know Mark wants to reconcile with his family. I hope and pray that is possible,” Graham said in a statement that avoided a call for resignation . “Second chances in life are not guaranteed or required. But if they are afforded they can be a real blessing.” While Jenny Sanford did leave her husband, Graham remained loyal to his friend. In , he rallied support for Sanford during a special election for the House and helped him win back that seat. It wasn’t Sanford’s messy personal life that ended his relationship with Graham. In the end, the Republican Party they both were a part of had shifted. It was less about conservative ideology and more about being in good company with Trump. Graham saw the reality and moved with it. Trump ( , AR: 1.50) “Along comes Trump: ‘I'm gonna burn the whole place down.’ I actually can relate to that because that's where I used to be,” Graham told me in that June interview. Trump won’t attack critics who he thinks want to “add value” to his success, traditional conservatism be damned, Graham said. “The head of our party is the least ideological person in the history of the Republican Party.” Graham’s longtime bond with Sanford couldn’t protect the anti-Trump Republican from Trump’s fury during his losing primary. Graham said he learned from McCain that bygones should be bygones in politics, having gone from being prisoner of war in Vietnam to dealing with that government as a senator, and working with President Barack Obama despite his loss to him in . And instead of fighting against Trump’s takeover of the party, Graham jumped on board. “So one thing I've learned from John is, when it's over, it's over,” Graham said then. Graham still held out hope for Sanford’s fourth act in politics if he figured out how to repair things with Trump. But with Sanford, it was never over. AP331347709959 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Sanford launched a brief run in the Republican presidential primary. This spring, he considered running for the House seat that Republican Rep. Nancy Mace is vacating after her failed bid for governor. Then, he announced he would start a foundation dedicated to taming the national debt. And now, he’s running for Graham’s seat. Sanford remains an anti-Trump Republican, preaching to a smaller and smaller choir but still hopeful that his decades of experience can win enough support. He thinks that South Carolina’s voters want a truly competitive primary and will want to know more about Sen. Darline Graham’s views on policy, particularly the debt. “I don’t think they like this idea of a coronation,” he said in a local TV interview this week. But even after his last act in politics appeared closed back in June , Sanford was not shutting the door on another comeback. “Believe me, if there's anybody who ever learned you never say never, it's me,” he told me then.

title: Mandela Barnes Drops Out of Chaotic Wisconsin Governor's Race
author: Christa Dutton
summary: The former lieutenant governor exited as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel said it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety.
content: Former Lt. Gov Mandela Barnes dropped out of the crowded and chaotic Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin on Thursday. Nam Y. Huh/AP Photo Former Lt. Gov Mandela Barnes dropped out of the crowded and chaotic Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin on Thursday. Shortly after he dropped out, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported that it was looking into allegations that Barnes had used his position to have “sexual encounters with young adult women.” The outlet initially provided few other details, adding only that it was continuing to report on the story. The Journal Sentinel soon updated its story to add that the state Democratic Party hired a law firm last year to look into “similar claims,” but the information it received was “anonymous and unspecific” and was not actionable. The outlet also reported that the Democrat has not been accused of committing crimes. “There are no allegations of misconduct or wrongdoing against Mandela," a campaign spokesperson told NOTUS. Barnes’ statement announcing that he was suspending his campaign did not address the Journal Sentinel’s reporting. “Last night I had a very difficult conversation with my staff,” he said in a video posted on X . “We’re incredibly proud of all the things that we’ve accomplished and all the resources that we have raised to spread our message, but it’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be.” Leading the pack in the race is Francesca Hong, a state representative and democratic socialist. She has gained momentum in the final weeks of the primary campaign, with one poll by Marquette University Law School showing her more than 20 percentage points ahead of Barnes . He did not explicitly endorse Hong in his announcement, but said he would work to help defeat Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is leading the Republican field. That leaves four Democratic candidates ahead of the Aug. 11 primary, a race that is being closely followed given that it’s playing out in a battleground state. Barnes’ exit is yet another shakeup in a primary in which Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out after she reported “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her financial campaign filings. That prompted Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who had already dropped out of the governor’s race because his campaign was not gaining traction, to reenter with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement. Hong’s rise as the primary’s front-runner is being closely watched, as it’s a test of democratic socialists’ political strength outside of solidly blue districts and states. Early voting is already underway in Wisconsin, which has created another twist in the race. On Wednesday, the Dane County circuit judge ruled that voters who had cast absentee ballots for Rodriguez would not be able to request new ones — a decision likely to apply to voters who cast ballots for Barnes too. Democrats in the state were already concerned about Barnes’ electability . From the outset, his gubernatorial bid was haunted by his failed Senate run in , when he lost to Sen. Ron Johnson by just 1 percentage point in a year that Evers won reelection by more than 3 percentage points. Until his announcement, Barnes’ social media accounts hadn’t otherwise posted since Wednesday. Door-knocking events scheduled for Saturday still appeared on his campaign website, and his social media accounts encouraged supporters to vote early on Wednesday. Editor’s note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

title: Centrist Democrats Are Staring Down Disaster in a Michigan Swing District
author: Alex Roarty
summary: Two establishment-friendly Democrats are battling it out in Lansing. Unfortunately for them, they’re not alone in the race.
content: “I am the strongest candidate to win both the primary and the general election,” said onetime Ukraine ambassador Bridget Brink. (Andrew Kravchenko/AP) LANSING, Mich. — The Democratic Party establishment is on the verge of another big problem ahead of November’s midterm elections. In Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, party leaders believe either of two candidates running — former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam or onetime Ukraine ambassador Bridget Brink — could win the battleground district. The problem? There’s a third candidate. And Maasdam and Brink have attacked each other relentlessly while drawing from the same pool of supporters — giving a progressive activist a chance to win instead. Democratic strategists in Michigan and Washington are deeply worried that the party is on the verge of nominating William Lawrence, co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement. Doing so, they fear, would be an electoral disaster in a swing district — held by Republican Rep. Tom Barrett — that narrowly backed Donald Trump in . The situation has left some Democrats frustrated at the inability of its centrist and establishment-friendly factions to unify behind one candidate, in the joint goal of blocking a candidate whose unabashedly progressive politics they agree are a poor fit for the district. “It’s a mess,” said Emily Cherniack, founder and CEO of New Politics, which backs candidates with a service background and has endorsed Maasdam. “People aren’t coalescing to say, ‘This is going to be the candidate because, mission first, we gotta win. That’s not happening.” Cherniack, in an interview last week, said she expected Lawrence would win, even if he gets far less than 50% of the vote. On Wednesday, a pro-Maasdam group released a poll showing Lawrence leading the primary field with 38% support, followed by Maasdam in second and Brink in third. Other recent surveys have shown Brink in second place. Michigan’s 7th District, a mix of suburban and rural communities that includes Lansing, is rated a “toss-up” by The Cook Political Report, and Democrats have targeted it as one of their best chances to flip a GOP-held district in November. “It’s an insane thing to say about what should be a top-5 pickup opportunity this year, but I think we might be about to shoot ourselves in the head on this one,” said one Democratic strategist in Michigan, who requested anonymity to speak candidly. It’s the latest instance of the Democratic Party’s sometimes stumbling efforts to block progressive candidates from winning races in key states or districts, one that threatens to complicate its efforts to win congressional majorities in the House and Senate this fall. In Maine, for instance, progressive newcomer Graham Platner toppled a sitting governor in the state’s Senate primary, before being forced from the race after being accused of sexual assault. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, meanwhile, has setbacks in places like California and Arizona, where its preferred candidates lost their primaries. The DCCC has not publicly expressed a preference in the 7th District race. But other centrist Democratic leaders say the party needs to be able to better navigate races like these, whether led by party committees or the candidates themselves. “It’s vital that in winnable but tough swing districts, mainstream Democrats take their cues from Amy Klobuchar and Pete Buttigieg and step aside to avoid a more extreme candidate from winning,” said Matt Bennett, co-founder of the center-left Democratic think tank Third Way. In interviews this week, neither Brink nor Maasdam gave any indication they were planning to step aside, each calling themselves the candidate with the best chance to win a primary and general election. “It seems a little awkward to have the person who's in the lead of that group drop out of the race to give it to the person who’s not in the lead,” Maasdam told NOTUS in an interview, reflecting his campaign’s belief that he has pulled ahead of Brink and sits within striking distance of Lawrence. “I would say, the person who’s not in the lead should drop out, but that would just be my opinion.” Brink, whose campaign maintains she leads Maasdam in the polls, said in an interview with NOTUS that it’s a sign of weakness for her opponent’s campaign that outside groups have spent millions of dollars backing his candidacy. “I am the strongest candidate to win both the primary and the general election,” she said. The two candidates have continued to attack each other publicly, while outside groups working on their behalf have also launched negative ads against their opponent. Lawrence has also been the recipient of attack ads from at least one outside group, part of a significant, if belated, effort to siphon support from his campaign. He’s also been the beneficiary of more than $1 million in ads widely believed to be funded by a Republican group, Michigan Sunrise PAC — an effort to meddle in Democratic primaries that the GOP has undertaken in a handful of key districts this year. Brink and Maasdam have also split the endorsements of local power brokers: Maasdam has the support of Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who held the 7th District seat before running for Senate in and took the unusual step of appearing in a pro-Maasdam ad. Brink has the support of an array of local Democratic leaders, including former Gov. Jennifer Granholm. Lawrence has campaigned explicitly on the acrimony between Maasdam and Brink and the deluge of outside spending trying to assist their campaigns. On Tuesday, he said he spent much of the day walking more than 12 miles through Lansing in an effort to talk to voters and business owners about policies that could help make life easier. “I think the voters are sick of it, and we’ve been running a positive campaign all along, fighting hard for what we believe,” he told NOTUS in an interview. “Not afraid to draw a contrast but keeping it focused on policy rather than baseless, personal attacks, like my two opponents have been throwing at each other.” Lawrence ended his walk Tuesday at a campaign rally in Lansing, sharing a stage with Abdul El-Sayed, an ideological ally who is himself on the ballot next week as a Senate candidate. Like El-Sayed, Lawrence backs single-payer health care, denounces Israel’s treatment of Palestine, and argues that he represents a fresh start from the failed status-quo politics of yesteryear. He’s also campaigned aggressively against data centers, an issue he said would help him win over Republican voters in November. Lawrence denied he would be the weakest candidate to the Republican this fall, saying his opposition to the establishment in both parties will make him an attractive candidate for a wide array of voters. “The Democrats have let us down so many times, and they also participate in the cover-up of the Epstein files, and they’ve also voted for these endless and pointless wars over the last 25 years,” he said. “And so, I’m not here to play partisan games. I’m not here to play Team Red against Team Blue. I’m here to represent the people of these districts.” Brink and Maasdam allies say they think their preferred candidate still has at least an outside chance to win, if they’re able to muster a late surge in momentum. But each side is also deeply frustrated with the other. Maasdam and his allies think he has the late momentum in the race, driven by his military background (Maasdam carried the “nuclear football” for President Barack Obama, a biographical fact supportive groups have cited in ads) and the perception he’d give Democrats a formidable nominee to back in the fall. At a campaign event Wednesday in Williamston, he also made an explicit electoral argument against Lawrence, saying his radical approach to politics won’t sit well with many voters of the district. “I want work within the bounds the Constitution provides. I think he wants to burn that down,” he said to an audience of about 20 voters. “He’d rather burn it down and start with a new system than to work within the bounds of what we have created in America. And I think that’s the wrong way to go.” Brink and her allies see the race differently. They believe Maasdam is only competitive because of a relatively late surge of millions of dollars in outside spending, much of which ultimately did more to boost Lawrence’s candidacy than his own. “What’s happening in our race is that there’s a ton of dark money in this race — it's a kind of super PAC money, and it’s unaccountable,” said Brink, who that $5 million of the $6 million spent in the primary by outside groups had gone toward helping Maasdam’s campaign. “It’s not transparent.”

title: LCV Victory Fund Will Spend at Least $50 Million Backing Democrats
author: Elena Schneider
summary: The climate group’s midterm push will focus on affordability and rising utility costs.
content: The LCV Victory Fund will boost Democrats including former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio. Jeff Dean/AP. A leading progressive climate group is planning to spend at least $50 million on the midterms — a boost to Democrats looking to retake both chambers of Congress. The LCV Victory Fund, the super PAC affiliated with the League of Conservation Voters, is targeting House Republican candidates in five battleground districts, with plans to expand that list heading into the fall, and will be boosting former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina and former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio in their respective Senate bids. It will also spend on gubernatorial and state legislative races in Michigan, Nevada and Georgia — a trio of states with competitive down-ballot races. The details of LCV Victory Fund were shared first with NOTUS. The spending will go toward advertising, field programs and work with content creators. LCV Victory Fund is particularly targeting voters who feel the affordability pinch — voters who are more likely to be women, Black or Latino, noncollege educated and less politically engaged, said Sara Schreiber, LCV Victory Fund’s senior vice president of campaigns. “A key part of the electorate is affected by this affordability crisis, and they are really looking for candidates who have plans and are creating solutions that will keep costs low,” Schreiber said in an interview with NOTUS. “These are the folks that you need to win in a midterm, and they're going to be critical in .” The eight-figure pledge is “on par” with previous midterm campaigns from the group, Schreiber said. During the cycle, LCV Victory Fund spent more than $40 million on independent expenditures and contributions to candidates. LCV Victory Fund’s pledge comes as Democrats a widening gap in fundraising between Democratic-aligned entities and Republican-backed groups. Some Democrats are concerned about the party’s ability to keep up with Republican spending in vital races. The Democratic National Committee, for example, remains in debt , while the Republican National Committee has built a $ million war chest. LCV Victory Fund’s ads — some of which started running earlier this month — drill Republicans on rising utility costs, complimenting House Democrats’ larger focus on affordability. In Michigan, LCV Victory Fund is out with a new ad attacking Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga for “votes to cut our clean energy supply” that “made our utility rates go up.” Public polling suggests those attack lines could be effective, particularly around rising energy costs. Nearly two-thirds of voters said President Donald Trump’s policies have “worsened” economic conditions in the country in a CNN poll released this week. Nearly eight in 10 voters said the Trump administration is not focused enough on lowering prices in a recent CBS News poll . LCV President Pete Maysmith called energy costs a “potent issue” for voters, one that already had success for Democrats in off-year victories in the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial elections. “It’s the central message because Republicans have broken trust with voters,” Maysmith said. “They're causing real pain in people's pocketbooks, and that shows up both in their utility bills, which are up 18% since Trump took office, when he pledged to cut them in half.” A handful of candidates are already leaning into utility cost messaging in their own ads. Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running for governor, touted his record of suing “big utilities and drug companies to lower costs” in his first TV ad . In Pennsylvania, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, who is challenging Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, hit data centers for “raising our electric bills” in her ad .

title: Democrats Can’t Recast Ballots Ahead of Wisconsin Gubernatorial Primary, Judge Rules
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: The state party filed a lawsuit earlier this month after multiple candidates dropped out of the governor’s race and one candidate re-entered.
content: Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker denounced Conway’s decision and tied the commission’s decision to larger efforts to “suppress” mail-in voting. Morry Gash/AP Wisconsin voters returned more than , absentee ballots before one of the front-runners in the governor’s race dropped out and another contender jumped back in — but a judge ruled Wednesday that those voters are not allowed to request new ones. The ruling shut down a lawsuit filed by the state’s Democratic Party against the Wisconsin Elections Commission to allow the absentee voters to submit new ballots because of the race’s changing nature. “The unambiguous language of the statute does not allow a voter to spoil an absentee ballot after it is returned,” Dane County Circuit Judge David Conway wrote in his ruling, referencing the guidance the state elections commission rolled out earlier this month on voters’ ability to receive new ballots. Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker denounced Conway’s decision and tied the commission’s decision to larger efforts to “suppress” mail-in voting. “The decision to change the rules around voting that were a long-standing practice before Republicans' attempts to suppress absentee voting was wrong, and we disagree with the ruling today,” Remiker wrote in a statement — adding that the state party intends to “examine all of [their] options moving forward.” “Their primary is already chaotic enough,” Wisconsin Republican Party Chairman Brian Schimming told The Associated Press earlier this month about the lawsuit. “Election laws should not be changed to rescue one party from the consequences of its own actions.” Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, who was seen as a front-runner in the governor’s race, dropped out on July 17 after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her campaign finance filings. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley jumped back into the race on July 18 — after he’d dropped out on July 8 and endorsed Rodriguez — with support from retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Missy Hughes, former Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation CEO, suspended her campaign earlier this month — triggering a decision by the state elections commission to block the ability to revote if a candidate drops out. The commission voted 4-2 on July 9 to issue the guidance limiting voters’ ability to “spoil” their ballots and excluded circumstances like someone deciding to vote for another candidate. In their suit, Democrats urged the court to issue a temporary restraining order against the policy. Rodriguez’s and Hughes’ names remain on ballots, and the primary election is Aug. 11. Five Democratic candidates — Crowley, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, former Milwaukee mayoral chief of staff Joel Brennan, state Rep. Francesca Hong and state Sen. Kelda Roys — are still in the running for the Democratic nomination.

title: Schumer Says He and Troy Jackson Are 'Working Together'
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: The Maine Senate candidate has said in past interviews that he would not support Schumer as leader next year.
content: It’s the first time the New York Democrat has publicly commented on the race since calling for Graham Platner to drop out of the race after sexual assault allegations. Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he met with Democratic Maine Senate hopeful Troy Jackson Wednesday morning. “We had a great meeting this morning,” Schumer told reporters. “We're working together to win the seat, beat Susan Collins and take back the Senate.” It’s the first time the New York Democrat has publicly commented on the race since calling for Graham Platner to drop out of the race after sexual assault allegations . None of Jackson’s potential Senate colleagues have endorsed him since the Maine Democratic Party selected him as the new nominee last Saturday, according to his endorsements page . Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) had endorsed Jackson during his earlier gubernatorial run this year. That support has not carried over to Jackson’s Senate campaign: Sanders campaigned heavily for Platner before the allegations broke. Jackson, like several Senate candidates this cycle, has said he would not support Schumer as leader next year. “The Democratic Party needs to have a different approach — getting people back in the party, getting working-class, everyday people back in the party — and I don’t believe it’s going to happen with Senator Schumer,” Jackson said in an interview with The New York Times earlier this month. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee backed Jackson’s nomination after it was made official. “Troy Jackson is a fifth-generation logger with a demonstrated ability to win,” Schumer and Chair Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) said in a statement that day. “A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been.” Jackson has also earned the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris, who won Maine by nearly 7 percentage points during her presidential run in .

title: Former CHC Chair Nanette Barragán: Latino Trump Voters Have ‘Buyer’s Remorse’
author: Oriana González, Ed Demaria
summary: The California Democrat says Trump misled Latino voters on the economy.
content: Barragán said that Democrats faltered with Latino voters in the election because of a failure in communication. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) Rep. Nanette Barragán, the former chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, said Latinos who voted for President Trump in the election have “buyer’s remorse” over his promises on the economy and immigration. “They’re saying, ‘I’m worse off, I’m paying more in higher cost, higher prices. I can't afford this anymore,’” Barragán said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “‘We thought he was going to go after the worst of the worst, the criminals.’ He's not, he's going after our gardeners, our housekeepers, even doctors, DACA recipients.” “They're looking at what's happening and saying, ‘This is not what we voted for,’” Barragán said. According to the exit polls, Trump carried 46% of Hispanic and Latino voters in the election, up from 32% in the demographic in the election. Barragán said that Democrats faltered with Latino voters in the election because of a failure in communication . “I think Democrats got so much done that we didn't know what to focus on,” Barragán said. “People were not feeling what we did. And a lot of this is how people feel. … If they don't feel it, they're not going to give us credit. They're going to try something else.” Barragán said it was “unfortunate” that sitting Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat lost his primary to Darializa Avila Chevalier, but she believes it was likely due to the New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s endorsement of Chevalier rather than the weakness of the CHC. “I don't know the politics of New York, but I know one thing, and that is the mayor there has been popular,” Barragán said. “His messaging is resonating with a lot of Americans.” Chevalier expressed interest in joining the Hispanic Caucus if she’s elected in November — Barragán said she expects Chevalier to be approved by an admission vote of the members. With more self-proclaimed socialists expected to join her in Congress, Barragán said she does not know what values socialists stand for but that Democrats of all stripes were united to oppose President Trump. “My understanding is whether you're a Democrat or you're a democratic socialist, you don't agree with this president and what he's doing on raising costs,” Barragán said. “I believe we should be welcoming of anybody, even if Republicans want to make the switch.” Barragán was one of more than House Democrats who voted yes on an amendment from Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to end all aid to Israel. The California Democrat said the amendment was “overbroad” and cut necessary humanitarian aid, but defended her vote as the will of her constituents. “At the end of the day, it was about listening to constituents and also sending a message that we are not going to continue to support [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu's wars and the killing of innocent people with our money,” Barragán said. “Just like I vote against President Trump and his money for war, it's the same rationale.” Barragán supported a measure to send military aid to Israel in , but said Netanyahu’s leadership led her to change her stance. “Things have changed, the landscape has changed,” Barragán said. “It was time to say we're not just going to keep funding something because we've done it in the past. We're going to look at everything going on, and we're not going to support a president in Israel who is just frankly doing whatever he wants.” On NOTUS is a weekly podcast where NOTUS reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here .

title: Debbie Wasserman Schultz’s Run Is Infuriating Black Democrats. She Might Win Anyway.
author: Oriana González
summary: If Wasserman Schultz wins the race to represent a historically Black district, it would be “the greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today,” one Democratic candidate said.
content: U.S. Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz (Democrat of Florida) during a Democratic Steering and Policy Committee in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday October 28, . Democrats are facing increasing pressure to reopen the government as the government shutdown enters its 28th day. (Photo by Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA)(Sipa via AP Images) Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA via AP When candidates running for Florida’s 20th Congressional District gathered for a forum hosted by the local chapter of the NAACP in late July, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the only white candidate in the race, wasn’t there. “If someone didn’t come, it wasn’t because they weren’t asked, it’s because they chose not to come and ask for your vote,” Marsha Ellison, president of the NAACP Broward County chapter told the audience, which was mostly made up of people of color.
