The candidates never directly named Wasserman Schultz — but her decision to run in the district, which has historically been represented by Black lawmakers and has a plurality Black population, has drawn the ire of her opponents and overshadowed much of the race. Wasserman Schultz lives in Florida’s recently drawn 22nd District, which leans Republican. The 20th District is now the safest blue seat in the state. The anger at Wasserman Schultz is palpable and doesn’t seem to be going away anytime soon, but it may not matter: Polling in the race has been limited , but Wasserman Schultz is seen as the lead candidate in the race due to the rest of the field splitting the vote. The four Black Democratic candidates in the race initially planned to consolidate behind one person to defeat Wasserman Schultz. However, they were unable to decide who should run and who should drop out. While the NAACP forum was largely focused on the candidates’ legislative ideas, many candidates criticized Wasserman Schultz’s decision to run. Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell, a rapper and Democratic congressional candidate, said that allowing Wasserman Schultz to represent the historically Black district would be “the greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today.” “If we allow her to win, we will not win the general,” Campbell said. “The world is watching congressional district 20, and don’t you miss this opportunity.” The NAACP forum was convened after the Broward County Democratic Black Caucus condemned Wasserman Schultz for suggesting that the group was endorsing her in the race. Wasserman Schultz’s campaign website listed the caucus in its endorsements page, then quietly deleted it after the caucus complained. The group accused Wasserman Schultz of “dishonest intentions” at the time, but Corey Shearer, the caucus’ president, told NOTUS that Wasserman Schultz apologized for the incident and explained that the endorsements listed were from . However, he said, that doesn’t change his anger that she’s running in a district that has long been represented by a Black representative. “This is a historical seat for many of us,” Shearer said. “There’s no way, no how, that we want to give that legacy up. And so that’s what Debbie Wasserman Schultz is forcing upon us.” “The Black community should be able to celebrate that, and our celebration is just ripped away by this move from Debbie Wasserman Schultz, somebody who we looked at as an ally, but it just seems like she was more familiar , and she’s using that familiarity to take an easy way out and look to take our seat,” Shearer said. The caucus held a debate for candidates in the race last Monday, but Wasserman Schultz also did not attend. Wasserman Schultz’s campaign did not respond to a list of questions from NOTUS. In a statement, a spokesperson said the “Congresswoman was representing her constituents in DC for votes during both the events in question. Both organizations were informed of this conflict that prevented her from attending.” Some of the candidates challenging Wasserman Schultz also denounced the Congressional Black Caucus for not publicly speaking out against Wasserman Schultz. “Our House is not in order because the Congressional Black Caucus … is not on our side,” Campbell said at the NAACP forum. “They allowed a white woman to come in this district knowing that [Republicans] are trying to … gerrymand the vote and take Black representation that has been here for 30 years.” Former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness, a Democrat, concurred. “It’s very discouraging, disappointing that the Congressional Black Caucus has not sought to make statements and to stand and say, ‘Look this is wrong,’” Holness said. The CBC and its campaign arm declined to comment for this story. CBC Chair Yvette Clarke has said she did not encourage Wasserman Schultz to run in the district, despite Wasserman Schultz’s suggestions to the contrary . The CBC PAC does not generally get involved in primaries with multiple Black candidates, though members have endorsed in races in an individual capacity. Three members of the caucus previously told NOTUS they do not expect the CBC PAC to back the congresswoman in the race. One member at the time called Wasserman Schultz a “friend” to the caucus, so the CBC would likely remain “neutral.” But House Democrats aren’t running to defend Wasserman Schultz either. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, for example, has declined to endorse Wasserman Schultz in the race. “I’m looking forward to getting involved in the August primaries, of which there’ll be primaries on Aug. 4th; there will be primaries on Aug. 11th; and then the Florida primaries will be in Aug. 18th,” Jeffries said last Thursday when asked if he’d be endorsing Wasserman Schultz in the race. He called her a “highly effective member of the U.S. Congress and a valuable member of both the leadership team and the House Democratic Caucus.” Outgoing Rep. Frederica Wilson , who refers to herself as the highest-ranking Black elected official in Florida and represents a neighboring district, recently wrote an op-ed calling the 20th District “a seat paid for by generations of Black sacrifice.” Wilson’s piece does not name Wasserman Schultz. “If Black lives matter, then the history of Black representation matters too,” Wilson wrote. “We deserve a seat at every table where decisions about our lives, our children, our communities and our future are made. That seat was not given to us. It was earned through generations of Black sacrifice.” “It is the seat that Black history built,” Wilson continued. “Now it is our responsibility to make sure history never has to build it again.” Wilson told NOTUS in mid-July that the op-ed was not meant to urge voters to not support Wasserman Schultz but to give context to voters. “I just wanted the district to know the historical nature of that district.” She that she had not spoken to Wasserman Schultz since she first announced her candidacy. “She feels like she should be able to run where she wants to,” Wilson said. But she , “It took us years to get that district, so I wanted them to be sure when they voted that they were willing to make that sacrifice and go back.” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) has weighed in on the race and formally endorsed activist Elijah Manley over Wasserman Schultz. Khanna called Manley “bold and progressive” and told NOTUS that his staff had reached out to Wasserman Schultz’s team before the endorsement was announced. “At a time where Black political rights are under attack, I find it wrong for a heavily Black majority district not to be represented by an African American who connects in that community,” Khanna said. While some candidates acknowledged it would easier to beat her if she was running against just one person, they’re hoping the backlash over this race will be enough for her to lose the primary. “If she gets back to Congress, if she somehow wins this race, she will be persona non grata,” Manley told NOTUS in June. “Nobody is going to want to touch her because she will have proceeded in doing what the Republicans want: taking away not just Black representation, but pushing her own career at the expense of the public because this is all about Debbie.”

title: Lawmakers Are Riding the AI Wave to Stardom
author: Samuel Larreal
summary: Politicians who can speak to the high-profile issue are positioned to grow their credibility among voters and with their party.
content: Rep. Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, argues that AI policy is going to be “a decisive issue” in the presidential election. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Artificial intelligence is upending the internet, warfare, science and the economy. It is also disrupting power in Washington by providing a pathway to relevance for politicians willing to grapple with it. Ask lawmakers on Capitol Hill who work on AI policy why they’re doing it, and they’ll tell you it’s one of the most pressing issues of our time. Observers point out it’s also politically astute of them to embrace the issue: It’s a fast track to higher name recognition, credibility within their party and the groundwork for a platform to run on. “Whenever there's a developing policy or technology that’s also in the news a lot, you always have a lot of ambitious politicians who love to go running towards the light,” said Eddie Vale, a Democratic political consultant. “It is definitely growing exponentially, both in terms of like groups and also politicians trying to get involved,” Vale told NOTUS. “When AI first came out, people were thinking about it more as a tech policy issue, but as people learned more about it, they realized it is starting to impact almost every policy area.” In practice, that means members of Congress across the political spectrum have introduced hundreds of bills aimed at shaping how AI is developed and used. While few AI-related bills have passed , AI regulation is becoming a prized policy space which can be leveraged for political power. Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, argued AI policy is going to be “a decisive issue” in the presidential election and beyond. Casar isn’t considered a possible candidate, but he has recently introduced bills to protect children using AI chatbots and stop AI-powered algorithmic pricing. He’s also proposed taxing large companies' AI use. “Democrats have this huge opportunity to be on the side of everyday people and leave JD Vance and the Republicans on the side of scumbags like David Sacks and Elon Musk,” Casar told NOTUS. But it’s not just Democrats whose careers could end up being hoisted by AI. Three-term Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California) has long been the point person in the House Republican Conference for AI policy. He co-led a bipartisan AI working group that established the largest bipartisan AI regulatory framework in Congress. Earlier this year, he became the conference policy chair. When NOTUS asked Obernolte, who was previously a computer scientist and game developer in California, if AI has boosted his career in Congress, he said he hadn't “really thought about it.” U.S. Congress ( , AR: 1.50)“For most of us, this is not why we’re doing this. We’re doing this because we care deeply about this issue and we feel that federal action is desperately necessary,” Obernolte said. “We rely on silos of expertise ... on the issues having to do with technology policy, those of us that have a background in technology, I think, we have people that listen to us.” That background may have helped land his spot in leadership, according to Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), who was policy chair before Obernolte and endorsed him for the role. “He's done a lot of work on many things, but he’s somebody who certainly understands AI,” Hern told NOTUS. “And that's an area where we have quite a deficiency in Congress. Maybe even more so on the House side.” “He’s somebody who is obviously educated on it. And I've always said I want people talking about important issues that have actually had experience on the outside, and he's certainly the right person,” Hern . Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), who is planning to run for vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus in the next Congress, according to a source familiar with her thinking, recently joined forces with Obernolte to introduce an AI safety bill. The bill would allow the federal government to intervene in the deployment of AI models and create safety transparency requirements for AI companies. Her involvement drew criticism from some members of her party after the release of a discussion draft last month which included language that could limit state-level AI regulation, a policy that is toxic among many Democrats. U.S. Congress ( , AR: 1.50)The lawmakers have reportedly continued to make changes to their proposal, but early on it managed to get support from some AI safety advocates and AI industry insiders, which could translate into credibility for her leadership bid. “Taking on big problems and working across the aisle to solve them is what folks back home elected me to do,” Trahan told NOTUS in a statement. “Automation and offshoring took our jobs a generation ago ... Is this good politics? That's not really how I think about this work. But sure, good politics is being responsive to the people you represent.” “There's earth-shattering AI news practically every week. It's only going to get more frequent and more serious as these models get more powerful,” she . “Every member of Congress knows next week will bring something else just as alarming, if not worse. We're responding with the urgency this moment demands.” The specifics of how AI will change the future remain uncertain, but for people jumping on AI regulation, the uncertainty in the space is part of the appeal. “It's just the next frontier of policymaking, you know? You can't be here knowing that we're in an era of technological advances and, you know, still on a rotary phone,” Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-New York) told NOTUS. Candidates are also seeing the political opportunity around focusing on AI and staking their campaigns on it, with mixed results. In June, New York State Assembly member Alex Bores lost his bid in a Democratic primary to replace retiring Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-New York) after making AI regulation a central part of his campaign; AI-backed super PACs spent millions of dollars in the race both for and against him. Abdul El-Sayed, who’s running to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), released a populist AI policy agenda that includes public ownership of AI companies. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tennessee), who is running for governor in her state, has leaned heavily into AI regulation with a platform that would create protections for children using AI chatbots and safety standards for AI companies. Election Michigan ( , AR: 1.50)“AI, being arguably the most important technology of our time, both in the immediate future and long-term future, will continue to attract a lot of people. Many are trying to get in early at the ground floor,” Caleb Knapp, an AI safety lobbyist at the Alliance for Secure AI, told NOTUS. “A lot of folks both anticipate and are expecting AI to become much more of a kitchen-table issue because of how it impacts culture and the economy and everything in between,” he said. Other candidates who might be angling for a presidential to run in have also tried to shape the AI regulation debate. Vice President JD Vance, who has long advocated for a relaxed AI regulatory state, has recently advocated for stronger restrictions on the technology. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) has made AI populism central to his politics, advocating for strict regulations that would bar kids from using AI chatbots and force safety-compliance measures for AI companies. And Gavin Newsom, the Democratic governor of California who signed one of the first AI safety laws in the country, has said the U.S. government should own a stake in large AI companies. U.S. Congress ( , AR: 1.50)Some members of Congress whose districts house tech companies, and therefore whose work on AI regulation began years ago, argue that the public is pressuring more candidates to weigh in on the issue. “People are getting more and more questions by their constituents back home, so it's understandable that they're waking up to the issue,” Rep. Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat who represents parts of Silicon Valley, told NOTUS. And others say they welcome the input of more members of Congress. “It's a good thing that more of my colleagues are rolling up their sleeves on this issue,” Rep. Sam Liccardo, another Silicon Valley Democrat, told NOTUS. “Ambition in this regard can be positive because for too long, too few of us have been delving into the details.”

title: Democrats Fret Over DNC Woes but Don't Call for Martin to Go
author: Igor Bobic
summary: Few would criticize Chair Ken Martin directly, but they said the organization’s growing problems and fundraising issues were “alarming.”
content: Most Democrats are holding their fire on Martin for now, even as they acknowledge issues with the organization. (AP Photo/Erin Hooley) The internal turmoil at the Democratic National Committee has alarmed some top Democrats, who worry the national party organization is not well positioned to make gains in this year's midterms elections. “Obviously, the amount of money they're raising is alarming,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), a potential contender who has been stumping for Democratic candidates ahead of November. The DNC has been plagued by money woes since Kamala Harris’ loss in the presidential election. The committee even put its physical headquarters in Washington, D.C., up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, NOTUS reported over the weekend. Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC, is facing growing scrutiny. He was the subject of an internal human resources inquiry after throwing a cell phone in the direction of a young aide in early July, though the phone did not hit the staffer. Then there’s the promised and botched election autopsy Martin apologized for earlier this year, and many in the party blame Martin for the DNC’s paltry fundraising numbers. Most elected Democrats are holding their fire on Martin for now, even as they acknowledge issues with the organization under his leadership. “In a year like this, where there is such enthusiasm among rank-and-file Democratic voters and voters generally, you obviously want to have the strongest organizational footing possible, and so I'm concerned about that,” Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) told NOTUS. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada) said that she was “concerned” but believed it was “up to the DNC to decide how they want to handle.” Potential Democratic presidential contenders are so far staying mum. Representatives for Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “You know, I think they're struggling,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), another potential candidate, told NOTUS. “Like, Democrats have been struggling. We're still struggling. A year and a half later.” Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), who’s also been mentioned as a possible White House contender, said Martin started the job with some “tremendous challenges.” “He inherited a DNC that had tremendous problems,” Booker said. “He inherited a DNC that was in debt, and he inherited a party that does not have a central leader that we're all looking to.” But Booker did draw the line at Martin’s reported treatment of the junior aide. “You should not throw things at staff,” he said. But the drip, drip, drip of bad news about Martin did prompt some calls for him to step aside. “As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies,” Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-California) wrote in an X post on Sunday, calling on Martin to step down from his post. “We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward—and our children will not forgive—torpidity.” Rufus Gifford, a former aide to President Joe Biden who served as finance director for Barack Obama's presidential reelection campaign, said that under Martin’s leadership, the DNC is “spiraling towards irrelevance,” its staff is losing faith, and there is “no saving Martin’s chairmanship.” Shannon Watts, an author and political activist who served as a member of the DNC’s finance committee in , said she has heard from frustrated donors and lawmakers who have complained about Martin. “I've heard from very wealthy donors that they are done with the DNC and that they're sitting on donations and giving to individual candidates,” Watts told NOTUS. “And the Congress members who have reached out to me have just expressed frustration because they've brought ideas to Ken and he's just sort of strung them along and never acted on them.”

title: A Former Platner Aide Says Morris Katz Has ‘Main Character Energy’
author: Alex Roarty
summary: Katz “needs to take some time for reflection and consider if he is serving the Democratic Party well,” Genevieve McDonald said.
content: Robert F. Bukaty/AP Photo Democratic strategist Morris Katz’s public mea culpa last week for his role in promoting and protecting Graham Platner didn’t sit well with at least one person familiar with the inner workings of the former candidate’s political operation. “I don't believe him,” Genevieve McDonald, who served as the Platner campaign’s political director until resigning last October , said of Katz. “I mean, consultants shouldn't have main character energy. We have lost the plot when consultants are doing PR tours for themselves, for their own redemption, and that is what this felt like.” Katz — one of the people most responsible for helping elevate Platner to national stardom — appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show ” last week, saying he now believes some of the initial revelations about Platner, including his online history , should have been enough to end his Senate candidacy last year. Platner would go on to win the Democratic Senate primary in June, only to be forced out of the race weeks later after he was accused of sexual assault . It was a notable admission from Katz, a rising star in his own right after helping mastermind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s winning race in . But it rang hollow to McDonald, who said Democratic voters were robbed of a real primary because top members of Platner’s campaign dismissed the seriousness of the candidate’s actions and failed to properly vet rumors of other potential misdeeds. “I appreciate the recognition that those things should have been enough,” McDonald told NOTUS in an interview on Monday. “However, they weren't enough in the moment, and so it doesn't repair the damage.” Katz’s admission that he misjudged the situation is an effort to protect his career rather than a genuine admission of wrongdoing, she said, and another chance for him to build out a political status that she thinks has a tendency to overshadow his actual political clients. “We've gotten to a point where it seems as though I've read as much about Morris Katz as I have about the candidates that he works for,” she said. Katz and McDonald have publicly tussled before over the former political director’s decision to talk to The Wall Street Journal about allegations that Platner had sexted multiple women while he was married. During last week’s interview, Klein asked Katz whether he owed McDonald an apology, which he declined to give. Katz’s response angered McDonald, who says he and his company, the Fight Agency, have tried to disparage her and her professional reputation since she resigned last year. “I don’t need an apology from Morris Katz,” McDonald said. “I think Morris Katz needs to take some time for reflection and consider if he is serving the Democratic Party well.” McDonald’s remarks mark a continuation of one of the most damaging controversies in recent party history, one that forced Democrats to pick a new nominee only this past weekend against Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Platner’s eventual decision to leave the race also led to a round of finger-pointing at some of the officials who worked for him and for months defended him vigorously from criticism. “I do think the process was irresponsible,” McDonald said. “You know, it appears Fight Agency and Daniel Moraff were so eager to launch him and push out any potential competitors in the primary that they did not do their due diligence.” Katz declined to comment for this story. Katz said in the interview with Klein that Fight Agency “is not a vetting agency,” but that it’d be “fair” to critique him and the firm for “putting more pressure on people to ensure that the vetting process taking place is responsible and robust.” McDonald said she just hopes that everyone can move on. “The past several months have been deeply challenging to me, both, you know, personally and professionally,” she said. “I'm very much ready for the nation to move on from the Platner campaign.”

title: The Latino Voters in These Districts Could Decide the House Majority
author: Daniella Diaz
summary: Both parties are fighting over a handful of Latino-majority districts across five states.
content: Angelina Katsanis/Angelina Katsanis/POLITICO Republicans and Democrats are fighting over Latino voters in a handful of House districts, keenly aware that they could determine who wins the House majority. Those districts are places where President Donald Trump made significant gains in , but now polling shows they are frustrated with the stagnated economy. For Democrats, that’s an opportunity to try to win back some of the constituencies they lost in . “I think we need to continue to educate and inform Latino voters of the impacts of what this administration has done, and I think there’s a lot of buyer’s remorse,” said Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat in a tough bid for reelection in Texas’ 34th Congressional District. “We can’t be critical of people who voted for Trump,” said Gonzalez, whose district Trump won in . “We need to just have a very honest conversation that, 'Hey, a lot of us were duped and we’ve made a mistake, and we need to fix that mistake.’ And we do that by showing up this next election and vote to change the power in Congress and put the stop to some of the policies, the painful policies to Latino communities that have come out of this administration.” The congressional districts that both parties are paying attention to span five states: Texas’ 15th, 23rd, 28th 34th and 35th; Arizona’s 6th; California’s 22nd; New Mexico’s 2nd; and Colorado’s 8th. All are seats with majority-Latino electorates, and all are considered within reach for either party depending on how voting breaks. A spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democrats’ campaign arm, said the organization is working with candidates and incumbents to make clear to Latino voters in these battleground districts that a House Democratic majority would mean change to the economy. “The DCCC has been committed to earning the Latino vote since day one by investing early and aggressively to reach these voters. While House Republicans are focused on making life more expensive for hardworking Latino families, the DCCC is showing voters exactly how the Democratic majority will deliver for them,” Bridget Gonzalez, a spokesperson for DCCC, told NOTUS in a statement. But some Republican candidates are betting that pocketbook issues will help them keep the Latino voters they’ve gained in recent years in their coalition. “I believe that [high prices are] temporary, the spike that we’re seeing with the conflict we’re having in the Middle East is temporary, and to hang on, we’re going to get through it,” said Greg Cunningham, a Republican trying to unseat Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez in New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District. Cunningham, who is Hispanic, said his own background gives him an advantage in reading the mood of Latino voters in his district. “Because I am Hispanic and because I am pretty sensitive to what’s going on here in New Mexico, I am listening and I am addressing those concerns, and I feel confident that the way that we are speaking to Hispanic voters, being Hispanic myself, and the plan that we’re putting forth really addresses those things,” he said, referencing Republicans’ agenda in Congress. “I'm not worried about a huge swing coming back the other way and going away from the Republican Party, but I am addressing and acknowledging the needs of the people here.” Republican-aligned Latino organizers argue Democrats’ values don’t match what they see in these Latino communities. “We’re hearing a lot that Democrats have failed to give Latino voters something to vote for, that they’re focused more on who to vote against, and that is not good enough,” said Daniel Garza, president of the Libre Initiative, a conservative Latino advocacy group. An UnidosUS bipartisan poll from May suggested economic anxiety is the driving force behind voter sentiment, and that rising costs and inflation are shaping daily life for Hispanic families and fueling broader dissatisfaction with the country’s direction. Nearly 7 in 10 respondents (68%) said they believe the U.S. is on the wrong track, and two-thirds (66%) said Trump and congressional Republicans aren’t prioritizing economic improvement. Garza acknowledged that Latinos across the country are disappointed with the stagnating economy and said he recognizes that the Trump administration may have played a role in that. “I think Latinos, even though they’ve expressed certain disappointment, to be honest, with the economic results of the Trump administration thus far, I think a lot of us are seeing that Democrats ain’t offering viable pro-growth policy alternatives,” Garza said. With control of the House hanging on a small number of seats, both parties say the races in majority-Latino districts will be decided less by national messaging than by which side does the more convincing job of showing up. “Over the past , Hispanic voters have steadily moved toward the Republican Party because Republicans are earning their trust and delivering on the issues that matter most: safer neighborhoods, lower costs, lower taxes, secure borders and the opportunity to achieve the American Dream,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Christian Martinez told NOTUS in a statement. “Democrats spent decades taking Latino voters for granted. Republicans are showing up, listening and earning every vote."

title: Some Pennsylvania Democrats Are Skeptical of Washington’s Sway
author: Kadia Goba
summary: Democrats are trying to nationalize their affordability message, bringing big names to swing districts.
content: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, congressional candidate Bob Brooks and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries campaign in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, even as voters say they don’t like Washington politicians inserting themselves. Kadia Goba/NOTUS BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Some voters in Pennsylvania think Democrats have a Washington problem. Which is why it was a little confusing that Democrat Bob Brooks, a former firefighter backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, was hardly the main attraction at his own campaign rally Sunday. The congressional candidate addressed roughly attendees at the United Steelworkers Union Hall here. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and then House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries followed Brooks — rather than serving as the warm-up to their featured candidate. “I'm a little angry with the way they've inserted themselves in local races,” Ian Carlis of Upper Saucon Township told NOTUS. He said that in the Democratic primary, he’d supported Brooks’ opponent Ryan Crosswell . “Then the national people and Josh Shapiro inserted themselves in the race and turned it.” Democrats are trying to make every competitive House race focus on affordability. The lineup at the rally illustrated a broader strategy, and one that comes with potential risks: National leaders want to have a big imprint on local elections, even as voters express skepticism over Washington’s input. Brooks won a hotly contested primary in May for Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District and will now Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, who flipped the seat when Donald Trump was at the top of the ballot in . The evenly divided district is rated a toss-up, according to The Cook Political Report. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has suffered several losses in primaries it has weighed in on, underscoring some of the frustration voters have with a national thumb on the scale. Democrats aren’t the only ones who have a Washington problem. Four current House Republicans have lost their bids for statewide office this year. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who ran for governor of South Dakota, pointed to the attacks on career politicians as a “really potent argument” that he was unable to fight against. In Pennsylvania on Sunday, some locals came to get a sense of how in sync national politicians are with their own needs and concerns. “It's more so like, what are the headlines they're talking about?” said Meg Kane, 42, who described her party affiliation as “frustrated.” She also wanted to know “what they think are important” and how much that aligns with what voters see as important. Local politicians also acknowledged that their national counterparts haven't always been in lockstep with their community. “I think that Democrats at the national level have finally realized that we need to get the economic message out, and that really resonates here locally. Some of the other social issues need to take a back seat,” Lori McFarland, chair of the Lehigh County Democratic Committee, told NOTUS. Carmen Bell, the second vice chair of the county party, said there’s “always some massaging” that can be done to the national message. “Regardless of what the national message is, we could talk about being a big tent, but when we get into these small communities, we have to actually listen to the people who are there and say, ‘What's resonating with you?’” Jeffries’ message, unsurprisingly, centered on affordability. But he also made some day-one promises, days out from the November midterms. “We're going to cut down on corrupt price gouging. We're going to clean up the mess at the United States Supreme Court. And we're going to ban the president, vice president and members of Congress from trading stocks,” he said before vowing action on two additional topics that have motivated Democrats. “We can vote for an America that keeps our promise to our cherished seniors by protecting your Social Security and your Medicare. We can vote for America when we release all of the Epstein files.” Jeffries’ highly charged speech did get the most reaction from the audience. And Brooks said he didn't mind being the warm-up act, either. “I was very cool with introducing,” he said. McFarland, the local party chair, argued that it isn’t national Democrats who are hurting the party’s message. “I think the national level has gotten that message. I don't think these democratic socialists have,” she said. “And they're the ones that I think are throwing a wrench into a coordinated, unified message because they're more worried about some of those other social issues that we all embrace, but that's not our No. 1.”

title: Troy Jackson Will Officially Be Maine's Democratic Senate Nominee
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Jackson will have just under days to mount a new campaign against Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
content: Jackson is a progressive Democrat and a fifth-generation logger who initially entered politics as a Republican before being elected to the state House as an independent in . Robert F. Bukaty / AP Photo Former Maine state Sen. Troy Jackson handily won the state Democratic party’s support in a last-minute party convention vote on Saturday. He will take on Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November. Former candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the race on July 8 after facing allegations of sexual assault. A dozen candidates quickly launched campaigns after Platner’s announcement, though the field had whittled itself down to Jackson and Saundra Pelletier by Friday after a televised debate last week. The state Democratic party backed Jackson nearly unanimously via hundreds of delegates who were selected through a series of county meetings July 18-19. The deadline to submit the new nominee’s name is Monday. “The easy solution would have been to task a party committee with making that choice,” Democratic State Committee Chair Charles Dingman said in his opening remarks, prompting lighthearted groans from the audience. “Instead, we responded to the growing grassroots movement in our state to build power for ordinary working people.” Now, Jackson will have just under days to mount an entirely new campaign against Collins after having rallied with Platner several times during his gubernatorial run earlier this year. The incumbent senator has already characterized Jackson as a “Bernie bro” and a socialist. Before the nomination vote, Jackson acknowledged that many people had likely already supported “different candidates” before Saturday’s convention kicked off — declining, as all speakers had throughout the event, to say Platner’s name. He said the hope Democrats had built during the primaries does not belong to “any one campaign,” but rather a list of progressive ideals. His speech concentrated on praising the organizing power of working-class people and bashing votes Collins had made on Medicaid cuts or boosting spending on federal immigration agents. “For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is ‘concerned,’” Jackson said in his opening remarks, addressing a room full of attendees with “Troy Jackson for Maine” signs and state flags. “But concern does not lower the cost of groceries or gas,” he said. “Concern does not restore all of the rights she’s taken away. Maine does not need another six years of concern.” The first challenger to form an exploratory committee, Jackson emerged as the clear favorite throughout the replacement process after he dominated the initial delegate voting process. As it became clear that he would be the nominee, other prominent candidates like Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, former gubernatorial candidate Nirav Shah and former congressional candidate Jordan Wood dropped out of the running. Shah and Wood both endorsed Jackson. The only one to not drop out of the race ahead of Saturday was little-known candidate Pelletier, a biopharmaceuticals executive originally from Caribou. She garnered five delegate votes. Jackson is a progressive Democrat and a fifth-generation logger who initially entered politics as a Republican before being elected to the state House as an independent in . He switched to the Democratic Party two years later, eventually becoming the state Senate president from to . Jackson’s campaign announced this week that the candidate has raised more than $1 million since entering the race. But he will still have to contend with Collins’ $11 million war chest.

title: Who’s on First?
author: Marissa Martinez
content: Voters cast their ballots in the South Carolina Republican presidential primary in Columbia, South Carolina, on Feb. 24, . Michael Nigro/Sipa USA via AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 24, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST South Carolina will be the first up to vote in the Democratic primary, the DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee voted today . The state’s 26 votes beat out Nevada (19) and New Hampshire (4). The proposed presidential nomination calendar puts South Carolina’s primary on Jan. 22 and Super Tuesday on March 7. The dates will go to the DNC’s August meeting for ratification. “Now, instead of reacting to whomever’s left, we now get to shape what the field actually looks like, and I think that’s important,” said Jaime Harrison, a former DNC chair and South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “It’s a different role for us.” President Donald Trump (jokingly?) said the U.S. will put a “major tariff" on Mexico "because of the lettuce” that has been linked to illnesses across several states. “We’re going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke, all right? Which would you rather — the lettuce or the smoke?” Trump asked a reporter in the Oval Office. “I think I’ll take the smoke.” THE ADMINISTRATION FDA advisers with ties to the peptide industry recommended the government expand access to six unapproved peptides. The CDC’s website still cites a retracted study linking vaccines and autism. U.S. firefighting resources are already maxed out — and it’s only July. The National Guard signed a $ million housing contract for troops deployed in D.C. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will travel to D.C. next week to meet with Trump at the White House and attend Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral. THE HILL Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma) was months late in disclosing personal stock trades, together worth millions and conducted within a week of officially entering Congress in March. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of the Michigan primary . Republicans fret Trump could sink Rep. Mike Collins’ Georgia Senate run. As he battles terminal heart disease, Rep. Neal Dunn (R-Florida) is taking on Big Auto — hoping his Trump connection helps. THE STATES The U.S. has now recorded more cases of measles this year than any other year since the virus was declared eliminated in . BABY BLUES Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kate Nocera and Erik Schutz. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

title: Republicans Fret Trump Could Sink Mike Collins’ Georgia Senate Run
author: Ben T.N. Mause
summary: The president’s approval rating is underwater — could he bring down their candidate in one of the country’s most significant races?
content: Brynn Anderson/AP Republicans are wary that a visible President Donald Trump in Georgia could do more harm than good as they try to win back Sen. Jon Ossoff’s seat. Ossoff was widely seen as one of the most vulnerable Democrats up for reelection this year — particularly after Trump won the state in . But with Mike Collins’ campaign already in a rut, they’re worried Trump's underwater approval rating in the state could further sink his chances. “We're already seeing Ossoff at every turn trying to tie Collins to Trump,” a Republican operative, who requested anonymity due to his role on an active campaign, said. The operative that when Trump’s approval rating sits below 40%, as it does now , “there's headwinds there.” Collins’ general election campaign has struggled with scandal. One longtime staffer was fired after Collins' campaign account mocked a woman by referencing the fact that she said she was a victim of sexual assault; Collins called the post “ despicable and unauthorized .” Another official aide reportedly said in a group chat that he tried to leverage his position to get a Holocaust denier out of prison . And CNN reported that Collins’ son-in-law has a history of antisemitic statements and white nationalist ties. A Fox News poll released on July 1 showed Ossoff with 56% support from registered voters, while Collins trailed with 43%. An AARP poll released on Thursday showed Ossoff with a 9 percentage point advantage. Some Georgia Republicans feel that if Trump becomes more involved, Collins' chances will further erode. “Collins is gonna get smashed,” Eamon Keegan, a Republican pollster in Georgia, said. But, Keegan , Trump's dismal approval ratings would only exacerbate the issue — particularly if the president is unable to resolve the ongoing war in Iran, which continues to drag down Republicans' election prospects. “One-hundred percent,” said another operative when asked if he believed that Trump could hinder Republican efforts in Georgia. Trump visited Georgia on Wednesday for an official White House event in Marietta, an Atlanta suburb. Several state and federal officials joined him, including Kelly Loeffler, a former Georgia senator and head of the U.S. Small Business Administration, Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Billed as an official event about Trump savings accounts, much of his speech was about politics, including Collins. Collins, however, didn't attend. He posted a video to X before the event, saying he needed to be in Washington for House votes, and he knew “the president and the great leaders of Georgia could hold the line today until I get back home.” During his speech, Trump gave an extended shout-out to Collins. “Maybe the most important man in this room right now is not here. His name is Mike Collins, and he’s going to beat Pee-wee Herman,” Trump said, referring to Ossoff. “I said, ‘Mike, I’m sort of here because of you,’” Trump . “I said, ‘Mike, if you’re here I’m going to be extremely upset with you.’ Because he has to vote.” Sam Densmore, deputy communications director for Collins’ campaign, disputed in a statement that Collins’ campaign is in tenuous territory. “[Collins] is going to win this race because he has the business background, bipartisan record of results and positive vision to make life more affordable, safer, and better off for every person in this state, while Jon Ossoff has never had a real job, has gotten nothing accomplished and has a radical voting record,” Densmore said. The RNC and White House also disputed that Trump could hinder Collins. “Democrats can spin all the fake narratives they want, but Georgia is President Trump country, and Jon Ossoff’s days in the Senate are numbered,” RNC spokesperson Emma Hall told NOTUS in a statement that targeted Ossoff’s voting record in the Senate. White House spokesperson Olivia Wales called the president “the Republicans’ best messenger and motivator” to contrast his agenda with congressional Democrats’. Trump’s focus on the Georgia Senate race was welcome to Democrats and the Ossoff campaign. “If they could bring back Trump every week, we’d love it,” David Brand, a Georgia Democratic operative supporting the Ossoff campaign, told NOTUS. The Ossoff campaign has sought to amplify Collins’ relationship with Trump, with ads that feature Trump using Collins’ name at rallies and events over the years. Collins has aligned himself closely with Trump during his time in the House. “We welcome anything that brings Mike Collins out of hiding and forces him to address his latest scandal, including visits from an increasingly unpopular president who has driven up costs and cut access to health care with the help of his puppet, MAGA loyalist Mike Collins,” Valeria Rivadeneira-Crandell, an Ossoff campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. The counterargument among Republicans is that Trump’s knack for drawing low-propensity voters to the polls could provide a needed boost to Collins’ chances. The first Republican operative also said that Collins could benefit from the president’s ability to stoke the MAGA voting base. Trump carried a significant advantage with low-propensity Republican voters in Georgia in , particularly in rural areas . That advantage is harder to calculate compared to his poll numbers before Election Day, but it paid dividends in battleground states for him and his party in . While he is not on the ballot in , operatives hope his visible support for Collins in the state could still bolster turnout. “But Collins is going to wear the negative of it as well,” the first Republican operative said. During the Marietta event, the president avoided the topic that makes Georgia operatives sweat most: complaints about election integrity. Just last week, the president made a prime-time address on the topic — a speech that Georgia Republican operatives were relieved didn’t specifically mention their state — while his dedication to passing the SAVE America Act, a voter-ID bill, has derailed congressional Republicans’ agenda this year. Georgia has frequently been at the epicenter of Trump’s attacks on elections. After former President Joe Biden’s narrow victory in the state in , Trump demanded that Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger find him additional votes to flip the outcome. “Those issues are definitely net negatives for Republicans in the state,” the first Republican operative said. “A general election electorate doesn’t have much patience for that.” Other Georgia Republicans feel it shouldn't be overanalyzed. He's the president, his supporters are incredibly loyal, and his words and presence have wooed middle of the road people before , they argue. One Republican member of the Georgia congressional delegation said as much — with an essential caveat. “If he stays on message,” the Republican member said, then asked of the Marietta speech: “Did he?”

title: South Carolina Keeps the Top Spot on the 2028 Calendar
author: Elena Schneider
summary: The DNC narrowly voted to make it first over Nevada.
content: Erin Hooley/AP South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia — that’s the Democratic presidential primary lineup. Members of the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws panel voted Friday on its presidential nominating calendar, adding two additional states and preserving South Carolina’s first-in-the-nation status. The slate will now go to the DNC’s August meeting for ratification. The decision comes after days of last-minute negotiations and lobbying , as members privately debated the slate into the wee hours of Friday morning before their public meeting. The early-state selections will shape how presidential campaigns define their own strategies in , ahead of a wide-open and likely crowded primary contest. “Now, instead of reacting to whomever's left, we now get to shape what the field actually looks like, and I think that's important,” said Jaime Harrison, a former DNC chair and South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “It’s a different role for us.” South Carolina narrowly edged out Nevada for the first-place slot, after several impassioned speeches by boosters from both states. New Hampshire, which lost its first-in-the-nation primary status in , was a distant third. It’s not clear how New Hampshire will respond to the new calendar, given that its state law requires it to host the first-in-the-nation primary. In a statement after the vote, the New Hampshire Democratic Party reiterated that the DNC’s decision “does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party.” Several DNC members suggested New Hampshire could hold a party-run primary process, separate from its state-run primary. But it’s not clear whether New Hampshire Democrats would agree to that suggestion. “Among other issues, it would cost millions of dollars,” said one New Hampshire Democratic operative. “Is the DNC with all of their cash reserves going to pay for that?” The state’s delegation released a blistering statement, which said the DNC’s decision “is wrong for Democrats, wrong for New Hampshire, and wrong for the country.” When pressed by reporters on how the DNC would respond to New Hampshire, should state Democrats opt to ignore the DNC’s schedule, DNC Chair Ken Martin said they’d “have to cross that bridge when we get there,” adding that “we don't want to presume anything at this point” about how the state might respond. Martin went on to cite the tougher sanctions. “We laid the marker down. This is a calendar this party is actually going to protect. And unlike the past, it’s not going to be a wink and a nod, 'we’ll let you do what you want and you can get away with it,’” Martin said. “If they decided to do that, they know what the consequences are and we’ve been very clear.” By adding New Mexico and Virginia, the DNC is opening its early window even wider, further diversifying the regions and racial makeups of the states at the front of the contest. Nearly two decades ago, ahead of the presidential primary, the committee Nevada and South Carolina to the opening lineup in efforts to highlight the voices of more voters of color. Martin strongly supported the expansion, urging members on Thursday to add a fifth state that "needs to be from the South." It was only four years ago that Democrats upended their process ahead of the election. Then-President Joe Biden elevated South Carolina and pushed to eliminate Iowa, after its disastrous caucuses. New Hampshire ran an unsanctioned primary in , though the DNC stiffened its penalties on states and candidates that would participate in rogue contests in . Now, South Carolina will lead off the primary on Jan. 22, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1. The DNC scheduled New Hampshire for Feb. 8, though it’s not clear if it will follow that guidance. New Mexico would hold its primary on Feb. 15, followed by Michigan on Feb. 22 and Virginia on Feb. 29. Super Tuesday is March 7. South Carolina’s hold on the influential, first-place perch, as well as additional Southern representation, gained greater salience after the Supreme Court further gutted the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, several members said. Christale Spain, South Carolina’s Democratic Party chair, said her state provides “the most reliable read" on Black voter "sentiment." “The South is not the past, it is the future,” she . There was some disagreement among members over scheduling New Mexico ahead of Michigan, skipping the midwestern region. But given the speed at which states needed to move their dates, it’s unlikely Michigan could have changed its date, given a Republican-controlled state House. “Over the period of six weeks, every one of those states is going to get a lot of attention, and so, I don't think it matters where Michigan fell in that calendar, although I understand the concern,” Martin said. “When you think of all the other states and the number of delegates that will come out of Michigan and Virginia, compared to the other states, there's no way they're going to be overlooked by the process.” Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell said she’d back the calendar because she wanted to leave the meeting “united.” "What we are doing this time is building, as we vote for six states, building the story of the Democratic tent," Dingell said. “No one state should ever have a lock on going first." This story has been updated with additional reporting.

title: Democrats Want a DCCC Reset After Three High-Profile Losses
author: Oriana González
summary: House Democrats say the stinging losses could threaten everything from the DCCC’s ability to win in general elections to its ability to collect member dues.
content: Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Some House Democrats want the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee to rethink its primary strategy after its third high-profile loss this season. The election is far from over, but Democrats are already making specific demands for the DCCC to consider in future cycles: The committee needs to improve how it communicates with members, find ways to take more feedback and stop interfering in Democratic primaries. House Democrats have heavily criticized their campaign arm over its involvement in primaries during an election cycle that has been defined by anti-establishment sentiment. This week, DCCC-backed Marlene Galán-Woods lost the primary in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District to Amish Shah, the latest in a stinging set of losses for the group. “I think that it should certainly result in a pretty significant reevaluation of the strategy, the decision-making and the approach around primary endorsements and support,” one House Democrat, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, told NOTUS. “The leadership of DCCC has a fiduciary responsibility to reevaluate things, given the several notable examples of non-DCCC-supported candidates winning.” The lawmaker that members who pay dues to the DCCC “would have much greater confidence if we feel like there's a genuine reevaluation of this approach.” Other House Democrats echoed the sentiment. “There's no reason for us to put our thumb on the scale when you have a healthy field of many viable candidates,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told NOTUS. Ocasio-Cortez said the DCCC believes that “one type of candidate, or one type of approach, or one type of ideology is what will win in every swing seat in America.” Instead, she said, what the committee needs “to be doing is have an approach that is more tailored and is listening to every community.” Before Galán-Woods lost her race, Maine state Sen. Joe Baldacci lost to progressive Matt Dunlap in that state’s 2nd Congressional District, and California Assembly member Jasmeet Bains lost to another progressive, Randy Villegas , in the 22nd Congressional District. To some Democrats, these races illustrate breakdowns in the way the DCCC communicates with its members and allies. For example, the DCCC failed to inform the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC that it was adding Bains to its “Red to Blue” flagship candidate program before she won her primary, even though the committee had agreed to keep the CPC PAC informed about its decisions, according to multiple sources. The CPC PAC only found out about the DCCC’s move the day before it was announced — and only because Villegas heard about it in California and then called the progressive group, which was backing him. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), a CPC PAC co-chair, told NOTUS that the progressive group “immediately set up a call” with DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries after learning about their involvement. They “apologized profusely,” Jayapal said, and “said it never should have happened that way, it was an oversight.” “I think it begs the question of engaging in any Democratic primary,” Jayapal . “At a minimum, if they’re going to engage, we need to know if we have a candidate in that race, and we need to have a really thoughtful discussion about it.” The DCCC did add Villegas to its “Red to Blue” program after he defeated Bains in June, and a spokesperson for his campaign told NOTUS in a statement that since the primary, “DCCC has been extremely helpful in our shared goal of defeating David [Valadao].” But the miscommunication around the DCCC’s primary involvement came at a time when the CPC PAC “is mobilizing our members to give the most amount of DCCC dues we’ve ever given,” said Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Florida), another CPC PAC co-chair. If the DCCC doesn’t change its election strategy, it runs the risk of members not paying their dues to the committee. Dues are already being affected by redistricting, which has cut the number of members who pay the party’s campaign arm, as NOTUS first reported . “It makes you think, ‘I’m giving my dues to win in November, not for primaries,’ and so you’d think it could discourage members from giving dues,” Frost said. In a statement to NOTUS, DCCC communications director Courtney Rice defended the group’s involvement in the primaries. “When the DCCC decides to put a candidate in a competitive primary on Red to Blue, it is done after polling and research into different general election match-ups and discussions with Caucus members, local leaders, labor, and other stakeholders,” Rice said. “Given Democrats’ big tent, there is not always consensus, but the decisions are never made in a vacuum.” Under the leadership of DelBene, the DCCC has been involved in 10 contested primaries in and won seven. But the three losses have been high profile enough to take up much of the oxygen, and opened the group to attacks. Republicans' campaign arm put out a press release Wednesday calling DCCC’s most recent primary loss a “humiliation.” “I have complete and total confidence in Suzan DelBene, her leadership of the DCCC, and as a result of that leadership, I’m confident we’re going to take back control of the House of Representatives in November,” Jeffries said at a press conference Thursday when asked about DCCC’s involvement in primaries. Some members said there’s a desire in the caucus for the DCCC to create more avenues for members to provide feedback to the committee. Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-California) told NOTUS the DCCC needs to “listen to members from the states where candidates are running to really understand what's happening on the ground, to understand the local dynamics, and to either support the candidates that are best connected to the community, or to let the dynamics play out in the primary.” The DCCC, Kamlager-Dove said, holds regular “listening sessions” where members can keep the committee informed about “what they’re seeing, what’s happening” in their states. However, attendance does not appear to be mandatory; when asked if the DCCC seemed receptive to the feedback from those meetings, the lawmaker said, “I couldn't say because honestly, I don't join many of them. I stay focused on my own state and how I can be helpful to the ‘Red to Blue’ candidates that are running.” Some House Democrats are floating the idea of creating a committee that gives members more say over the DCCC’s decisions. Axios first reported lawmakers’ interest in a formal body to give that feedback. “It would not be a bad idea for us to really consider what leadership will look like that's beyond one person,” Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois), an outspoken critic of the DCCC’s involvement in primaries, told NOTUS. “A coordinated approach, a table convening of six or seven members of Congress, that represent different parts of this big tent that can help provide adequate, intentional perspectives as they're making their decision.” “One person can’t possibly have the breadth of understanding and the dynamics of what’s happening on the ground,” Ramirez . “I certainly want to talk about that as we're thinking about how we move next year.” The DCCC’s primary election strategy has also been criticized by Democratic candidates. Joe Caiazzo, a consultant for Dunlap’s campaign in Maine, told NOTUS that the DCCC “has made some decisions this cycle that have been far from ideal.” But, he , “as we march towards November, we all need to unify in an effort to win back the House, and I think that there are many competitive races around the country that the DCCC could absolutely come to the table and support to ensure that we are broadening the map.” While Dunlap painted himself as an anti-establishment candidate during his primary, Caiazzo said Dunlap is still interested in getting the DCCC’s backing — highlighting how the party’s support remains valuable for the general election. “We’re talking to the DCCC, we have a good relationship, and I expect that they will eventually move him to ‘Red to Blue,’” Caiazzo said. In a statement released after the Arizona race was called Wednesday, Shah similarly touted his win as a “grassroots victory where Arizona voters made their voices heard,” adding that the “status quo in Washington, D.C., is not working for Arizonans.” The day before, he’d told reporters that if he won the race, “I’m sure we’ll have a phone call, and I will speak to the DCCC and I hope that I can get their endorsement.” “Any Democratic candidate would want to be on the ‘Red to Blue’ list,” a source close to Shah’s campaign told NOTUS. It is unlikely that the DCCC will stop becoming involved in Democratic primaries. Dan Sena, the DCCC’s executive director in the cycle, pointed to the Maine Senate race , where Graham Platner stepped down as the Democratic nominee after being accused of sexual assault — which he denies — as an example of what happens when “you allow things to just happen without heavy input.” “You either get involved in the primaries and you win seven out of 10, or you don't get involved and you come up shy in the majority,” Sena said. “Either way, the Democrats have to ask themselves, wouldn't you rather have the gavels in your hand?"

title: Democrats Lock Back In on Maine
author: Alex Roarty, Igor Bobic, Christa Dutton
summary: Whether they can win is an open question.
content: Troy Jackson’s nomination would cap what has been one of the party’s most tumultuous primary processes in recent memory. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Maine Democrats are on track to select a new Senate candidate later this week. Their likely pick? A former state lawmaker who lost the party’s recent gubernatorial primary, has no federal political experience and has only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent. Most party leaders — including Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, who said she’s “very optimistic that we will win Maine” — say they haven’t felt this good about the race in months. “I think it's going to be hotly contested, but I think it's very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. On Saturday, Democrats in Maine are expected to pick Troy Jackson as their Senate nominee against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, less than a month after the party’s former nominee, Graham Platner, was accused of sexual assault , the latest in a string of controversies he throughout his campaign. Jackson’s nomination would cap what has been one of the party’s most tumultuous primary processes in recent memory, a series of mishaps that could — and is widely expected to — jeopardize the Democrats’ ability to defeat Collins. That’s especially the case with a candidate like Jackson, who even allies acknowledge is an underwhelming orator with little time to build out a campaign infrastructure. But Democrats in Washington and Maine insist they think he’s still in a better position than Platner, who, despite denying the allegations, carried baggage into the race that party strategists feared would undermine his electability. “Turbulence is never the friend of politics, but I think there’s plenty of time,” Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado told NOTUS. “There's some history, and people have done attack ads, and you know, have in some way vetted him a little more thoroughly than some candidates get.” The sentiment reflects just how anxious many Democrats — especially moderates — had become about Platner’s chances against Collins, so much so that they are relieved to throw in with a candidate few national Democrats know well. More importantly, it indicates that Democrats remain committed to trying to win the Senate race despite everything that has happened there. Democrats likely need to win the race in Maine — the only Senate seat held by a Republican in a state won by Kamala Harris in that is up for grabs this year — to have a chance at flipping majority control of the Senate. Platner’s baggage had made his path to victory “very likely insurmountable,” said Lauren French, spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democrats. “Now we have the opportunity to refocus this conversation where it should be, which is Susan Collins,” she said. National Democrats have pointedly stayed out of the race to replace Platner. Asked if he would support Jackson, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer expressed confidence in defeating Collins, a formidable and well-funded incumbent who is seeking her sixth term in Washington. “We're going to win Maine. Susan Collins is going to lose, and we are going to take back the Senate,” Schumer told NOTUS. “People in Maine don't like Donald Trump, and they don't like that Susan Collins always votes with him.” Jackson told The New York Times this week that he would not support Schumer being the party’s leader in the Senate. He was also wary of receiving support from the minority leader. “I’d have to find out what that entailed,” Jackson told the New York Times. “I mean, if his help comes, absolutely no strings, I would say, you know, possibly. There’d have to be no strings.” Jackson’s team did not comment for this article. Among voters, Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, appears to start the race in a competitive position. He edged out Collins by 3 percentage points in a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire, and, unlike Collins, he is viewed quite favorably by Maine voters. The poll’s margin of error is 2.8 percentage points. But that could change with the onslaught of Republican attacks waiting for him in the general election. Republicans have already begun drawing parallels between Platner and Jackson. They’ve pointed to Jackson’s reported history of growing angry in meetings, and attacked him for views Republicans have cast as extreme, like support for a single-payer health care system. “He's had quite a transformation over the years in his political views, but now seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” Collins told NBC News , referring to Jackson’s conservative positions on social issues, like abortion, more than a ago. Democrats acknowledge that Maine will still be a difficult place for Democrats to win, but President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and rising costs give the party a chance to make a compelling case. “While the Democrats will have a new candidate by the end of this weekend, the fundamental motivation around winning the Senate race hasn't changed at all,” said Emily Cain, a Democratic strategist in Maine. Platner’s departure is a second chance at the seat without the distraction of controversy, some Democrats argue. An open question is whether Jackson can raise the money needed to beat Collins, who had nearly $11 million in the bank at the end of June. He’s raised $1 million in the less than two weeks since he entered the race, Politico reported . “All 49 states of Democratic Party activists and donors — small donors and large donors — are now all eyes on Maine,” said Democratic strategist Mike Trujillo. One Democratic donor who gave the largest contribution they could to Graham Platner told NOTUS they plan to give the maximum donation to the new candidate as well. “Maine is Maine,” the donor said. “My priority is winning in the general in every state where we're competitive, and that definitely includes Maine. No matter who's running, I'm sold.” Still, other Democrats are less than certain about their chances of flipping Maine’s Senate seat after Platner’s collapse and the rushed process for selecting his replacement. “They had to come up with somebody, and they did,” Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono said of Maine Democrats’ likely nomination of Jackson. Asked if he had a better shot than Platner, Hirono burst into laughter. “Let's just say that we have a candidate,” she said.

title: Mark Sanford Jumps Into Crowded Race for Lindsey Graham’s Senate Seat
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Graham’s sister is running. So are Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman.
content: Republican presidential candidate Mark Sanford takes part in a political forum in Nashville, Tennessee. (AP Photo/Mark Humphrey) Mark Sanford, the former congressman and governor of South Carolina, announced Thursday that he will run for the Senate seat held until recently by the late Lindsey Graham. “Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can't sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every days,” Sanford said in a post on X. “I've spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I'm running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.” The post was accompanied by a video of Sanford saying Graham’s death is a reminder of “how short and precious life is.” Graham’s seat is temporarily being filled by his sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve out his term by Gov. Henry McMaster. She also announced this week that she would campaign for a full term, joining a crowded primary field that also includes Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman. The primary is set for Aug. 11. Sanford was South Carolina’s governor from to , and he represented the 1st Congressional District twice, between and and between and .

title: States Are in a ‘Fight to the Death’ for the Democratic Primary Calendar’s Top Spot
author: Elena Schneider
summary: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan are expected to be early states, according to interviews with DNC members.
content: South Carolina held the first Democratic presidential primary in the cycle. Mike Stewart/AP A last-minute, aggressive lobbying campaign is underway over the phone and through the media, as Democrats from a handful of states jockey to lead off the presidential nominating calendar. South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain appeared on Roland Martin’s YouTube show Monday to declare , “we’re first, and we maintain that.” At a private reception Wednesday night, Democratic National Committee members mingled with Nevada Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto, while New Hampshire boosters reached DNC members with one-on-one phone calls. The all-out push will culminate at the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee meeting later this week. The 49-person panel is charged with setting the early-state window, ahead of what’s expected to be a wide-open and unwieldy Democratic presidential primary . Ahead of Friday’s meeting, tensions are already running high. “It’s going to be a bloodbath,” said one of the members, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Most states represented have at least one or two members on the committee, and I think they’re all going to fight to the death for this.” Interviews with nearly a dozen DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee members revealed some certainty about which states will likely be inside the early window — South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan — but not necessarily the order. South Carolina and Nevada appear to be front-runners for the first spot over New Hampshire, according to these interviews. Members aren’t sure if they’ll add a fifth state to the slate, though if they do, New Mexico and Virginia lead that discussion. “I believe South Carolina is in a good position, and our vote count is good. We made the case in May to be first, and we’ve been talking to members ever since then,” said Spain, the South Carolina party chair. “I believe we have the votes, but I think Nevada is the next-highest vote-getter.” Setting the presidential primary calendar is one of the DNC’s most consequential tasks ahead of the presidential primary, and the Rules and Bylaws Committee must contend with its own internal politics over which states to elevate or demote — triggering debates over racial diversity and representation. Members said they hoped to recommend a slate by Friday and send it to a full vote of the DNC at their meeting in Austin, Texas, next month. At least a few members are pushing to delay the decision until after the upcoming midterms, though others insist they must wrap it up as soon as possible. “We need to rip the Band-aid off,” said a second rules committee member. “We’re going to make people mad no matter what, and it’s not going to get any easier after the midterms.” Reordering the slate also made people mad in , when then-President Joe Biden eliminated Iowa as an early state, elevated South Carolina to first and Michigan. The party came under pressure to shake up its calendar after the presidential primaries, when technical difficulties upended the Iowa caucuses and candidates criticized Iowa and New Hampshire for their lack of racial diversity. “There’s real ramifications, long-term ramifications, if we don’t make the right decision on the calendar,” said Jaime Harrison, the former DNC chairman who also served as the South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “Black voters are paying very close attention to this.” Jim Clyburn AP- ( , AR: 1.50)South Carolina’s boosters are making their pitch publicly and privately, sharpened by the Supreme Court’s decision to further gut the Voting Rights Act this spring. They also argue that South Carolina’s relatively cheap media market, compactness and majority-Black primary electorate will be the best proving ground for future presidential candidates. In a letter to DNC members and obtained by NOTUS, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) warned in May that it would be a “profound mistake for our Party to retreat” from Black voters and Southern states in the nominating process, adding that South Carolina’s role in the nominating process “has been about ensuring that candidates engage deeply with the diverse coalition.” Officials from Nevada are also campaigning aggressively to be first. They, too, leaned into their state’s racial diversity, particularly its Latino population. Over the last year, Nevada’s elected officials have made personal appeals to DNC members and frequently hosted events to promote the state. More than 20 Latino leaders and groups signed on to a letter Wednesday, urging members to elevate Nevada in order to “reverse” the trend of losing Latino voters to Republicans. “Choosing Nevada to go first is a strategic decision, as we work to win back the coalition we need to win back the White House in ‘28,” said Daniele Monroe-Moreno, the Nevada Democratic Party chair. “That coalition of rebuilding has to be a broad coalition, which has to include Black voters, Asian voters.” Some members have suggested that the battle for first may include horse-trading on a fifth addition to the line-up. If Nevada were selected to go first, then members may add Virginia, putting two Southern states in the early window. And if South Carolina were to go first, then they could add New Mexico, another western state with strong Latino representation. But DNC members have raised concerns about Nevada’s mail-in balloting, which could delay the results of the primary. Monroe-Moreno said the Nevada secretary of state’s office is “implementing adjustments and improvements” to its mail-in ballot counting. “It may take a little more counting than another state,” she said. “I want to make sure that everyone's votes are counted.” Without a Democrat in the White House, the 49-person committee is charged with making its own decision on the calendar. DNC Chair Ken Martin has largely remained hands-off, but that could change over the next few days, the committee members said. “I don’t think Ken needs any more headaches than he’s already got,” said one Democratic operative involved in the calendar process and granted anonymity to speak candidly. The chaos of selecting a new calendar comes during a rocky year for the DNC. Martin has questions over his leadership after presiding over an incomplete autopsy of the election and staring down serious fundraising challenges. The Republican National Committee is sitting on $ million in cash, while the DNC holds $16.3 million with $18.5 million in debts, according to the most recent Federal Elections Commission filings. It’s not clear whether states or candidates will follow the DNC’s decision on the primary calendar, given the committee’s weakened position. At least three potential Democratic presidential candidates told NOTUS last month they were considering skipping the DNC’s debate schedule, while Iowa’s backers have already said they are seriously considering hosting a rogue caucus. Last month, the DNC instituted stiffer penalties if a state jumps the line to head off these challenges. For example, if a candidate campaigns in a rogue contest, they’ll sacrifice debate stage access and the state will lose its delegates at the party’s convention. New Hampshire already tested those boundaries in , when it ran its own unsanctioned primary after Biden demoted the state from its first-in-the-nation status. The state is still expected to be in the early window, but several DNC members said “New Hampshire is a very distant third” behind Nevada and South Carolina for first. “They just don’t have the votes,” a third DNC member said.
