New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Raymond Buckley defended the state’s position, arguing in a statement that “anyone who suggests New Hampshire isn’t in a strong position is mistaken.” “We’ve been focused on having conversations one-on-one with committee members, and we’re encouraged by how those have been going,” Buckley continued. “New Hampshire serves as a critical testing ground for whether candidates can attract independent voters — an issue that couldn’t be more pressing for the Democratic Party nationally.”

title: Darline Graham? Republicans Don’t Know Her.
author: Igor Bobic, Al Weaver, Oriana González
summary: Graham decided to run for a full Senate term after being appointed to the seat after her brother’s death, but people are still learning what she stands for.
content: Republican senators are still getting to know Sen. Darline Graham, who cast her first votes in the Senate this week after a whirlwind appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. Tom Williams/AP Darline Graham made it official that she wants to run for a full term to represent South Carolina in the Senate. But unlike her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly earlier this month, few people know where she stands on most issues. President Donald Trump and top Senate Republicans quickly endorsed Darline Graham to become South Carolina’s next full-term Republican senator. But few Republican lawmakers personally know Graham, who was appointed to the seat just last week. The low profile could put Graham, a longtime disability advocate who previously served on the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, at a disadvantage, even with Trump’s backing effectively making her the frontrunner in next month’s special election. “These are people with legislative records that they can point to, that are proven to say, ‘Hey, prices are up, we can bring prices down if we do X, Y and Z. Here’s what I’ve done in the past,’” CJ Westfall, chair of the Dorchester County Republican Party, told NOTUS. Darline is “somebody that’s unproven and just has the stamp of approval by the president. I don’t think that’s the end-all, be-all for South Carolina,” Westfall . As a county party chair, he cannot endorse any candidate in the race. Republican senators are still getting to know Graham, who cast her first votes in the Senate this week after a whirlwind appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. Initially, many believed she would serve as a caretaker for the last six months of her brother’s term, with several South Carolina Republicans expressing interest in the job, until a surprise Trump endorsement for a full six-year term upended the race. “She certainly seems competent from the little bit I’ve seen. But competence isn't even a requirement in this job, as I can demonstrate and prove,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) joked to NOTUS. “That’s what primaries are for — to discover those things,” he . “It’s a very short time frame to prepare. Others who are in the business of politics may have that edge. On the other hand, her answers will be very instructive.” Graham doesn’t have long to convince South Carolina voters to keep her in Washington. The state will hold a special election on Aug. 11, giving her roughly two weeks to introduce herself to voters after her brother’s funeral plans take place next week. The winner will compete against Democrat Annie Andrews in the November election. Trump’s endorsement of Graham isn’t scaring off rivals from challenging her. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry have hopped into the race, along with businessman Mark Lynch . Former Gov. Mark Sanford and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette are expected to throw their hats in the ring. Evette, notably, came up short in her bid for governor last month despite having Trump’s endorsement, underscoring that Graham’s campaign for Senate is no sure thing. “Each candidate has a strength,” Tyson Grinstead, chair of the Richland County GOP and a former campaign adviser to Lindsey Graham, told NOTUS. “Darline’s a newcomer but she has Sen. Graham’s campaign and she's got Sen. Graham's structure in place to help her, and so I think that kind of evens out with some of the other candidates.” “Russell Fry’s definitely got longstanding relationships. Ralph Norman has just come out of the governor’s race,” Grinstead, who cannot endorse a candidate as a county party chair. “And then you’ve got Darline with Sen. Graham’s campaign, which was one of the only statewide campaigns that had a lot of money spent on it.” Fry and Norman are pushing for a debate in Charleston on Aug. 4, the day before early voting starts. While the details are still being worked out, Norman suggested that’s where voters will have the opportunity to “find out” more about Graham, who hasn’t yet indicated whether she will participate. Graham did give a hint about her priorities as senator in a recent interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity indicating she may focus more on domestic rather than foreign policy. “I used to see him on the talk shows,” she said of her brother. “I would watch him, and I’d be like, ‘Lindsey, are you just talking about national security all the time?’ And I understand that’s important. Protecting our borders, national security, absolutely. I said, ‘But talk about also what matters to the average person. The price of groceries, the price of gas, health care, insurance, those kind of things.’ That’s what I’m worried about,’” Graham said. She has moved to quickly align herself with Trump’s key legislative priority, a sweeping bill that would change some voting rules, known as the SAVE America Act. And she has the support of top Senate Republicans who immediately backed her campaign, including Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a staunch defense hawk. Senate Republicans are also hoping that Graham’s support for a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill, which her brother long advocated for, will help get the legislation across the finish line in Congress and to Trump’s desk. “Senator Darline Graham has worked for the people of South Carolina for almost 30 years, and now the U.S. Senate is an extension of that service. God calls on ordinary people to do extraordinary things, and it’s clear she has met the moment,” said Taylor Reidy, a Graham spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement. Touting her work so far, Reidy pointed to her votes to confirm judges and the president’s nominees and , “Sen. Darline Graham was sworn in eight days ago and in that time alone, she has led the introduction of major sanctions legislation, cosponsored the SAVE America Act and a host of pro-life bills. Still, policy groups have yet to decide on Graham’s qualifications. Students for Life America, a prominent anti-abortion group, has yet to decide whether it will endorse Graham in the primary, with a spokesperson telling NOTUS on Tuesday that the group is still evaluating her positions. The late senator was an outspoken anti-abortion ally in Congress, and SFLA backed some of his efforts to restrict abortion. Graham is working quickly to shore up support on the right. On Wednesday, she announced she is co-sponsoring more than a half-dozen anti-abortion rights bills, including the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act. Despite the questions about her background, Graham does have a number of things working in her favor. Due in large part to her brother and to Trump, she has high name recognition that others running may not enjoy. “It’s huge statewide. It’ll be low turnout so name recognition will be an even bigger factor,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), a member of Republican leadership who has endorsed Graham. One South Carolina Republican strategist who spoke to Graham recently said she wants to chart her own path in the Senate. “True to Graham fashion, she wants to own her own lane. And it’s not Lindsey’s lane,” the strategist told NOTUS. Republicans are expecting Graham to begin campaigning in earnest after her brother’s funeral services on July 28. The late senator died at age 71 from a rupture of his aorta due to a hardening of his arteries, according to a preliminary analysis by the D.C. medical examiner. “I know I’m a hard worker. I learned that from Lindsey,” Graham said in her interview with Hannity. “I feel like I can do it. I feel an inner peace about it. Will it be difficult? Yes. Absolutely.” Capito conceded that Graham could a challenge getting her message out in such a short time frame, but indicated she should be able to gather enough financial support. “I think she will have a challenge getting her own voice out, and I don’t know if that’s a choice she’s going to make,” Capito said. “Is it her own voice, or is it just ‘I’m going to be the voice of my brother’ plus?”

title: Trump Celebrates After Election Deniers Sweep Arizona’s Republican Primaries
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: Some of the Republican nominees would have critical roles in overseeing the election if they were to win in November.
content: Andy Biggs will incumbent Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs in November. Ross D. Franklin/AP President Donald Trump claimed victory after his favored candidates — including deniers of the election results — won their Republican primaries in Arizona on Tuesday. At the forefront of Tuesday’s winners was Rep. Andy Biggs, the former chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, who will be the Republican nominee for governor after besting his colleague, moderate conservative Rep. David Schweikert. Biggs, a Trump ally, voted not to certify results of the election. Biggs will incumbent Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, in November’s general election. “MAGA candidates won everything last night in Arizona, a complete sweep!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social in all capital letters. “I won Arizona 18 months ago. The Dumocrats are dumbfounded. After decades, Arizona is becoming a Republican state.” If Trump’s preferred candidates prevail in November, they could play key roles in overseeing and certifying the election. And Biggs isn’t the only newly minted nominee who questioned the results in , when Trump lost the state. The second Trump administration has targeted Arizona’s Maricopa County as part of its efforts to investigate long-debunked claims that the election was rigged. The FBI subpoenaed election records from the county in March, which were handed over by state Senate President Warren Petersen. Petersen received the Republican nomination on Tuesday for attorney general. He previously assisted in launching a controversial audit of the election overseen by Cyber Ninjas, a Trump-friendly cybersecurity company. The audit found that former President Joe Biden won the election. State Rep. Alexander Kolodin secured the Republican nomination for secretary of state, the state’s top election official. Kolodin was disciplined in by the State Bar of Arizona for his role in various lawsuits attempting to overturn the election. Trump praised Petersen and Kolodin during a Turning Point USA rally in April, stating that they would help achieve his plans of “building a red wall.” Other Trump-backed candidates who won congressional primaries on Tuesday include Mark Lamb , who has been accused of sexual misconduct, which he has denied. Former NFL kicker Jay Feely and Rep. Juan Ciscomani also won their primaries for the House.

title: Wisconsin Democrats Ask Elections Commission to Allow Voters to Recast Absentee Ballots
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: The bipartisan panel blocked the ability to revote earlier this month after Democrat Missy Hughes exited the governor’s race.
content: Over 80, ballots have already been submitted, but the party argues many of these votes are going to waste due to candidates dropping or reentering the race. Morry Gash/AP Photo Wisconsin’s gubernatorial candidates keep shuffling before next month’s primary. Now, the state Democratic party is requesting Wisconsin’s elections panel allow voters who already cast an absentee ballot to vote again. After thousands of Wisconsinites had already submitted their absentee ballots ahead of the Aug. 11 primary, Democrats’ candidate slate shifted twice within days. Front-runner Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez ended her campaign last Friday. A day later, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley rejoined the race a week after he suspended his campaign, reentering with current Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement. Earlier this month, the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission blocked the ability to revote if a candidate drops out after a different Democrat, Missy Hughes, exited the governor’s race in June. Because of that ruling, Rodriguez voters and people who would have backed Crowley may have lost their chance to vote for a candidate who will actually be in the running through August, the state Democratic party argues. Over 80, ballots have already been submitted, but the party argues many of these votes are going to waste due to candidates dropping or reentering the race. The commission voted 4-2 on July 9 to issue the guidance limiting voters’ ability to “spoil” their ballots and excluded circumstances like someone deciding to vote for another candidate. Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker said “some voters will not be able to truly participate in our Democratic primary process” if the guidance is not reversed to allow new absentee ballots. “Allowing voters to spoil and recast their ballots was standard practice in Wisconsin prior to attempts by Republicans to file frivolous lawsuits to muddy the waters,” Remiker said in a statement . The state Democratic Party argues the new guidance should be rescinded because it reverses the commission’s own rule that was in place in . It is also inconsistent with a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that stated voting rules should not be changed close to an election, they said. In the past, Wisconsin voters were able to cancel submitted ballots and then request a new one up to three times, for any reason. But in October , a county circuit judge ruled that this “ballot spoiling” practice was illegal. The 2nd District Court of Appeals reversed the ruling in February, finding that the lawsuit was not properly served.

title: Cleo Fields Won’t Seek Reelection After Redistricting in Louisiana
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Fields’ district was at the center of the Supreme Court’s decision that largely eliminated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of .
content: “I tell people all the time, the issue is not whether or not I serve another day in Congress,” Fields said. “The issue is whether or not a person like me will have the opportunity to serve in Congress." Tom Williams/AP Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields — whose Louisiana district was at the center of the Supreme Court decision gutting a key part of the Voting Rights Act — announced Tuesday that he will not seek reelection and will instead run for his old state Senate seat. Fields represents the 6th Congressional District, a majority-Black district that encompasses part of Baton Rouge and currently leans Democrat. After the Supreme Court declared the district’s existence an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander,” Louisiana lawmakers passed a new congressional map that eliminated Fields’ district to heavily favor Republicans. The new lines left intact only one of the two majority-Black districts in the state ahead of the midterms. “After a great deal of prayer and reflection, I have decided not to seek re-election to Congress, in the 6th District or any other district in Louisiana,” Fields said in a statement . “I feel my calling to serve the people is better put to use back home than here in D.C., and I intend to answer that call.” The National Republican Congressional Committee announced earlier this week that it was targeting his district to flip from blue to red. “I tell people all the time, the issue is not whether or not I serve another day in Congress,” Fields told NOTUS in May . “The issue is whether or not a person like me will have the opportunity to serve in Congress. And that’s the big focus.” He will now look to fill the unexpired term of the late state Sen. Larry Selders, a Democrat from Baton Rouge who died July 7.

title: Democrats Ditch Their Old Pick in a Competitive Arizona Seat
author: Christa Dutton
summary: The DCCC is supporting Marlene Galán-Woods in her primary, even though she’s running against Amish Shah, the candidate it backed in the general election.
content: Mike Stewart/AP Voters in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District are looking at something of a rematch in their Democratic primary. Unlike in , when House Democrats’ campaign arm let the race play out, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now has a clear preference. The group’s pick in the primary is Marlene Galán-Woods, a former broadcast journalist who has never held public office, was registered as a Republican until and came in third when she ran in . On Tuesday, she’ll off against several Democrats, including Amish Shah, an emergency-room physician and former state legislator who beat her in the primary in and competed in the general election with the DCCC’s backing. Shah narrowly lost to Republican Rep. David Schweikert in . This year, the DCCC hopes Democrats in the district will choose not to give Shah a do-over, but to go in a new direction with Galán-Woods. While the DCCC put Shah on its Red to Blue list in the general election but did not intervene in that year’s primary, now it’s Galán-Woods who’s in the DCCC’s Red to Blue program. “She’s on paper a better fit, but you're dealing with the rather uncomfortable question that she already lost a primary to him,” said a Democratic strategist and DCCC alum who has worked on previous races in the district. “So, was it a resource problem? Was there something else that has changed? No doubt that DCCC has analyzed this, weighed all of this, and still come to the conclusion that intervention enhances their odds of picking up a seat.” The candidates have few ideological differences and are running in the country’s only open toss-up seat, since Schweikert is running for governor. The Democratic race is one of several primaries the DCCC has weighed in on, along with contests in Pennsylvania and Texas battleground districts. This type of intervention in competitive primaries has prompted backlash from some corners of the party, who say the committee should let voters decide rather than putting its thumb on the scale. “It's unfair because out of respect to him for winning such a competitive primary, I think they should have either stayed out or at least waited until after the primary,” said Arizona state Sen. Flavio Bravo, who endorsed Shah. So far this year, most of the DCCC’s picks have succeeded in their primary races, but two candidates have lost: state Sen. Joe Baldacci in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District and Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains in California’s 22nd Congressional District. Those losses left some Democrats questioning the committee's use of resources and cheering the defeat of the establishment. This Arizona race has become another test for the DCCC in a primary that lacks the progressive-versus-pragmatic dynamic that has defined other races. “Unless there is a clear and obvious reason, the DCCC should not intervene in Democratic primaries, including the race in AZ-01,” said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) in a statement to NOTUS. “These resources should be focused on flipping this seat in November and winning back the House majority.” Shah was frustrated about the DCCC’s decision to weigh in. “I think they got it wrong,” he told NOTUS. “I think the Democratic Party voters do not want to see meddling from D.C. here in our district.” If he pulls off a win, he said he will “work with anybody and everybody, including the DCCC, to make sure that we do everything we can to stop this guy in the White House.” The DCCC determined that Galán-Woods has “undeniable momentum, a broad coalition, and strong fundraising,” a spokesperson said. “This designation signifies that we believe this candidate — and this campaign — are the one best positioned to flip the Republican-held district,” the spokesperson said. Galán-Woods has accumulated support from other major players in the party. She received a powerful endorsement from Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly in the final days before the primary. She also has the backing of several national Democratic groups including Planned Parenthood Action Fund, EMILYs List, the Bench and BOLD PAC. She’s proved herself to be an effective fundraiser, raising about $2.1 million as of July 1, according to Federal Election Commission filings, compared to Shah’s $1.3 million . She also has allies spending mountains of money on her behalf, far outpacing the spending on Shah’s behalf. Galán-Woods said she decided to run again because Shah, who lost the general election by 4 percentage points, underperformed Kamala Harris and Ruben Gallego in ’s presidential and Senate contests. When asked about the DCCC’s backing, Galán-Woods said she’s most proud of her local backing. “I'm happy to have the support, but I'll be honest with you, here in the district, people aren't talking about it,” she said. “People are talking about the issues that keep them up at night, and most importantly, how do we win? How do we win in November?” There’s been limited polling in the primary. HighGround, a public affairs firm that has worked on Republican campaigns, showed Shah up by 22 percentage points in a February poll. Most voters in the district are registered Republicans, but voters who did not select a party at all outnumber Democrats. “This district is a really good bellwether for how the country's going,” said Eric Chalmers, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not involved in the race. “The independents who live in this district, they went one way for three cycles voting for Dems, and then last cycle, it was almost a complete .” Some Democrats see Galán-Woods — who grew up in a Republican household with parents who emigrated from Cuba and who is the widow of Grant Woods, the former Republican state attorney general and chief of staff to John McCain — as just the right kind of Democrat to win over independents. “The appeal of a different candidate who's got a lot of support from the business community and a lot of the ‘Republican-lites’ or kind of McCain-Republican types out in CD 1, which makes up a lot of that district, led to the appeal of wanting to try Marlene,” Chalmers said. Shah, meanwhile, is pitching himself as an experienced politician. He served in the statehouse for three terms and ran in the general election before, while Galán-Woods lacks public office experience. He is known for his shoeleather campaign style and touts that he’s knocked on 28, doors in the district. But Arizona strategists said he will have to scale it up. “On paper he's just a normie Democrat with a really interesting, compelling background and compelling voice,” said DJ Quinlan, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not working on the race. “In practice on the campaign trail, he has a number of unique views.” Quinlan said one of Shah’s challenges is his apparent dislike of negative campaigning and TV ads. “He seems to have an aversion to the sort of campaign tactics that you need to be successful as you scale from a legislative race to a congressional race,” he said. Shah, however, calls that a mischaracterization. He pointed to his fundraising numbers and television ads to show that his last campaign did put up a congressional-level fight. Door-knocking helps the campaign keep an ear to the ground, he said. “We understood in that there's no way that you could run a door-knocking campaign over the course of six or eight weeks directed at , people,” Shah said. “That was nowhere in my arguments. We ran a mass communication campaign that involved mailers, that involved TV ads, that involved digital, all at the direction of the DCCC during that cycle.” The primary’s winner will advance to either former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik, business executive John Trobough, or the Trump-endorsed former NFL kicker Jay Feely.

title: Will Incoming Progressives Give Hakeem Jeffries Their Support?
author: Daniella Diaz
summary: Brad Lander backed his New York colleague but warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.”
content: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP New York’s Brad Lander said he would support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker if Democrats win back the House — an olive branch from a candidate expected to become one of Congress’ highest-profile progressives. Lander and several likely members of Congress — including Melat Kiros, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez and Chris Rabb — are part of a group of uber-progressive Democrats, many aligned with the leftist Democratic Socialists of America, who recently won competitive primaries in safe blue districts. The majority of them have not committed to supporting Jeffries if Democrats win in November. Lander’s support for Jeffries, who is a fellow New Yorker, is a tacit admission that the members are willing to give leadership a chance as they’re on the cusp of winning back the majority — but still he warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.” “I look forward to voting for Hakeem to be the speaker of the House,” Lander said in a recent interview with NOTUS. “At the same time, I want a party and party leadership that can listen to the passion and anger that voters feel and be responsive to it, and that means showing people much more clearly than leadership have so far what we're fighting for.” DSA-aligned candidates built their campaigns around a direct challenge to the Democratic Party’s “status quo,” casting themselves as insurgents willing to break with establishment leadership. Their message centered on economic populism — even when that meant taking on moderate Democrats rather than Republicans. Now that several of them are on track to easily win in November, the tug-of-war over the Democratic caucus’s center of gravity is about to grow even more pronounced. And many of the people who will be trying to pull it left will be from congressional districts in Jeffries’ backyard. Landers has previously said he plans to support Jeffries for speaker. "There will be a good opportunity for leadership to create a framework in which we can cut the line as fighters versus folders and show that it will be possible to win the majority in a strong way and to hear what voters are saying about their frustrations and the bolder posture they want to see from Democrats,” Lander, who beat incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman in a primary that attracted national attention, told NOTUS. Lander said Jeffries called to congratulate him and that the two have continued to talk, along with Jeffries' team, about how Jeffries envisions progressives working in the next Congress. When asked for comment, Jeffries team pointed to his remarks at a recent press conference. “I've talked to several of them, and we'll have more to say about it in the future,” Jeffries told reporters when asked about the winners of the competitive primaries in his home state. Building new working relationships between drastically different wings of the party isn’t an entirely new dynamic for Democratic lawmakers to navigate. In , after Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Ayanna Pressley arrived as the “Squad,” the then-new lawmakers had to establish a working relationship with then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi. They often broke with leadership on marquee votes, including when Omar and Tlaib opposed the bipartisan infrastructure bill, and several backed primary challenges against sitting Democratic incumbents in the years that followed. Pelosi, who’s retiring, said she has no concerns for Jeffries after November. “Hakeem is a very unifying force. He's eloquent. He listens,” Pelosi said in an interview. “He's very respected by the members. I was a different kind of voice, and I always had a race, except for my first time. Every single time I had a race. I don't see that for him. I think he will have a very unified caucus.” Ocasio-Cortez, who told NOTUS she’s made herself a resource for the incoming members, said she understands the candidates have to listen to their constituents who elected them for change. “Movement-based candidates don't just make individual calculations. Movement-based candidates generally try to be — especially when they're elected from their communities — I think they just conference a lot with their communities,” she said. Some centrist lawmakers, however, are already concerned that the DSA-aligned candidates will use tactics similar to those used by conservatives in the House Republican Conference, whether it be voting down a rule or refusing to back measures supported by moderate Democrats. Rep. Brad Schneider, chair of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, which has more than Democratic members, argued there should be more attention to the moderate candidates running in battleground races. He argued that candidates like the ones who have beat out incumbents are “not adding to the Democratic majority” because they’re in already-blue districts. “I am concerned about the rhetoric when [the progressives] come in and they say, ‘We are going to take down the rules, take down the speaker,’ and do these things,” Schneider said. “That just locks it up. We see that with the Republicans.” While none of the soon-to-be members of Congress have said they plan to vote against Jeffries, they’re noncommittal about supporting him. Several progressives said the fear expressed by Schneider is disconnected from reality. “I think if their fear is simply that these will be people who are more interested in division for its own sake or attention for its own sake, they've got something else coming,” said Andrew Bard Epstein, who worked on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign and Valdez’s campaign. (Mamdani backed several of the New York progressives on track to win seats in Congress.) “These are people who are smart and determined and strategic.” Lander was optimistic that in the general election, once primaries are wrapped up, Democrats will come together to win the majority. He dismissed any concerns about members of t he caucus being able to work together in that scenario. "I'm much more worried about Donald Trump and the danger that he presents to the country than I am about the divisions within the party," he said.

title: Darline Graham Will Run for a Full Term in the Senate
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: “I’m in,” Darline Graham told Fox News, setting up a campaign pushed by President Trump.
content: Sen. Darline Graham (R - South Carolina) said there is a "tremendous amount of pressure” surrounding her decision about whether to run for the Senate seat. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was recently appointed to temporarily serve in place of her late brother Lindsey Graham, said on Monday that she is running for a full term. “I’m in,” Darline Graham told Fox News host Sean Hannity in an interview. She said there is a "tremendous amount of pressure” surrounding her decision about whether to run for the South Carolina seat, which her brother had held for over two decades. “I have been praying a lot, talking to my family,” Graham said. “I feel like I can do it. I feel an inner peace about it. Will it be difficult? Yes. Absolutely.” Graham was sworn in July 14 after being appointed to the seat by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social encouraging her to run for a full, six-year term. “I hope Darline does this, in that there would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement,” Trump wrote. However, some are staying out of the race for the time being. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) declined to endorse in the race, but that Graham is a “strong candidate.” “Sounds like the field is taking shape and we’ll let the voters in South Carolina decide it,” Thune said. “She obviously carries on Lindsey’s legacy, but I think she's a very accomplished person in her own right.” “I'm not endorsing anybody at the moment,” he . This story has been updated with comments from Trump and Thune.

title: Republican Russell Fry Launches a Bid for Lindsey Graham’s Senate Seat
author: Brett Bachman
summary: The congressman may get the backing of President Donald Trump if Darline Graham opts not to run, a source previously told NOTUS.
content: Bill Clark/AP Republican Rep. Russell Fry announced Monday that he was launching a campaign for the Senate seat held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, entering a brief and potentially crowded field in South Carolina. He could be up against Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to hold his seat through this November’s election. President Donald Trump endorsed her last week but she has not yet officially launched her campaign for a full term. In a statement , Fry sought to position himself as a champion of Lindsey Graham’s legacy and a staunch ally of Trump’s. “There is no other way to put it: Lindsey Graham was one of a kind. There is no replacing him,” Fry said. “But I believe the best way to honor his legacy is to fight alongside the President just as steadfastly as he did.” Fry also said that he intended to focus on cost-of-living issues that he said were crushing ordinary Americans, both in his state and across the country. “Too many South Carolina families are struggling to make ends meet,” Fry said. “High gas prices and soaring grocery costs are hurting hardworking people every day.” source familiar with Trump’s thinking told NOTUS last week that the president would consider supporting Fry in the event that Darline Graham does not run for her brother’s seat. Trump met with Darline Graham on Friday at the White House, writing in a subsequent post on Truth Social that he urged her to run for the seat. “There would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, ” Trump wrote. “Should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.” “RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” he . Darline Graham was appointed early last week by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to complete her brother’s term following his death due to a heart issue last Saturday. Trump quickly decided to back her for the interim appointment and was considering backing her for the full term, NOTUS first reported last week. The window for candidates to file for the truncated Republican Senate primary opens Tuesday and is expected to include a number of boldface names including Rep. Ralph Norman, who has already announced his intention to run, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, businessman Mark Lynch and former Gov. Mark Sanford, as well as Rep. Nancy Mace. Fry’s decision to run for Senate could leave the House Republican caucus in a bind. If he — or any other member of the lower chamber — were to win the race, their seat would likely sit empty for several months. Republicans already hold a razor-thin majority in the House, one that is expected to tighten or even flip after November’s midterms. Mace appeared to call out Fry in a post on X following his announcement, pointing to the repercussions if he were to win the race: “This is an escalation that harms our country, our state and our values at such an important time in our nation’s history.”

title: Maine’s Troy Jackson Is on a Path to Become Senate Nominee
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: Two contenders, Nirav Shah and Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the Democratic race after Jackson picked up a majority of delegates.
content: Troy Jackson, the former Maine state Senate president, has a majority of delegates heading into Saturday’s convention to choose the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson may have effectively clinched the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine. Jackson, who is seeking to replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket after Platner dropped out, has the backing of more than half of the delegates who will attend next weekend's nominating convention, according to an analysis by the Bangor Daily News . His position strengthened Sunday as two rivals, former state Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the contest. On Saturday, delegates and members of the state’s central committee are scheduled to meet in Bangor, Maine. Those delegates were being chosen this weekend. The Bangor Daily News reported that York County, which borders New Hampshire, put Jackson over the top, bringing his total of pledged delegates over . “Thank you, York County. We’re organized, we’re ready, and we’re going to win. Solidarity forever,” Jackson wrote on X. The delegates are formally unbound, meaning they are not legally required to vote for a specific candidate even if they promised to during the delegate selection process. Shah said he would withdraw from the race to put the party’s energy into defeating Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November. “Today I am stepping aside, and I am doing it for exactly the same reason that led me to get in: we must defeat Susan Collins, and the Democratic Party must be unified to do it,” Shah wrote in a statement posted to X . Shah’s and Bellows’ exit leaves former congressional staffer Jordan Wood and 10 other candidates seeking the nomination. The race to become the Democratic nominee for Senate reopened earlier this month after Platner withdrew amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied. This story has been updated to include the withdrawal of Nirav Shah from the race.

title: Shenna Bellows Exits Senate Race in Maine
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: The Maine secretary of state’s withdrawal comes less than a week before Democrats hold a state convention to replace Graham Platner on the ballot.
content: Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who was behind on endorsements by potential delegates, said she wanted to focus on her job overseeing elections. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows dropped out of the race for U.S. Senate on Sunday, leaving three major candidates to off at the Democrats’ state convention this week. Bellows said she was withdrawing to focus on her role as the state’s chief election officer amid attacks on ballot integrity by President Donald Trump. “Donald Trump’s attacks are only accelerating, and the best way that I can serve our state and country at this moment is by focusing exclusively on my role as Secretary of State,” Bellows wrote in a statement posted to X. Trump addressed the nation on Thursday, arguing that recently declassified documents show rogue state actors are intent on disrupting U.S. elections and charging that hundreds of thousands of non-citizens were registered to vote, though evidence provided by the White House largely did not back up those assertions. Per the Constitution, state and local officials oversee elections. The Justice Department sent a letter to all 50 states this month threatening to prosecute election officials if any noncitizens are found to have voted in any upcoming elections. Bellows also pointed to the urgency for Democrats in this race, saying the party doesn’t “have a day to waste in unifying around” beating incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November. Twelve Democrats, including Bellows, have entered the race to replace Platner, the party’s nominee who dropped out this month amid sexual assault allegations, which he denied. A gathering of delegates will join the members of the state’s central committee to choose a nominee Saturday in Bangor, Maine. With Bellows’ departure, the frontrunners are considered to be former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, former Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and former congressional staffer Jordan Wood. Support for Jackson has surged among delegates after a televised debate last week, according to an analysis released Friday by Bangor Daily News . Among the 3, people who could fill those delegate seats, Jackson carried stated endorsements, Shah had and Bellows had 48. The delegates were being chosen this weekend at county caucuses. Jackson celebrated Bellows’ decision to leave the race, highlighting their “friendship” and “shared values.” “Defeating Susan Collins will take all of us, and I’m grateful for your commitment to bringing Democrats together around that mission,” Jackson wrote Sunday on X. “Let’s get to work.” Bellows did not immediately endorse any of the remaining Democratic contenders.

title: Ralph Norman Announces Campaign to Fill Lindsey Graham’s Vacant Seat
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: The South Carolina Republican told Fox News that he was not deterred by President Donald Trump’s early endorsement of Darline Graham.
content: The day before he announced his plans, Norman received nods of support from other lawmakers, including Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Rep. Ralph Norman announced on Saturday his plan to run in the special primary election to fill former South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham’s vacant seat, becoming the first major candidate to enter the race. Graham’s death on July 11 immediately spurred interest among conservatives, including Norman, in securing the GOP nomination in South Carolina Republicans’ first contested open-seat Senate primary in over two decades. “I'm running for the United States Senate because our country is at a crossroads,” Norman said in a message posted to his campaign’s website Saturday. “President Trump needs proven conservative fighters standing with him — not politicians who fold when the pressure comes. Washington doesn't need more talkers. It needs people who will do exactly what they told the voters they'd do.” By state law, candidates have from July 21 to July 28 to register their campaigns. Whoever wins the special election on Aug. 11 will Democrat Annie Andrews in the fall. The day before he announced his plans, Norman received nods of support from other lawmakers, including Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida. But complicating Norman and other future contenders’ plans is Trump’s early backing of Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham, to run for a full term. Republican Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s term days after his death, making her the first woman Senator in state history. She has not formally filed to run in the special election. Norman told Fox News on Saturday that Trump’s endorsement of Darline Graham did not deter his plans. “I’m in this to win,” he said. Norman said on social media that, if elected, he’d vote to pass the SAVE America Act, Trump’s priority elections bill. The president also said Lindsey Graham advocated for the bill prior to his passing.

title: Democrats’ Nebraska Senate Nominee Wants Off the Ballot. The State Might Not Let Her.
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Cindy Burbank ran for the seat in hopes of clearing a path for independent candidate Dan Osborn.
content: Burbank jumped into the race to prevent Forbes from advancing in the Democratic primary, eventually securing nearly 90% of the vote in May. BRAD NORTON/AP Nebraska Senate candidate Cindy Burbank secured the Democratic nomination in May. On Friday, she submitted a request to the office of Nebraska’s secretary of state to be taken off the ballot — but a legal challenge could ensue. Burbank’s campaign website says she ran to ensure that Sen. Pete Ricketts, the incumbent Republican, could not prop up a “stooge” Democratic candidate in William Forbes, an anti-abortion pastor who voted for President Donald Trump. By announcing plans to drop out, Burbank hoped to clear a path for independent candidate Dan Osborn, who received the state Democratic party’s endorsement and has the best chance to beat Ricketts in November. But even before she sent in her official request, Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, a Republican, said he may move to keep Burbank on the ballot. “I’m going to wait and see if she wins that primary,” Evnen said at an event after Burbank publicly stated she intended to drop out. “If she submits a withdrawal, then I’m going to ask, ‘Well, what is my obligation with respect to this now? Do I have to accept it?’ So I’ve submitted this question to the attorney general to see what happens.” A spokesperson for Evnen’s office confirmed to NOTUS on Friday that they have received Burbank’s request and will write to state Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office asking if they are required to honor it. Hilgers’ team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “But I will be back, and I’m not going to just sit on the sidelines either,” Burbank told Courier Nebraska on Friday. “I do want to thank everybody who supported me, voted for me, and cheered me on. And it was a great, fun adventure. It reinforced to me that I grew up in a wonderful state with wonderful people.” Burbank jumped into the race to prevent Forbes from advancing in the Democratic primary, eventually securing nearly 90% of the vote in May. Since winning her primary, her campaign has been largely quiet, save for promoting nonpartisan House candidate Austin Ahlman. Limited polling suggests that Ricketts still has an edge over Osborn ahead of November. The incumbent senator raked in over three times what Osborn raised last quarter.

title: Trump Is Weighing Backing Darline Graham for a Full Senate Term
author: Kadia Goba, Reese Gorman
summary: The late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister was sworn in as an interim senator and is considering running for a full term. A White House endorsement could clear the field.
content: Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was sworn in to take the seat on an interim basis, but is considering running for a full term. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite President Donald Trump is considering backing Darline Graham for the full Senate term to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsay Graham of South Carolina, two sources tell NOTUS. Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster last week to fill out the remainder of her late brother’s term after he unexpectedly died early Sunday morning. Trump backed her for the “interim” appointment but has not publicly endorsed her to run for a full term. In recent days, however, Darline Graham has expressed to the White House that she wants to run for the Republican nomination for the full term, sources told NOTUS, and Trump is considering backing her. Her late brother was competing for another term in November against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a physician who ran unsuccessfully for a House seat in . Semafor first reported that Darline Graham had expressed interest in the position. One of the sources told NOTUS that she is Trump’s first choice and endorsing her would help avoid a messy Republican primary that would take place over the span of a few weeks. The special election is scheduled for Aug. 11 and a runoff, if necessary, on Aug. 25. Multiple other South Carolina Republicans have been mulling a run, including Reps. Ralph Norman, Russell Fry and Nancy Mace, but none of them have made an announcement one way or another. Darline Graham or Andrews would be the first female elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate. One source familiar with the discussion told NOTUS that Trump would consider backing Fry if Darline Graham decides not to run. The White House and Darline Graham’s office did not immediately respond to requests from NOTUS for comments. Memorials for Lindsey Graham have been scheduled for July 28 in Washington and July 29 in South Carolina, according to his office .

title: Wisconsin Governor Candidate Drops Out After Reporting Financial ‘Inaccuracies’
author: Brett Bachman, Elena Schneider
summary: Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez’s exit from the race comes less than a month before the state’s Aug. 11 primary.
content: Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, a Democratic candidate for governor in , speaks at a news conference at a food bank on Tuesday, Nov. 4, , in Sun Prairie, Wis. (AP Photo/Scott Bauer) Scott Bauer/AP Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez suspended her gubernatorial campaign on Friday, just days after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in campaign finance filings and accusing her former campaign manager of vastly overstating her fundraising totals. “I am deeply hurt and betrayed by what happened,” Rodriguez said in a video message posted on social media . “I cannot in good conscience let these questions become a cloud over an election that Democrats need to win. Wisconsin deserves better than that.” The Democrat’s exit from the race comes less than a month before the state’s Aug. 11 primary. decision to drop out also kickstarted a Democratic effort to convince David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, to reenter the race, one person familiar with the situation told NOTUS. Gov. Tony Evers is considering supporting the movement to get Crowley back into the race, the source said. Crowley, who endorsed Rodriguez after dropping out of the race last week, is "strongly considering" it, according to a second person directly familiar with his thinking. A crowded field remains for the party’s nomination — former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, state Rep. Francesca Hong, state Sen. Kelda Roys and former state Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan are all still vying for a spot on November’s ballot. Whoever wins is likely to Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is leading the Republican field. The financial misconduct allegations that roiled Rodriguez’s campaign were first revealed over the weekend, when the lieutenant governor issued a statement revealing she had fired her campaign manager, Kara Spencer, after discovering discrepancies in her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez said at a press conference Monday that she first knew something was wrong when television ads for her campaign that were supposed to air last week did not run. “I was given excuses from my campaign manager that did not make sense,” Rodriguez said after confronting Spencer about the unpaid invoices. “There was clearly a double-counting of contributions that inflated how much money we had raised,” Rodriguez said, while blaming her campaign manager for the situation. “There was also a significant failure to report certain expenses that had been paid.” The discrepancy between the reported fundraising total and the actual amount in her campaign’s coffers amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars, Rodriguez said. As of Monday, the campaign had a total of roughly $ , on hand. A campaign lawyer for Rodriguez has reached out to the Wisconsin Ethics Commission to report the situation, the lieutenant governor . “Part of being a leader is taking swift action, doing the right thing and being as honest as possible when there’s a problem,” Rodriguez said in her video message Friday. This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Where Republicans’ Cuts to Medicaid Could Cost Them
author: Zara Norman
summary: The race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District tests the politics of Republicans’ social safety net cuts.
content: Rep. Rob Wittman, a ten-term Republican, initially said he wouldn’t support the “One Big Beautiful Bill” because of its sweeping cuts to Medicaid. Tom Williams/AP CHESTERFIELD, Virginia — Democrats think they can flip a President Donald Trump-supporting congressional district blue. Their message: The incumbent, Virginia Rep. Rob Wittman, voted to cut Medicaid. Wittman, a ten-term Republican, told party leadership last summer that he wouldn’t support the “One Big Beautiful Bill” because of its sweeping cuts to Medicaid, a program one in eight of his constituents rely on for coverage. But ultimately, he did. Local Democratic Party committees are using Wittman’s vote to stir up their base. The official campaign arm for House Democrats says his district, the suburban and rural communities surrounding Richmond and the state’s eastern shore, “represents one of our best pick-up opportunities.” Shannon Taylor, the Democratic candidate who secured a spot on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” list , said his about- should be “the No. 1 issue” on voters’ minds as they head to the polls in November. “Wittman knew that voting for that budget bill was going to be cutting health care services and that's exactly what's happened,” Taylor, a county prosecutor, told NOTUS. “He owns that responsibility, and that's what we're out there telling people. We are letting them know that these terrible choices that they're being with day in and day out are his responsibility.” Republicans have publicly and privately fretted that their cuts to the social safety net could be a liability in battleground states. The race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District is a test of just how much. It’s a contest taking shape around the future of health care, and particularly Virginia’s rural hospitals. Three such clinics shuttered last year in Virginia, directly citing the One Big Beautiful Bill as a reason. A state legislative committee deemed that 13 more hospitals risk the same fate, though the two in Wittman’s district have no immediate plans to close . Taylor and the six other candidates vying for the Democratic nomination feel fairly confident in their odds, despite the fact that Wittman has already raised about twice the amount Taylor has, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings. Though the district voted for Trump by 5 percentage points, it also broke for Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger last year. Shannon Taylor AP- ( , AR: 1.50)“This is the first time this seat is actually up for grabs,” Elizabeth Dempsey Beggs, one Democratic candidate, told voters at a June town hall in Chesterfield. Republicans disagree. They don’t think Wittman’s vote on Medicaid is the silver bullet Democrats think it is, for his seat or for the other Republicans who voted for the bill. One House Republican strategist said they feel pretty good about securing the 1st District, citing Trump’s win. Rural hospitals struggled to stay open long before last summer’s cuts, they argue. A National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson told NOTUS they plan to “take Democrats to task” for opposing Republicans’ solution for that: a $50 billion rural health fund which was included late in budget bill negotiations to address moderate Republicans’ concerns around Medicaid cuts. “The Commonwealth of Virginia received $ million from this program, which will be used to modernize facilities, address workforce challenges, and expand life-saving services,” Wittman told NOTUS in a statement. “I was proud to advocate for this funding, and I will continue to work with our rural providers to ensure they have the resources they need to serve our communities.” Democratic lawmakers in Congress called the rural health fund a “ fig leaf ” that did little to address the budget hole the policy created. The law cut more than $ billion dollars from Medicaid over 10 years, primarily by limiting the ways states can raise revenue to cover their share of the bill, restricting noncitizen coverage and introducing new work requirements. Virginia is part of a 23-state coalition suing to stop those work requirements from being implemented. “These policy changes risk shifting care from lower-cost preventive services toward higher-cost emergency and inpatient care, which is not the best outcome for patients or the healthcare system,” a spokesperson for Augusta Health, which operated the three shuttered rural clinics, told NOTUS in a statement. Hospitals have to provide emergency care regardless of a patient's ability to pay. About 13% of Augusta Health’s patients are covered by Medicaid, meaning the company expects to see more uncompensated care. That can be make or break for rural hospitals that operate on thin profit margins, see fewer patients and have more that rely on Medicaid than their urban counterparts. Virginia’s rural health providers are waiting until later this year to assess how much damage Medicaid cuts will do, but they’re not feeling optimistic. More than , Virginians are expected to lose coverage. “The challenges facing rural healthcare are not new. In recent years, however, those headwinds have intensified,” a spokesperson from Bon Secours, which operates one of two at-risk hospitals in Wittman’s district, told NOTUS in a statement. “We are continually monitoring this shifting landscape and remain committed to addressing these challenges thoughtfully and responsibly.” The $50 billion rural health fund aimed to move rural hospitals away from reimbursement-based funding, as that model works better in urban areas with more patients. But while any funding for rural healthcare is welcome, providers said they don’t see it as a solution. “While it may help address certain needs, it is unlikely to replace the ongoing reimbursement reductions hospitals are expected to experience,” wrote the Augusta Health spokesperson. Though Virginia received $ million of the fund this year, it asked for $1 billion. To access that money, clinics must apply to the state with an innovative idea. Giving the funds without strings attached might have been preferable, Jack Hensold, a rural oncologist in Montana, told NOTUS. “All they are trying to do is keep their heads afloat. So how many of them really have a sweeping, innovative idea?” said Hensold. “That money is just going to go to waste.” In June, four of the seven Democrats running for the seat participated in a town hall where they swiped at Wittman for his record on health care. Wittman wasn’t present. Chesterfield Town Hall ( , AR: 1.33)Health care attorney Ericka Kopp said she entered the race on the back of Wittman’s vote last summer — calling it a “slap in the .” Tim Cywinski, the communications manager for the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter, said his family lost their home to medical debt. Jason Knapp, a former naval officer, said he was born to a 19-year-old single mother and they relied on Medicaid and food stamps when he was growing up. “We have seen good candidates here before, but they didn't win,” said Knapp at the town hall. “To win this seat we have to consciously get people to fire Wittman who have been voting for him all this time.” Democratic candidates hoping to oust Wittman a truncated timeline to get that message across. A statewide redistricting battle delayed Virginia’s primary elections until August 4. In the meantime, local party committees are focusing on the downstream effects of Trump’s budget bill rather than any one candidate. “There are so many parts of the Big Beautiful Bill that made things less affordable for people,” Jen Tierney, chair of the Historic Triangle Democrats, told NOTUS. “We have rural hospitals in the 1st Congressional District that are at risk because of those cuts, so it is hard to find a person who is not impacted in some way.” Republicans have known the political implications of cutting Medicaid for a while. Most adults report some kind of connection to the program, according to the health policy research organization KFF . Politico found that 11 Republicans in competitive seats represent larger-than-average Medicaid populations. “I see him gradually resented more and more,” Michael Hill, a 72-year-old retired teacher from Chesterfield, said of Wittman. “I just feel like, at this point, you might be persuaded to move in a different way.”

title: Haley Stevens Is Getting Flamed Online. Will It Matter in Michigan?
author: Elena Schneider, Daniella Diaz
summary: The Michigan Senate primary is turning personal. “I think that we should bring the conversation back to the more substantive issues,” said an El-Sayed backer.
content: "Is she the most effective communicator? The answer is no," Amanda Litman said of Rep. Haley Stevens. Kristen Norman/AP Photo/Kristen Norman A 19-second video clip of Rep. Haley Stevens — a stilted, clenched-fist pep talk with a gym-teacher affect — zinged across social media this week, triggering mockery from Democrats and Republicans of the Michigan congresswoman locked in a tight Senate primary. And on Michigan voters’ TVs this week, a pro-Stevens outside group funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee dropped another ad slamming her opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, for his “sexist attacks” on Stevens. That spot adds to the 10-to-1 advertising advantage for Stevens, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. This split screen in the Michigan Senate primary — what’s going viral online versus what’s airing on voters’ televisions — encapsulates much of what’s defined Democratic Senate campaigns throughout : debates over electability, virality, dark money spending and U.S.-Israel politics. That dynamic, now freshly injected with accusations of sexism, stands to define the closing weeks of Michigan’s Senate primary, a must-win battleground state for Democrats. Stevens’ defenders accuse El-Sayed backers of attacking Stevens’ appearance, voice and on-camera presence — of taking the “low road,” as Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), who endorsed the congresswoman this week, put it to NOTUS. El-Sayed supporters said the discourse over Stevens’ persona distracts from her actual policies and her support from AIPAC, one of the most divisive groups for Democratic primary voters. “I think that we should bring the conversation back to the more substantive issues,” said Emily Dievendorf, a Michigan state representative who endorsed El-Sayed. “[Including] how much funding is being thrown into the race in order to spread misinformation and frankly lead people on wild goose chases.” Democratic operatives and strategists, in Washington and Michigan, argue two things can both be true — that there can be a sexist streak in the campaign chatter and that Stevens can be a flawed candidate. Amanda Litman, a co-founder of the progressive recruitment group Run for Something, said that while the criticism of Stevens is “absolutely sexist,” she’s also “a bad candidate, both on camera and for her position on Israel.” “The need to be telegenic, while always important, is even more so now, and because the world is sexist, women pay a higher cost for that,” Litman said. “You have to meet the reality of what is the most effective communication, and that's video. Is she the most effective communicator? The answer is no.” Judging a candidate’s electability remains a Democratic Party obsession, one that’s inextricably woven with preexisting biases around sexism and racism. In , Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Kamala Harris of California called out sexism during the Democratic presidential primary, arguing it clouded how pundits viewed the electability of the women in the race. Those arguments have only gotten louder since Harris’ loss in , ahead of the presidential campaign that could see fewer women run . And they’ve become a flashpoint this year after Graham Platner, who was accused of sexual assault , dropped his Senate bid in Maine. In a statement, Stevens spokesman Arik Wolk said “Haley’s been clear from Day One that she will run through anyone or anything to fight for Michigan and stand up to Donald Trump. Haley is leading with actual Michigan voters because she is focused on their concerns, not chasing likes on the Internet.” In Michigan, El-Sayed has come under fire for his comments about his female opponents. Earlier this month, he told Semafor that Stevens’ backers should “teach her how to string together two coherent sentences.” He said state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the primary earlier this month, “doesn’t quite understand” some basic health care policy. And the AIPAC-backed TV ads litigate El-Sayed’s comments about former first lady Michelle Obama and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. “A campaign that said their woman opponent can’t string two sentences together may want to consider cooling charges of sexism by pushing back against those attacks, not sitting silently by,” said Neera Tanden, the president of Center for American Progress and a friend of Stevens’ who has worked with her in the past. But El-Sayed’s team has pushed that he is the better option, sending a memo Thursday pointing to fundraising success and favorable polling. “Between the massive amounts of outside spending by corporate billionaires, AIPAC, and Trump donors and a barren ground game, Haley seems to be content letting corporations buy the election for her — a clear sign that she’d struggle to engage voters in a general election matchup,” the memo said. In a statement in response to questions about the dynamics of the race, El-Sayed spokesperson Sophie Pollock kept the focus on health care and the “fight to keep our tax dollars here in Michigan,” saying the campaign is building “a 10, volunteer strong movement on a vision for a future where working people come first.” El-Sayed has leaned into cheeky, viral videos of his own. He’s biking , lip-syncing and weight-lifting . There’s a strategy to El-Sayed’s omnipresence online, which reflects aspects of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s digital-savvy campaign that’s inspired progressive candidates nationally. El-Sayed “really needs people under 40 to vote in much higher numbers, and they’re most likely to be online,” said Adrian Hemond, a Democratic strategist in Michigan who is not working on the Senate primary. “To be extremely online has two targets: One is getting small-dollar donors outside of Michigan, and two, he needs extremely online elder millennials and Gen Z to vote for him, and that’s a tough nut to crack,” Hemond said. “Stevens can afford to be less online and be focused on the median Democratic primary voter, which is a Black woman in her 60s who is sitting in a church pew.” Stevens hasn’t leaned heavily into in-person rallies and has largely left her communications to TV ads. One on heavy rotation includes a clip of former President Barack Obama, praising Stevens’ work inside his administration. El-Sayed, meanwhile, is hosting Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) this weekend. That may work for Stevens in the end. The Detroit News released a poll this week finding Stevens with a 7-point lead over El-Sayed. She’s polling particularly well among Black voters in the state. But other public polling has shown El-Sayed with a single-digit lead. It’s also not clear whether the social media attacks on Stevens’ appearance are breaking through with actual voters on the ground. Michigan, like Texas and Maine, may be suffering from the “online fog of war,” said Kyle Tharp, a Democratic researcher who writes about online politics for his newsletter, Chaotic Era. “The online discourse about Abdul has been dominated by manufactured outrage around Hasan Piker, a streamer that has a relatively small audience nationally and even fewer viewers in Michigan,” Tharp said. “The online discourse about Stevens has been almost exclusively about her admittedly massive AIPAC funding and personal attacks on her accent and appearance. Both are things that have little to do with normie voters’ primary concerns.”

title: As Maine Goes, So Go Incumbents Winning
author: Paul Kane
summary: Democrats need to know how hard it is to defeat incumbents in choosing Graham Platner’s replacement.
content: Whoever is picked to be the Democratic nominee will Sen. Susan Collins, who’s won five Senate races in the previous three decades, and is the longest-serving senator in Maine history. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Before running for Senate in , Sara Gideon’s toughest race came in the Democratic primary for a seat in the state House. She won by 6 percentage points and eventually became speaker of the state House. Eight years later, her challenge to Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) went down in political flames, despite Gideon raising $75 million and the tailwinds from Joe Biden’s victory in Maine by 9 points. In Maine, as history has shown repeatedly, it is very difficult to knock incumbents out of top offices. Rep. Jared Golden (D), who first won in , is Maine’s only challenger to knock off an incumbent member of the U.S. House this century. The last time an incumbent Maine senator lost reelection was in , when Republican Bill Cohen won the first of three terms. And it’s been 60 years since a Maine governor sought re-election and lost. “Maine thinks they’ve chosen well to begin with,” Kevin Raye, a former state senator who lost three bids for the state’s northern 2nd Congressional District in , and , told NOTUS. It’s a central dilemma for Maine Democrats now as they choose a replacement for Democratic Senate nominee, Graham Platner, who dropped out amid sexual assault allegations. Whoever is picked will Collins, who’s won five Senate races in the previous three decades, and is the longest-serving senator in Maine history. Based on the state’s electorate, Democrats would seem favored to defeat Collins in November. Democratic presidential nominees have won Maine in nine straight elections. Four of the last six governor’s races went to Democrats, and for 26 of the last 30 years Democrats have held both of Maine’s seats in the U.S. House. Add in that recent polling shows President Donald Trump is approved by fewer than 4 in 10 Mainers , and it’s a politically toxic mess for Collins. And it comes in one of the nation’s most competitive races, one that will draw plenty of spending, as it could decide control of the Senate. But that favorable Democratic environment is running up against the state’s political inclination to support incumbents, regardless of party. “Maybe it’s because Maine people elect good people to start with, they don’t think they have to change them,” Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) told NOTUS, half-joking. King narrowly won the gubernatorial election as an independent, when Collins was the Republican nominee, but in his reelection bid his closest competitor trailed by 40 points. He came out of retirement in to run in an open Senate race, almost campaigning as a familiar incumbent. He won comfortably by about 20 points, similar to his margins of victory in and . Since Ronald Reagan won the election, Maine has had just five senators — the same number as other small-population states Alaska and Hawaii, which are notorious for sending their senators to Washington for very long stretches in order to bring home federal bacon. Ticket-splitting is a long tradition in Maine, even as it has disappeared from other states. From into , Maine voted repeatedly to send Republicans Collins and Olympia Snowe to the Senate while also voting every two years to send two Democrats to the House. Despite Trump’s poor showing in Maine in , Gideon received fewer votes in her bid against Collins than he did in the presidential race. King, who is not endorsing in this year’s Senate race, pointed to a unique factor in Maine’s state government. Elected statewide offices are limited to governor and two senators. There’s no lieutenant governor. The Legislature votes for the state’s attorney general, secretary of state and auditor – positions that go to those who play the inside game in the state capital, Augusta, not through statewide elections. “So there's not much of a pathway for people to achieve some statewide name-recognition or experience,” King said. Moreover, the Legislature is massive for such a small-population state: more than seats in the state House, leaving representatives with a constituency of about 9, , and 35 in the state Senate, with about 40, constituents. “State senators are not well known outside of their districts,” said Raye, the former state senator. Raye said Gideon, who served a couple terms as state House speaker, was an unknown entity across Maine. In that critical primary, Gideon won with only votes, about what it takes to win student council president at an average-size high school. Raye, a Republican who was chief of staff to Snowe in the 1990s, served four terms in Augusta, rising to state Senate president. Maine’s strict term limits forced him out in , when he decided to challenge the incumbent House Democrat. He lost by about 16 points, and two years later he lost the Republican nomination to Bruce Poliquin, who went on to win the state’s 2nd Congressional District, which had been left open when the incumbent ran for governor. Troy Jackson served as state Senate president for three terms, but even in a few competitive races for his northern district he never won more than 12, votes. When he ran in the Democratic gubernatorial primary this year, he finished in third place. He’s now considered among the top tier of potential nominees to replace Platner. The new standard-bearer will have to win over a collection of roughly Maine Democrats who will hold a convention on July 25, with a deadline two days later to announce the new pick. Golden, who is retiring in early January after four terms in Congress, will not endorse in any races this year. He said challengers need to offer a positive vision or Mainers will revert back to their comfortable previous choice. “Do I want to keep this person in the job? The answer is maybe not,” Golden told NOTUS. “Their second question is: But do I want to give the job to this other person? And if they don’t know, then they’ll default to the incumbent.” Golden had an opening in to defeat Poliquin because in the Republican had made statements suggesting he would not vote to repeal the Affordable Care Act and then did just that in . Golden’s ads hit on Poliquin’s votes, then pivoted to his own biography: serving in the Marines in Iraq and Afghanistan, working in the Senate for Collins and serving two terms in the state House. One ad ended with him saying he’s a “straight shooter” and firing a weapon. Democrats thought Collins’ vote for Trump’s nominees in his first term, particularly her decisive vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh, made her vulnerable in . But after the campaign, many Maine Democrats felt the race focused too much on a Supreme Court vote that didn’t resonate with many middle-of-the road Mainers. “You have to offer them a rationale for why you should have a job,” Golden said. “But so many people these days just campaign on why the other person shouldn’t have the job.” Also, Mainers expect their members of Congress to be statesmen with something of national profile. Ed Muskie (D), a Maine senator from to , was a serious presidential candidate in and served as secretary of state at the end of the Carter administration. George Mitchell, who succeeded Muskie, was Senate majority leader for six years before retiring in . Cohen, the former Republican senator, was confirmed as Bill Clinton’s final secretary of defense soon after retiring from the Senate in January . Collins, King and Snowe all have waded into tense bipartisan negotiations on a range of policy issues over the past several decades. King said there’s something existential about how Maine voters feel like they know their leaders in ways that are impossible in large states. They like to say they live in a big small town. “When I'm on the street in Maine, most people call me Angus, not senator,” he said. “They feel there's a connection.” Golden said voters will get past some ideological sins if the lawmaker publicly explains their position, something he did after his reversal to support a ban on assault weapons. He had a powerful case to make after a mass shooting had just left 18 people in his hometown, Lewiston, even in a pro-gun, rural district. He went on to a narrow victory in as Trump won his district by 9 points. “I didn’t shy away from having a daily, transparent conversation with my constituents, where I laid out, ‘Here's what I was thinking when I opposed the assault weapons ban,’” Golden said.

title: Democratic Voters Are Not Thinking About Abortion
author: Oriana González
summary: Support for abortion rights has taken a back seat to pocketbook issues during the Democratic primary season.
content: This election cycle, polling has continuously shown that voters are mostly concerned about the economy and cost of living, with abortion dropping as a top issue. Andrew Harnik/AP Photo Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado has long been a leading defender of abortion rights. But her record didn’t help much with voters earlier this month when she lost her primary to upstart democratic socialist Melat Kiros . Similarly, Maine state auditor Matt Dunlap beat state Sen. Joe Baldacci in the Democratic primary in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District in June, despite attacks about Dunlap’s past anti-abortion record being a major part of the messaging against him . These are the most recent examples of how abortion has receded as an issue in compared to the and elections, when it was one of Democrats’ top electoral focuses. In fact, more than three times as many abortion-related ads ran from January to mid-July — with candidates and organizations spending nearly double on them — as did in the same period of , according to a NOTUS analysis of data from AdImpact, an advertising tracking company. But Democrats’ focus on abortion rights didn’t deliver wins for the party in the way it did in . Democrats effectively prevented a red wave in the midterms by heavily messaging against the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade, the landmark ruling that protected abortion access. Republicans fended off Democrats’ abortion attacks in , with President Donald Trump formally declaring that the Republican Party did not support a federal abortion ban . This election cycle, polling has continuously shown that voters are mostly concerned about the economy and cost of living, with abortion dropping as a top issue. As a result, lawmakers and abortion rights groups are making adjustments. Abortion “is just as important, but I think what's happened is that back in , with the Supreme Court decision, people felt the immediate impacts, and now people are really feeling the increased cost of living, and you know whether it’s rent, groceries,” Democratic Rep. Nanettee Barragán of California told NOTUS. Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nevada) said abortion would definitely play a part in her race because Nevada is one of three states with a constitutional measure to protect abortion rights on the ballot. But, she said, “I think the economy is a far bigger issue for people on a day-to-day basis.” One House Democrat from a competitive district who declined to comment on the record told NOTUS that the party not prioritizing abortion messaging is a positive. “If you polled the American people in November of last year and you said, ‘What are the issues that you care about the most?’ they would say affordability, immigration, taxes, crime and health care,” the lawmaker said. “If you asked those same people, ‘What do you think the Democrats are pushing?’ they would say abortion rights, LGBTQ rights. … That’s why we were losing, because we weren’t talking about the things that people were talking about.” While Democrats have stepped back on their abortion messaging, abortion rights groups have announced major spending and are encouraging Democrats to message on abortion by tying it to affordability . Reproductive Freedom for All announced a $23.5 million campaign to mobilize voters and “hold anti-abortion politicians accountable.” It’s the most the group has spent in a midterm election.
